title: Towards a successful future: Personal development as today’s most important investment
description: By: Nozanin Bahodirova When does a person’s future begin? Perhaps on the day they dream big? Or when they make an important decision in life? In reality, a successful future begins today, with the choices we make and the small steps we take right now. The world is changing faster than ever before. The knowledge that was sufficient yesterday may not be enough today, and professions that are in high demand now may require entirely new skills tomorrow. In such circumstances, people cannot afford to stand still. They must continue learning, exploring, thinking and, most importantly, working on themselves. Personal development is not simply about reading books, attending courses or acquiring new knowledge. Above all, it is about understanding oneself, discovering one’s potential, recognising one’s weaknesses and striving to become a better person than one was yesterday. Real change begins when people stop being indifferent to their lives and take responsibility for improving them. Dreaming is not enough — action is necessary. Every person has dreams, plans they wish to achieve and goals they hope to reach. However, there is a considerable distance between a dream and its fulfilment. This distance can only be covered through discipline, patience, hard work and determination. A life without goals is like a journey without direction. When people do not know where they are going, their efforts may not lead to the desired results. Therefore, we should set clear goals, plan how to achieve them and take at least one small step towards them every day. Of course, difficulties, failures and unexpected obstacles may appear along the way. However, these challenges do not necessarily mean that our abilities are limited. Instead, they may indicate that we need to gain new experience. Psychologist Albert Bandura emphasised that people’s beliefs in their own abilities influence their actions and achievements. Therefore, self-confidence is one of the important steps towards success. Knowledge is the key that opens the doors to the future. In modern society, being knowledgeable is a valuable asset. However, being willing to learn is even more important. True progress is closely connected to a person’s desire to acquire new knowledge. Reading books, learning foreign languages, improving professional skills and exploring new technologies all contribute to broadening one’s horizons. In particular, independent learning and the pursuit of personal interests can create greater opportunities for young people in the future. Nobody can increase our knowledge on our behalf. A teacher can guide us, books can provide information and courses can introduce new opportunities. However, genuine enthusiasm for learning must come from within. Time is an opportunity that cannot be regained. People often say that they do not have enough opportunities to achieve their dreams. In reality, however, the problem is sometimes not the lack of opportunities but how we use the time available to us. Small tasks completed throughout the day, a few pages of a book read, new words learned or a skill developed can lead to remarkable results over time. To achieve this, we must value our time, prioritise important tasks and reduce unnecessary distractions. In his work, Stephen Covey highlights the importance of setting priorities in order to lead an effective life. Indeed, being busy does not always mean being productive. What matters is spending our time on activities that bring us closer to our goals. Change does not begin with external circumstances; it begins with an internal decision. A person’s attitude towards themselves and their abilities determines the direction of their development. Sometimes, people consider their abilities unchangeable and hesitate to try new things. However, abilities and skills can be developed through effort, experience and education. Psychologist Carol Dweck demonstrates the importance of a growth mindset in acquiring new knowledge and overcoming challenges. This means that something we do not know today can be learned tomorrow, and a task we cannot accomplish today may become possible after gaining experience. Therefore, instead of constantly comparing ourselves with others, it is more beneficial to compare our present achievements with our previous progress. Everyone has their own path, opportunities and pace of development. Personal development is not only for yourself. The achievements of a person who continuously works on themselves are not limited to their personal life. Knowledgeable, responsible, proactive and independent-minded individuals can also contribute to the development of their families, communities and countries. In particular, the younger generation’s commitment to education, willingness to introduce new ideas, interest in international experiences and desire to demonstrate their potential are essential for future progress. UNESCO also recognises education as an important force in shaping the common future of humanity. Thus, personal development is not merely a means of achieving individual success; it is also a value that benefits society as a whole. In conclusion Nobody else will build a successful future for us. We create it ourselves through the knowledge we acquire, the decisions we make, the ambitions we pursue and the actions we take today. We do not have to accomplish extraordinary things every day. Sometimes, reading a single page of a book, gaining one new piece of knowledge, making a small but courageous decision or completing a task on time can become the beginning of significant changes. Most importantly, we must never lose confidence in ourselves, appreciate our opportunities and continue developing. After all, the future is not simply a time to be awaited. It is an opportunity to be created today. A person who works on themselves today is someone who cares about their tomorrow. title: Belt and Road think tank cooperation, int’l communication forums start in China’s Xi’an
description: Source: Xinhua, Editor: huaxia XI’AN, Nov. (Xinhua) — The Belt and Road Forum for International Think Tank Cooperation 2026 and the 4th Silk Road (Xi’an) International Communication Forum opened in Xi’an, capital city of northwest China’s Shaanxi Province, on Tuesday. Themed “High-quality Belt and Road Cooperation Empowering Modernization and Mutual Learning among Civilizations,” these forums aim to pool global wisdom and promote new development of Belt and Road cooperation with higher quality and at a higher level. More than 300 diplomats, think tank experts, journalists, cultural and tourism experts, and business representatives from over 50 countries and regions are attending these forums to engage in exchanges and discussions. In his address, Zhao Gang, deputy secretary of the Shaanxi Provincial Committee of the Communist Party of China (CPC) and governor of Shaanxi, said Shaanxi has in recent years deeply integrated itself into the broader pattern of Belt and Road cooperation. Lyu Yansong, editor-in-chief of Xinhua News Agency, said that over the past 13 years, Belt and Road cooperation has grown from a vision into tangible and visible cooperation projects, making positive contributions to enhancing friendship between China and partner countries and promoting the economic and social development of partner countries. As the lead of the Initiators Council of the Belt and Road Studies Network (BRSN), Xinhua is ready to work with domestic and international colleagues to deepen research and interpretation of the connotations of high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, showcase the fruitful achievements of partner countries in advancing modernization and mutual learning among civilizations, and gather strong momentum for high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, Lyu said. The BRSN has continued to expand its influence since its establishment seven years ago. At the opening ceremony, four new member institutions, namely BRICS International Forum, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Manas National Academy of the Kyrgyz Republic, and the Development Strategy Centre, Uzbekistan were presented with signing documents. A think tank report titled “Building an Open World Economy Through Belt and Road Cooperation” was, meanwhile, released globally in both Chinese and English. title: Nyeri’s wage bill is eating our future
description: Nyeri County spends KSh 52 of every KSh 100 it receives on salaries — 17 percentage points above the legal limit — and the gap is costing residents roads, water, and health services. By Dr Grace Njine Nyeri County’s wage bill consumed 52 per cent of its total revenue last financial year — nearly double what the law allows and the highest proportion recorded among all 47 counties in Kenya. That figure is not contested. It comes from the county’s own County Budget Review and Outlook Paper 2026, which shows that by the end of FY 2025/26, Nyeri had spent KSh4.62B on salaries and allowances — 58.63 per cent of everything it actually spent that year. The Public Finance Management Act caps the wage bill at 35 per cent of county revenue. Nyeri is 17 points over that line. The scale of the problem becomes clearer when set against neighbours. The Controller of Budget’s review of all 47 counties for FY 2024/25 placed Nyeri at the top of the wage bill table at 55 per cent, ahead of Machakos and Baringo. In the same period, Murang’a spent 48 per cent of revenue on salaries, Embu 43 per cent, and Kiambu 42 per cent. Nyandarua held within the legal limit at 33 per cent. Kirinyaga’s trajectory is the most instructive comparison. In 2017/18, Kirinyaga spent 45 per cent of revenue on wages — worse than Nyeri is today. By FY 2025/26, the Salaries and Remuneration Commission ranked it among only five nationally compliant counties at 32 per cent. It achieved that by freezing recruitment, introducing performance incentives for revenue collectors, and growing its own-source revenue from approximately KSh300 million to KSh700 million. If Kirinyaga, working from a smaller economic base, can get under the line, so can Nyeri. The human cost of non-compliance is not abstract. Every shilling spent above the legal wage-bill ceiling is a shilling unavailable for roads, water infrastructure, dispensaries, coffee factories, and bursaries. If Nyeri brought its wage bill to 35 per cent, approximately KSh1.5B annually would be freed for development and services. That calculation is straightforward: the numbers are in the county’s own budget papers. This is not an argument against county workers. Nyeri’s nurses, agricultural extension officers, and ward administrators do essential work, frequently under difficult conditions. The problem lies in the structure of the payroll, not the people on it. How did Nyeri arrive here? There is no single cause and no single administration to blame. When devolution began in 2013, Nyeri inherited staff from former local authorities and from national government. By 2023, the county acknowledged to the Senate that many of those inherited employees lacked the technical skills required, forcing it to recruit new staff while retaining the old. Collective bargaining agreements and national salary reviews have repeatedly landed additional wage obligations on county budgets without matching transfers from the national government. Health workers alone account for 56 per cent of Nyeri’s wage bill, one of the highest proportions in the country. Payroll controls have also been weak: the Controller of Budget found Nyeri paying KSh109.65M in salaries outside the official payroll system in a single quarter — the kind of shadow payroll where ghost workers and irregular payments are hardest to detect. The county took a meaningful step in August 2026 by launching a payroll and personnel audit. The question is what follows. Audits matter only when they produce binding action. Neighbouring counties offer a practical map. Nyandarua conducted repeated physical headcounts and ordered staff found drawing double salaries to refund the money. Uasin Gishu now runs its entire payroll through the official system with no manual payments at all. Makueni links every department’s performance contract to staff appraisal, with both rewards and sanctions attached. These are replicable, proven approaches — not untested theory. For Nyeri, five steps are achievable within the current political term. First, complete and publish the payroll audit, follow it immediately with a biometric headcount, and set a firm target of zero manual payroll within twelve months. Second, establish an approved staff establishment for every department and freeze all hiring above it, except for critical health and technical positions. Third, reduce numbers humanely through natural attrition and redeployment rather than mass dismissals — Kirinyaga’s abrupt layoff of casual health workers in 2020 threw its hospitals into crisis and stands as a warning. Fourth, grow revenue: Nyeri’s hospitals, public markets, and county assets have unrealised earning potential, and every additional shilling of own-source revenue reduces the wage-bill ratio without cutting a single job. Fifth, extend performance contracts from the executive level down to ward administrators, and tie promotions and training allocations to measurable results. The law gives counties until June 2028 to reach the 35 per cent threshold. That deadline falls squarely within the term of whoever Nyeri voters elect in August 2027. The wage bill should therefore be a defining question of that election. When candidates come canvassing for votes, residents have one question that cuts through every promise: what is your specific, costed plan to bring the wage bill within the law? The answer — or the absence of one — will reveal more about an aspirant’s preparedness to govern than any campaign rally. Nyeri’s future is being consumed by its payroll. The county cannot develop what it cannot afford to build. Dr Grace Njine, CHRP(K), PMP, is a Human Resource Management and Public Service Reform specialist. She holds a PhD in Human Resource Management from Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology and an MBA from the University of Nairobi. She is an alumna of the Kenya School of Government’s Strategic Leadership Development Programme and writes on county public service reform, wage bill management, and the cooperative sector. title: Financial discipline: The missing key to Kenya’s youth prosperity
description: Young Kenyans are earning more than ever — but without financial discipline, income alone will not build the secure future they deserve. By Flora Jebet Financial discipline among Kenya’s young people has never mattered more. With the cost of living rising and economic competition intensifying, the gap between earning money and managing it effectively is widening — and it is costing a generation its financial future. Across the country, young people are generating income through employment, entrepreneurship, online businesses, and the informal sector. Yet earning is only half the equation. Social media, peer pressure, and lifestyle aspirations are driving uncontrolled spending on clothing, entertainment, and outings that consume income before it can work. Without a budget, there is no framework to distinguish needs from wants — and money that could build a future is spent on things that offer none. The solution begins with fundamentals. Every amount received should have a purpose: basic needs, bills, family obligations, savings, or investment. A simple written budget transforms vague intentions into accountable decisions. Saving need not wait for a larger salary — consistent small amounts, set aside as a habit, compound into meaningful security over time and reduce reliance on the high-interest digital loans that now trap many young borrowers. Financial literacy must also be treated as essential education. Schools, universities, families, and community organisations all carry responsibility for equipping young people with the tools to budget, manage debt, and invest intelligently. Financial independence is not built in a single pay cheque. It is built in the daily decisions that most people never see. title: Wenger considers shock bid for FIFA presidency
description: The former Arsenal manager is weighing a challenge to Gianni Infantino ahead of the November 18 candidate deadline for the March 2027 election. By Pascal Okoth Arsène Wenger is seriously considering entering the race for the FIFA presidency, with reports from The Athletic, BBC Sport and other international outlets indicating the 75-year-old Frenchman may declare his candidacy before the November 18 deadline. The election is scheduled for 18 March 2027, during the 77th FIFA Congress in Rabat, Morocco. Wenger would challenge incumbent Gianni Infantino, the Swiss-Italian administrator who has held the presidency since 2016 and is seeking a fourth term after re-elections in 2019 and 2023. No official declaration has been made, but influential figures within European football are actively encouraging Wenger to stand — UEFA among them, though the governing body is simultaneously evaluating other potential candidates. The push for an alternative reflects growing unease with Infantino’s leadership, particularly following a controversial proposal to allow private investors to acquire a minority stake in a company tied to FIFA’s commercial operations and World Cup activities. The plan drew sharp criticism from UEFA and several confederations before Infantino withdrew it. Wenger publicly distanced himself from the project, stating he had no involvement in its development and supporting its withdrawal. His FIFA credentials are substantial. Since joining the organisation in November 2019 as Chief of Global Football Development, Wenger has driven youth development initiatives, coaching education programmes, and the establishment of football academies across multiple continents — giving him an operational understanding of FIFA’s structures that few outside candidates could claim. The obstacles, however, are real. Infantino retains significant support among FIFA’s 211 member associations, particularly across Africa, Asia, and South America — the voting blocs that have historically determined presidential outcomes. Any candidate must also secure nominations from at least five member associations to qualify, a threshold that requires early diplomatic groundwork. Japan Football Association honorary president Kozo Tashima and former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega have also been named as potential challengers. Questions about Wenger’s age have surfaced — at 77, some observers have questioned whether he would commit to a full four-year term. Those close to him reportedly believe his experience and institutional knowledge outweigh that concern. The football world has not seen a credible challenge to a sitting FIFA president in years. If Wenger declares, that changes immediately. His 22-year tenure at Arsenal — three Premier League titles, seven FA Cups, and a redefinition of English football’s tactical and cultural possibilities — gave him global standing that no other candidate in this race can match. Whether that translates into the kind of association-by-association political support needed to unseat Infantino is the question his camp must now answer. The November 18 deadline is days away. What Wenger decides in that window could define not just his next chapter, but the direction of world football for years to come. title: UDA questions Gachagua’s status as DCP leader
description: The ruling party claims the former Deputy President is not formally recognised as party leader in Registrar of Political Parties records, adding to tensions ahead of 2027. By Yvonne Wambui The United Democratic Alliance yesterday questioned Rigathi Gachagua’s position as leader of the Democracy for the Citizens Party, claiming he is not officially listed in records held by the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties. According to information attributed to the Registrar, the position of party leader is not among the offices currently registered under DCP. The records instead identify former Kakamega Senator Cleophas Malala as the party’s registered Deputy Party Leader. The claim has reignited debate over the leadership and registration status of Gachagua’s party, raising questions about whether the procedures required to formalise his appointment were completed. Under the Political Parties Act, any changes to registered party officials must be submitted to the Registrar through the prescribed legal process — a requirement that applies regardless of how a party presents its leadership structure internally or publicly. Gachagua launched DCP in May 2025 following his fallout with UDA and has since presented himself publicly as the party’s leader, using it to mobilise supporters and build a national political network ahead of the 2027 General Election. He has worked to attract politicians, community leaders, and regional networks to the party as he consolidates his standing as one of the most prominent opposition voices in the country. UDA’s challenge introduces a fresh complication to that project — specifically the legal distinction between internal party appointments and offices formally recognised by the Registrar. Whether Gachagua’s leadership carries standing under registration law is now a live question, and one that his party will need to address directly if it is to avoid the issue being used as sustained political ammunition. The development comes against a backdrop of deepening tensions between Gachagua and the current administration, with both sides increasingly active in positioning ahead of the August 2027 poll. With the election drawing closer, the dispute over DCP’s registration status is unlikely to fade quietly. The post UDA questions Gachagua’s status as DCP leader appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: What TSC’s vision of a transformed, motivated and ethical teaching service really means
description: Kenya’s teaching profession is being asked to reinvent itself — and the Teachers Service Commission’s vision sets out exactly what that reinvention looks like in practice. By Ashford Kimani The Teachers Service Commission’s guiding vision — “a transformed, motivated, and ethical teaching service that is globally competitive” — is four words doing serious work. Each term is deliberate. Each carries concrete operational implications for what happens inside a Kenyan classroom every single day. Understanding what the vision actually demands of teachers is the first step toward delivering it. Transformation, as the TSC means it, is not cosmetic. It signals a fundamental departure from the traditional teacher-centred classroom toward learner-centred, competency-driven pedagogy aligned with Kenya’s Competency-Based Curriculum. A transformed teacher no longer positions themselves as the sole source of knowledge in the room. Instead, they facilitate — guiding inquiry, encouraging collaboration, and designing tasks that develop critical thinking in learners rather than passive reception of information. The difference is visible in practice. In a Literature lesson, a transformed teacher does not dictate notes on a set text. They organise learners into discussion groups, ask them to analyse themes, connect those themes to contemporary issues, and present their interpretations to the class. The classroom becomes interactive rather than performative. Transformation also means embracing technology — digital platforms for assigning work, tracking progress, and incorporating multimedia — and adapting to diverse learner needs, including those with special educational requirements. In short, transformation is about how teaching is done, not merely what is taught. Motivation, the second pillar, operates at two levels simultaneously: the internal drive that individual teachers bring to the profession, and the external conditions that sustain or erode it. A motivated teacher arrives in class with a clear lesson plan, engages learners actively, and follows up on their progress over time. They do not simply mark compositions and move on. They provide constructive feedback, hold remedial sessions, and track improvement — because the goal is understanding, not syllabus completion. But motivation cannot be reduced to individual willpower. It is also systemic. Timely salaries, fair promotions, recognition of excellence, and supportive school leadership all shape teacher morale in ways that individual commitment alone cannot compensate for. A school culture where outstanding teachers are acknowledged during assemblies or offered opportunities to mentor colleagues reinforces the message that effort is valued. Even in resource-constrained environments, a motivated teacher improvises — using locally available materials, adjusting strategies, and maintaining high expectations. That improvisation is the visible difference between a teacher who gets through the content and one who ensures learners genuinely understand it. Ethics, the third element, is non-negotiable precisely because teaching operates at the intersection of young minds and societal values. An ethical teaching service is one grounded in integrity, fairness, and accountability — qualities that must be active rather than assumed. In practice, ethical teaching means honest assessment. An ethical teacher does not inflate marks to satisfy administrators or reassure parents. They assess objectively, providing an accurate reflection of learner performance. During national examinations or school-based assessments, they resist any form of malpractice, even under pressure. Ethical conduct extends further — into punctuality, proper lesson attendance, respectful interaction with learners, and the maintenance of appropriate professional boundaries. A teacher who consistently misses lessons or practises favouritism undermines both the credibility of the profession and the outcomes of their learners. Ethics also encompasses safeguarding: protecting learners from abuse, discrimination, and exploitation. A teacher who reports bullying or intervenes in harmful situations is not going beyond their mandate. They are fulfilling it. Ultimately, ethics is about doing the right thing especially when no one is watching. Global competitiveness, the fourth component, places the Kenyan teacher within an international frame of reference without severing their connection to local realities. It means that a teacher trained and practising in Kenya should demonstrate standards comparable to those in high-performing education systems worldwide. This requires integrating global best practices — critical thinking, digital literacy, communication, and collaboration — with the specific contexts in which Kenyan learners live and grow. A globally competitive teacher designs assessments that go beyond recall, uses technology effectively, engages learners in genuine problem-solving, and pursues continuous professional development through courses, reading, and engagement with international education trends. The measure of that competitiveness is ultimately visible not in the teacher, but in the learner — in whether Kenyan students can compete confidently in academics, innovation, and the job market. The vision’s power lies precisely in the interaction of these four elements. Transformation without motivation produces mechanical compliance. Motivation without ethics risks well-intentioned harm. Ethics without transformation yields honest but outdated practice. Global competitiveness without local grounding becomes irrelevance dressed in ambition. For the vision to be realised, each teacher must embody all four simultaneously — and understand that they reinforce rather than compete with one another. This is not an abstract mission statement. It is a practical blueprint for redefining teaching in Kenya — one classroom, one lesson, and one learner at a time. Ashford Kimani teaches English and Literature in Gatundu North Sub-county and serves as Dean of Studies. title: McCarthy unbothered by Harambee Stars selection storm
description: The Harambee Stars head coach says public criticism of his squad picks will not alter his vision for Kenya football as the side prepares to face South Africa in a double-header Afcon qualifier. By Martin Weche Benni McCarthy has dismissed mounting criticism over his Harambee Stars team selection, declaring that outside noise will never dictate how he builds Kenya’s national football programme. The South African head coach made the remarks yesterday ahead of Friday night’s 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against South Africa in Soweto — a fixture that places his selections under immediate and unforgiving scrutiny. McCarthy has faced persistent questions throughout his tenure over his preference for certain players who have struggled for consistent club minutes. His answer to those questions has remained consistent: the players he calls up fit his philosophy and possess the mental strength his project demands. Yesterday, he went further. “In Kenya, they say whatever they want to. Freedom of speech is really freedom of speech. People say whatever they want to,” McCarthy said. “I think if I had listened my whole life to what people have said, do you think I would be sitting here or I would have achieved whatever I have achieved?” The former Manchester United and Blackburn Rovers striker, who won the UEFA Champions League with Porto in 2004, has never been a man easily rattled by opinion. That psychological resilience, forged across a playing career that made him one of South Africa’s greatest footballers and a coaching career that has taken him through three continents, appears to be the frame through which he manages Kenya’s expectations as much as its tactics. “I think the noise outside is always the noise, and you’re never going to be able to please everyone,” he said. “We know, the players know, what we’re building and what we’re trying to do. Of course, not everybody’s going to like it if your favourite player is maybe not selected. And then, of course, you criticise the coach or you criticise the team.” He added: “That comes with this job — being a manager, making decisions that not many people will be able to make, the difficult ones. You’re going to have to be prepared to be criticised for it.” The timing of those remarks carries particular weight. Friday’s fixture in Soweto pits Kenya against the nation McCarthy grew up in — a psychologically layered encounter that he will be expected to navigate both tactically and emotionally. The two sides meet again on Tuesday, 17 November, at Nyayo Stadium in Nairobi, giving the double-header the character of a mini-series rather than a single qualifier. For McCarthy, both legs are an opportunity to demonstrate that his vision is producing a team capable of competing at the continental level. Kenya’s qualification for the 2027 Afcon is already secured by virtue of co-hosting the tournament alongside Uganda and Tanzania. That removes the existential stakes from these qualifiers but introduces a different kind of pressure: the obligation to show that Kenya belongs among Africa’s elite, not merely as a host nation granted passage but as a side prepared to compete. A heavy defeat in Soweto — or across both legs — would reignite questions about readiness that squad selection debates alone cannot answer. McCarthy’s response to that pressure is to accelerate the building process rather than retreat into caution. His insistence on players who embody his football philosophy over those with higher public profiles reflects a coaching approach that prioritises system over reputation — a method that requires time, patience, and an acceptance that the results on the pitch must eventually make the argument that words cannot. Harambee Stars have shown flashes of genuine progress under McCarthy’s watch. The question that Friday night in Soweto will begin to answer is whether that progress is structural or superficial — whether McCarthy’s vision is a plan or simply a posture. He remains unconcerned by those asking the question. The coach who lifted the Champions League trophy with Porto and helped fire South Africa to Afcon glory has heard louder doubters than the ones currently filling Kenyan football’s online commentary sections. They did not stop him then. He is betting they will not stop him now. The post McCarthy unbothered by Harambee Stars selection storm appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: Ruto and Sifuna tied at 31% as Kenya’s 2027 race sharpens into a two-horse contest
description: A new TIFA poll places the President and the Nairobi Senator level on popularity, with fragmented opposition support representing Sifuna’s clearest path to the fifty per cent threshold. By John Kamau President William Ruto and Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna have tied at 31 per cent each as preferred winners of the 2027 General Election, according to a new poll by TIFA Research based on face-to-face household interviews with 2,036 randomly selected Kenyan adults across all 47 counties. The findings, released this week, mark a significant moment in Kenya’s pre-election landscape: for the first time, a single opposition figure has drawn level with an incumbent president in a credible national survey — and the arithmetic that follows that parity is what will define the next nine months of Kenyan politics. Behind the two frontrunners, the field drops sharply. Wiper Party leader Stephen Kalonzo Musyoka stands at nine per cent, Jubilee’s Fred Matiang’i at five per cent, former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua at four per cent, and Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro at one per cent. The combined opposition total — excluding Sifuna — sits at 19 per cent. TIFA’s analysis notes that if those voters consolidate behind a single candidate, that bloc alone is sufficient to push Sifuna past the 50-per-cent-plus-one threshold required to win a Kenyan presidential election outright. The strategic implication is unambiguous: Sifuna does not need to convert Ruto voters. He needs to inherit the opposition. The regional breakdown reveals two distinct Kenyas. Ruto’s support is dominant in the Central Rift at 59 per cent, Northern Kenya at 62 per cent, the Coast at 40 per cent, and Nyanza at 35 per cent — a cross-regional coalition built through the machinery of incumbency, infrastructure spending, and targeted political patronage. Sifuna’s support is strongest in Mt Kenya at 32 per cent, Nairobi at 39 per cent, the South Rift at 31 per cent, and Western Kenya at 55 per cent. That Western Kenya figure is the poll’s most striking regional number. It suggests Sifuna has successfully extended his political network beyond his Luo Nyanza base into a region that has historically been contested and that carries significant parliamentary weight. Mt Kenya, however, tells the most consequential story of the entire survey. With 21 per cent of respondents in the region declaring themselves undecided — the highest undecided proportion in any region nationally — the country’s largest vote-rich bloc remains genuinely in play. Nairobi follows at 17 per cent undecided. Together, these two zones represent the electoral prize that will determine the presidency. Ruto won Mt Kenya comprehensively in 2022 by consolidating it behind his Deputy President William Ruto ticket in a moment of unprecedented political realignment. Holding it in 2027, against a Sifuna candidacy that is already polling at 32 per cent in the region, will require active and sustained political investment rather than the assumption of loyalty. The party landscape is shifting in ways that reinforce the poll’s headline findings. UDA has regained its position as Kenya’s most popular political party at 25 per cent, recovering ground after a difficult period of internal turbulence. Sifuna’s Linda Mwananchi Movement sits second at 17 per cent — a remarkable figure for a political vehicle that only formally launched on 30 October and held its National Delegates Conference today behind closed doors. ODM, the party that defined Kenyan opposition politics for nearly two decades under Raila Odinga, has seen its rating halved since TIFA’s June survey, falling from 20 per cent to ten per cent. That collapse is both a measure of Odinga’s irreplaceable personal political weight and a window into where his voters are going: the evidence points toward Sifuna and the Linda Mwananchi Movement as the primary beneficiaries of that redistribution. On the question of running mates, the poll captures an interesting divergence between presidential preference and deputy preference. Among those who favour Ruto’s re-election, 55 per cent prefer his current Deputy President, Prof. Kithure Kindiki, to remain on the ticket. Twelve per cent prefer Homa Bay Governor Gladys Wanga — a cross-coalition preference that reflects Wanga’s growing national profile — while nine per cent named Mining Cabinet Secretary Hassan Joho. These figures indicate that while Kindiki retains majority support as Ruto’s preferred running mate, there is a meaningful constituency within the pro-Ruto camp that is open to a different configuration. The political period between now and August 2027 will be defined by two parallel contests operating simultaneously. The first is the battle for opposition consolidation. Kalonzo, travelling this week to Washington for a seven-day lobbying and diaspora mobilisation tour, has made clear that his presidential ambitions must be taken seriously in any coalition negotiations. Gachagua, whose Democracy for the Citizens Party is building national structures even as fresh questions emerge about his formal registration status at the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties, represents a separate centre of gravity. Matiang’i, co-chairing The Ukombozi Alliance with Siaya Governor James Orengo, brings institutional credibility and a national security background that appeals to a specific voter profile. The challenge for Sifuna — and the central strategic question of Kenya’s 2027 race — is whether he can bring these competing egos and regional interests into a coherent coalition without triggering the defections that have historically broken opposition alliances at the moment they were needed most. The second contest is Ruto’s battle to defend his lead against an opposition that, for the first time since 2022, has a credible arithmetic path to victory. An incumbent tied at 31 per cent with a senator who launched his formal party vehicle six weeks ago is not a position of comfort. The pressure of incumbency — the expectation that a sitting president will show results — is compounding as economic conditions remain difficult for ordinary Kenyan households. The government’s infrastructure pledges and development messaging must compete with daily lived experience in a way that campaign promises never do. TIFA’s poll is a single data point, not a verdict. title: Kalonzo takes Kenya’s opposition campaign to Washington ahead of 2027 election
description: The Wiper Patriotic Front leader will lobby United States Congress members and rally diaspora communities across six American cities as the opposition race to build a credible challenge to President Ruto. By David Kimani Stephen Kalonzo Musyoka, leader of the Wiper Patriotic Front and head of The Ukombozi Alliance, will lead a nine-member delegation to the United States from Wednesday, 18 November, to Tuesday, 24 November 2026, presenting the Kenyan opposition’s alternative governance agenda on Capitol Hill and mobilising diaspora voters ahead of the August 2027 general election. The seven-day working visit marks a decisive international phase in the opposition’s campaign to unseat President William Ruto — and it arrives at a moment when the domestic political landscape is shifting faster than any single alliance can comfortably manage. According to a media advisory issued by the Office of the 10th Vice President in Nairobi, the itinerary blends formal legislative consultations in Washington, D.C., with academic forums, religious gatherings, and community town halls across Boston, Massachusetts; Germantown and Baltimore, Maryland; Minneapolis, Minnesota; and Cleveland, Ohio. The delegation departs Nairobi on Monday, 16 November, arriving in the American capital ahead of Wednesday’s flagship engagements inside the Capitol Hill complex, which conclude with a formal evening dinner alongside Washington leadership. On Thursday, 19 November, Musyoka travels to Boston for an institutional forum at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, meeting alumni, faculty, and members of the technology and investment community — an audience whose interest in East African economic governance and democratic resilience makes them natural interlocutors for an opposition leader positioning himself as a credible, institution-minded alternative. The tour returns to the capital region on Friday, 20 November, for a town hall with the Washington, Maryland, and Virginia diaspora and an East Coast dinner, before moving to Baltimore on Saturday morning for a Sabbath service at Living Springs Seventh Day Adventist Church. That evening, Musyoka flies to Minneapolis to join Ambassador Mohamed Abdi Afey at the Somali Hero Awards and Somali Book Fair — a deliberately symbolic appearance. The tour concludes with a two-day finale in Cleveland: a diaspora Thanksgiving dinner on Sunday and the Building Bridges: Cleveland-Kenya-Africa Reception on Monday before the return flight to Nairobi. Beyond the choreography of a transatlantic tour, the trip reflects the intensifying strategic calculations that now define Kenyan politics nine months before polling day. At home, the political landscape has entered a fluid and fiercely contested pre-election period. The passing of former Prime Minister Raila Odinga removed the singular gravitational force that had anchored opposition politics for more than two decades, fracturing traditional voting blocs and opening space for new configurations — and new ambitions. President Ruto has worked aggressively to consolidate his United Democratic Alliance base while leveraging his broad-based governing arrangement to make inroads into areas that once reliably returned opposition majorities. Against that pressure, opposition figures have rallied under The Ukombozi Alliance — co-chaired by Siaya Governor James Orengo and former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i — in an effort to construct a unified front capable of mounting a credible electoral challenge. The architecture of that front, however, remains contested. Musyoka has repeatedly made clear that his own presidential ambitions must carry genuine weight in coalition negotiations, signalling that he is unwilling to step aside after four decades at the heart of Kenyan statecraft without a serious conversation about the top of the ticket. Speaking during recent grassroots rallies in South Nyanza — where his convoy encountered disruptions in Migori County before moving on to Homa Bay — Musyoka urged voters to embrace a platform of national transformation while invoking Odinga’s legacy as both inspiration and political inheritance. His office reinforced that posture in a statement issued earlier this month: “Our party leader has always maintained that his presidential ambitions must be taken seriously, and we remain confident that the ongoing discussions within the opposition will give due consideration to this position.” Internal friction has complicated efforts to settle on a single flagbearer. Tensions involving former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua and emerging generational voices such as Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna have exposed competing regional interests and tactical disagreements over how best to confront the incumbent. Polling data released this week by TIFA Research sharpens the stakes: President Ruto’s ruling party has regained ground at 25 per cent national support even as opposition voters remain fragmented across multiple personalities and movements. The numbers make the cost of continued division legible and urgent in equal measure. It is against that backdrop that Musyoka’s Washington mission carries its dual purpose. Externally, it projects statesmanship to international observers — American policymakers, academic institutions, and diaspora communities — who represent both diplomatic legitimacy and financial resources. Internally, it signals to domestic rivals that he commands a level of diplomatic stature and organisational reach that no other opposition figure can currently match. In crafting his pitch to Capitol Hill lawmakers and MIT audiences, Musyoka is drawing on a career that spans four decades in law, diplomacy, and governance. Having served as Kenya’s tenth Vice-President between 2008 and 2013, and previously as Minister for Foreign Affairs, Education, Tourism, and Environment, the Senior Counsel occupies a rare position among Kenyan politicians: he has negotiated on the world stage, not merely observed it. His advisory highlights his central role in the negotiations that produced the Comprehensive Peace Agreement and the birth of South Sudan, alongside his mediation during Kenya’s 2007–2008 post-election crisis. For American policymakers focused on regional stability across the Horn of Africa and democratic governance in East Africa’s largest economy, Musyoka’s team is presenting The Ukombozi Alliance as a predictable, experienced alternative to the current administration. Equally central to the tour’s strategic logic is the Kenyan diaspora in North America, whose financial remittances constitute one of Kenya’s largest sources of foreign exchange and whose political influence reaches directly into rural homesteads and urban constituencies back home. Town halls in Maryland, Minnesota, and Ohio offer the opposition a fundraising avenue at a moment when state resources heavily favour the incumbent. title: Catholic bishops warn Parliament against electoral bills that could undermine 2027 vote
description: The Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops singles out a proposed ban on livestreaming presidential tallies as legislation likely to heighten tensions and erode public confidence in the polls. By Agnes Kilonzo The Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops yesterday cautioned Parliament against advancing electoral amendment bills that could compromise the credibility of the 2027 General Election, specifically warning that a proposed ban on the livestreaming of presidential vote tallies would generate unnecessary tension and undermine public trust in the electoral process. The statement, signed by KCCB Chairman Archbishop Maurice Muhatia Makumba, was issued following a gathering of Catholic bishops at the John Cardinal Njue Pastoral Centre in Embu on Wednesday, 11 November. “We are concerned that the introduction of bills — such as the banning of livestreaming of the presidential vote tally — raises unnecessary tensions in the country,” the bishops stated, urging the Speakers of both Houses of Parliament to ensure that divisive legislation does not advance. The Church’s intervention places one of Kenya’s most influential institutional voices squarely against a proposal that critics argue would restrict public access to real-time electoral information at the most sensitive moment of any election cycle — the presidential count. The bishops framed transparency not as a preference but as a democratic imperative. “Parliament has yet one more chance to redeem itself by totally rejecting such an attempt to muzzle free access to information,” they said. “There should be full transparency in the elections where Kenyans have access to all information.” The language is pointed — “redeem itself” is not the phrasing of a body offering gentle counsel, but of one that has watched previous parliamentary conduct on electoral matters and found it wanting. Their statement arrives at a moment of acute sensitivity in Kenya’s electoral calendar. With the August 2027 General Election nine months away and political competition already intensifying across coalition formations and presidential polling, any legislative change to the electoral framework carries disproportionate weight. The proposed livestreaming ban, if enacted, would remove a mechanism that has become central to how Kenyan voters and observers independently verify tallying in real time — a safeguard whose value is precisely its public, unmediated nature. Beyond the livestreaming proposal, the bishops directed separate calls at three institutions. They challenged the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission to strengthen its operational preparations — voter registration, logistics, official training, results verification, and complaints resolution — while resisting any attempts by politicians or external interests to compromise its independence. They called on the Judiciary to handle electoral disputes diligently and without partiality, warning against a repetition of past electoral violence that claimed lives and destroyed property. And they urged political leaders to conduct campaigns peacefully and responsibly, insisting that electoral reforms must build public confidence rather than deepen division. Kenya’s Catholic bishops speak to a congregation that spans every region, ethnic community, and political affiliation in the country. When they address Parliament in terms this direct — nine months before a consequential election — the message carries weight that extends well beyond the Church’s own membership. Parliament now has its answer from the pews. What it does next will be watched accordingly. title: Crystal Asige takes on KRA over disability tax rules she says undermine hard-won rights
description: The nominated senator warns that proposed exemption regulations introduce a hierarchy of disability, impose unlawful fees, and require the permanently disabled to prove their condition every five years. By Agnes Kilonzo Nominated Senator Crystal Asige yesterday publicly challenged the Kenya Revenue Authority over draft tax exemption regulations for persons with disabilities, warning that the proposed rules could erode constitutional rights and increase the financial burden on some of Kenya’s most vulnerable families. Asige, who is blind and has consistently used her Senate platform to advocate for disability inclusion, posted her objections on her X account on Thursday, 12 November 2026, targeting specific provisions in the Draft Income Tax (Persons with Disabilities, Parents or Guardians Tax Exemptions) Regulations, 2026, which KRA has opened for public comment until 24 November. “Nothing about us, without us — yet here we go again,” Asige wrote, framing the regulations not as a technical oversight but as a retreat from gains that Kenya’s disability community has fought to secure over many years. Her criticism was precise, directed at three specific provisions rather than the regulations as a whole — a legislative approach that reflects both her legal literacy and the seriousness with which she intends to pursue formal interventions. Her primary objection concerns Regulation 10(2), which she says introduces graduated exemption levels based on the severity of a person’s disability. Under the proposed framework, individuals classified with milder disabilities would qualify for partial tax relief while those classified with severe disabilities would receive full exemptions. Asige argued that this approach creates what she described as a hierarchy of human suffering — a scale on which one person’s access to rights is measured against another’s degree of impairment. “Equity isn’t a ladder,” she said, calling for a framework that treats the needs of persons with disabilities as a matter of right rather than degree. The concern is not merely philosophical. In practice, disability classifications are determined by medical assessors whose criteria, processes, and consistency vary. A system that ties tax relief to classification outcomes creates a gatekeeping mechanism that could disadvantage individuals whose conditions, though genuinely disabling, fall below the threshold required for full exemption. Asige’s objection is that the threshold itself should not exist — that access to relief should not depend on where a person sits on an administrative spectrum of disability severity. Her second objection targets a proposed KSh1,000 processing fee for parents or guardians applying for tax exemptions related to caring for a person with a certified severe disability. Asige argued that this fee directly contradicts the Persons with Disabilities Act, 2025, which she says repealed assessment fees. If that legal reading is correct, KRA has drafted a provision that is inconsistent with the statute it is meant to implement — a significant drafting error that would need to be corrected before the regulations are finalised. The senator said she intends to submit formal interventions on this point, suggesting the challenge may extend beyond public comment into legal proceedings if the fee is retained. The draft regulations provide for a separate tax exemption for a parent or guardian caring for a person with a certified severe disability who cannot meet their own basic needs. However, the application is restricted to one parent or guardian per person with a disability. Asige questioned whether this adequately accounts for families in which both parents share caregiving responsibilities, or households in which more than one child has a disability. The practical implications are considerable: a family with two children who have severe disabilities would, under the proposed rules, be entitled to only two single-parent exemptions rather than a recognition of the compounded caregiving burden that both parents carry. Her third objection addresses a proposed requirement for people with permanent disabilities to undergo reassessment every five years to maintain their tax exemption status. The requirement draws a sharp and direct response: “Permanent means permanent,” Asige said. She argued that compelling people with permanent disabilities to periodically prove their condition — at personal cost and inconvenience — treats disability rights as provisional rather than settled. The reassessment requirement also raises practical questions about accessibility: for many persons with disabilities, particularly those in rural areas or with limited mobility, travelling to assessment centres every five years represents a significant and recurring barrier. KRA has described the proposed regulations as procedural rules designed to implement the tax exemptions established under the Persons with Disabilities Act, 2025, and has invited submissions from the public, professionals, and stakeholders by 24 November. The consultation window is standard practice for draft regulations, but Asige’s intervention raises the stakes considerably. A nominated senator with direct lived experience of disability, a detailed knowledge of the relevant legislation, and a public platform has identified specific provisions she considers constitutionally problematic. That combination — legal precision, personal authority, and public visibility — is difficult for a regulatory body to dismiss as uninformed criticism. Kenya’s disability community has long argued that policy affecting their lives is too often made without meaningful participation from those it directly impacts. Asige’s opening line — “Nothing about us, without us” — is a phrase with a history that stretches back decades through disability rights movements worldwide. That she felt compelled to use it in response to regulations drafted in 2026 says something about how far the principle has yet to travel from statement to practice. The November 24 deadline is ten days away. What follows it will determine whether the regulations are refined to meet constitutional standards or challenged in a forum where Asige has already signalled she is prepared to go. title: Linda Mwananchi tops Nairobi as TIFA poll reshapes Kenya’s 2027 political map
description: Edwin Sifuna’s movement leads the capital with 26 per cent support while nationally UDA reclaims first place — but a presidential race tied at 31 per cent signals the most competitive election Kenya has seen in a decade. By Anita Njeri The Linda Mwananchi Movement has emerged as Nairobi’s most popular political party at 26 per cent, ahead of Rigathi Gachagua’s Democracy for the Citizens Party at 11 per cent, ODM at nine per cent, and President William Ruto’s UDA at eight per cent, according to a TIFA Research survey released yesterday covering 2,036 adults interviewed face-to-face across all 47 counties between 26 October and 5 November 2026. The findings land at a pivotal moment in Kenya’s pre-election calendar, reshaping assumptions about where political power is consolidating and where it is haemorrhaging — with consequences that will drive coalition negotiations for months to come. The Nairobi numbers are the poll’s most striking single finding. That Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna’s movement — formally launched only on 30 October and holding its National Delegates Conference behind closed doors today — already commands more than a quarter of the capital’s party allegiance speaks to the speed at which the post-Raila Odinga political landscape is being reorganised. Wiper and Jubilee each register seven per cent in Nairobi, while 31 per cent of the capital’s respondents say they identify with no party at all — a bloc of unattached voters whose eventual alignment may determine not just Nairobi’s parliamentary seats but the presidential result itself. Nationally, the picture is more nuanced. UDA has reclaimed its position as Kenya’s most popular party, rising from 17 per cent in June to 25 per cent in November — a recovery that reflects both the stabilising effect of incumbency and the resources available to a governing party in an election year. Linda Mwananchi sits second at 17 per cent nationally, overtaking ODM, whose support has been halved since TIFA’s June survey, falling from 20 per cent to ten per cent. That collapse is the poll’s most consequential structural finding. ODM retains its strongest regional foothold in Nyanza at 33 per cent, but beyond that base the party that defined Kenyan opposition politics for two decades is losing voters at a rate that suggests organisational erosion rather than a temporary dip. The regional breakdown of Linda Mwananchi’s support reveals both the movement’s strength and its current limits. Western Kenya delivers its highest regional figure at 40 per cent — a number that confirms Sifuna has successfully extended his political network beyond Luo Nyanza into a region that carries substantial parliamentary weight and that has historically been fought over rather than owned by any single political force. Nairobi follows at 26 per cent, Nyanza at 18 per cent, and the Coast at 16 per cent. The movement’s relative weakness in Mount Kenya, the Central Rift, and Northern Kenya — where UDA commands 56 per cent and 60 per cent respectively — defines the geographic challenge that any Sifuna presidential campaign must address before August 2027. UDA’s regional dominance outside the opposition’s core zones underlines why the presidential race remains genuinely open despite the headline tie. Ruto’s support is structurally embedded across Northern Kenya, the Central Rift, and the Coast in ways that reflect both political organisation and infrastructure spending targeted at those regions during his administration. Sifuna’s path to 50-per-cent-plus-one runs through consolidating the existing opposition vote — currently spread across Kalonzo Musyoka at nine per cent, Fred Matiang’i at five per cent, and Gachagua at four per cent — while simultaneously making inroads into the 21 per cent of Mount Kenya voters and 17 per cent of Nairobi voters who remain undecided. Neither task is straightforward, but the arithmetic is real. In Nairobi’s presidential preference numbers, Sifuna leads at 39 per cent against Ruto’s 13 per cent, with Kalonzo at 11 per cent and Matiang’i at ten per cent. That 26-point lead in the capital — Kenya’s largest single constituency — is a figure that will accelerate coalition conversations, as other opposition principals calculate whether their interests are better served by negotiating terms with Sifuna now or waiting to see whether his national numbers hold through the first quarter of 2027. The poll also captures a finding with significant implications for the broad-based government arrangement between UDA and ODM: 43 per cent of Kenyans oppose it, against 32 per cent who support it. In Nairobi, opposition runs at 57 per cent, with only 13 per cent in favour. Those numbers are a direct challenge to the political logic that brought ODM into government — and they help explain the speed of ODM’s national decline. Voters who backed Odinga’s movement as an opposition force appear unwilling to extend that loyalty to a junior partner in a Ruto administration, and many are evidently finding their new home in Linda Mwananchi. Kenya’s 2027 presidential election is shaping into something the country has not seen in a decade: a race with no predetermined outcome, no dominant incumbent, and no guaranteed coalition. The TIFA poll does not predict a winner — nine months of political realignment, coalition negotiations, and campaign dynamics separate these numbers from a ballot paper. What it does confirm is that Sifuna has transformed from a prominent opposition voice into a credible presidential contender in the space of months, that ODM’s post-Odinga decline is structural rather than temporary, and that the broad-based government arrangement has generated more public resistance than its architects appear to have anticipated. The map is being redrawn. The question is who draws the final lines. The post Linda Mwananchi tops Nairobi as TIFA poll reshapes Kenya’s 2027 political map appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: Oburu Oginga returns to Senate after two months of illness
description: The Siaya Senator received a standing ovation from colleagues as he made his first appearance in the House since travelling to the United Kingdom for medical treatment in September. By James Mwangi Siaya Senator Oburu Oginga returned to Parliament yesterday after nearly two months of absence due to illness, receiving a standing ovation from fellow senators as he took his seat in the chamber for the first time since departing for medical treatment in the United Kingdom in September. Oginga, who appeared visibly upbeat during Thursday’s sitting, used his return to deliver a message of political tolerance — urging Kenyans to maintain cordial relationships across political divides even as the country moves into an increasingly competitive pre-election period. “We can hold opposing political views and still treat one another with respect,” Oginga told the Senate. “Political differences should never be allowed to tear us apart as a people.” The appeal, delivered by one of Kenya’s most experienced legislators to a chamber that received him warmly, carried particular resonance coming from a senator whose own absence had been exploited to spread disinformation about his health and, in some quarters, his survival. Oginga departed for the United Kingdom on 10 September for what the Orange Democratic Movement described at the time as a routine medical check-up. As weeks passed without a public update, speculation filled the vacuum. Social media accounts circulated claims that the senator had died — a campaign of misinformation that his office and the ODM moved swiftly to counter. In a statement issued on 6 October, the Office of the ODM Party Leader described the claims as “malicious, unfounded fake news and propaganda” and urged the public to rely exclusively on official communication channels. “We wish to assure the general public, members of the Orange Democratic Movement, the people of Siaya County, and the entire nation that Dr Oburu Oginga is well, safe, and in good spirits,” the statement said. Oginga himself subsequently dismissed the rumours directly, saying reports of his death were entirely without foundation. Yesterday’s return gave the senator an opportunity to address not only his colleagues but the wider public that had followed his absence with concern. He spoke of the period of illness with candour, acknowledging the difficulty of being bedridden while away from the political arena he has inhabited for decades. What sustained him, he said, were the messages of goodwill that poured in from Kenyans across the country — across party lines, across regional boundaries, across the very political divides he was now urging the nation to bridge. That detail is not incidental. It speaks to something about Oginga’s standing in Kenyan public life that transcends his party affiliation. As the son of Jaramogi Oginga Odinga, the founding father of Kenyan opposition politics, and a veteran legislator whose career spans multiple political eras, Oburu Oginga occupies a place in the national consciousness that is partly personal, partly historical, and partly symbolic. His illness attracted concern from people who may have little in common politically with ODM or with Siaya County. His recovery, and the warmth of his Senate reception yesterday, reflected that breadth. His call for political tolerance, however, arrives at a moment when Kenya’s political temperature is rising rather than falling. With the August 2027 General Election now less than nine months away, the country’s political class is engaged in an increasingly intense process of coalition-building, candidate positioning, and strategic realignment. The TIFA Research poll released this week, which showed President William Ruto and Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna tied at 31 per cent each as preferred presidential candidates, underscored how competitive and consequential the coming months will be. ODM itself, the party Oginga serves as a senior figure, has seen its national support rating halved since June — from 20 per cent to ten per cent — as voters redistribute across the reconfigured opposition landscape following the departure of former party leader Raila Odinga from domestic electoral politics. It is into that landscape that Oginga has returned — a landscape that is simultaneously more fluid and more fraught than the one he left in September. The opposition is attempting to consolidate around multiple candidates, each with their own regional base and strategic calculus. The question of who leads that consolidated front, and on what terms, remains unresolved. Coalition negotiations are active, often fractious, and operating under the pressure of a ticking electoral clock. Oginga’s voice in those negotiations — measured, historically grounded, and now carrying the particular authority of someone who has faced mortality and chosen to speak about unity — may carry more weight than the transactional calculations of politicians jockeying for position. Whether that voice will be heard above the noise of a presidential race that is already generating considerable heat is another matter. For now, the Senate stood and applauded. In Kenyan politics, that moment of bipartisan warmth is rarer than it should be — and perhaps more necessary than the participants fully realise. title: Sifuna’s Linda Mwananchi Movement holds closed NDC as 2027 platform takes shape
description: The movement bars media from its National Delegates Conference today as it formalises its transition from The Equitable Party and ratifies a leadership structure built around Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. By James Mwangi The Linda Mwananchi Movement today holds its National Delegates Conference behind closed doors, with journalists barred from proceedings as the political outfit formalises its transition from The Equitable Party and ratifies a leadership structure intended to anchor its 2027 General Election campaign. The conference, whose venue has not been made public, is restricted to delegates drawn from members registered under The Equitable Party at the time the NDC notice was published, with each county allocated a fixed number of seats based on registered membership. “Kindly note that today’s NDC will be a closed-door meeting, with no media coverage,” said Pauline Njoroge, the movement’s Head of Communication, confirming the decision yesterday. The movement described the gathering as a statutory requirement under the Political Parties Act, necessary to approve the party’s name change and ratify the resolutions needed to complete its transition. “We ask for your understanding and cooperation as we undertake this important process,” its official notice stated. The decision to exclude the media is unusual for a political movement seeking national visibility ahead of a general election, and it has drawn attention precisely because of what the conference is being asked to approve. At the movement’s public launch on 30 October, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna was unveiled as the proposed party leader — a role that, once ratified today, would give him a formal institutional platform from which to prosecute his 2027 ambitions. Former Meru Governor Kawira Mwangaza, former Law Society of Kenya president Faith Odhiambo, and Mavoko MP Patrick Makau were named as proposed deputies. Vihiga Senator Godfrey Osotsi was proposed as chairperson, Suba South MP Caroli Omondi as secretary-general, and Njoroge as deputy secretary-general. Trans Nzoia Governor George Natembeya was unveiled as head of the movement’s presidential campaign — a signal that the Linda Mwananchi Movement intends to field a presidential candidate rather than serve as a junior coalition partner. The path to today’s conference has not been straightforward. The movement faced legal challenges at the Political Parties Disputes Tribunal, where party member Emmanuel Willyngtone Khamala filed a petition seeking to block the NDC over alleged irregularities in leadership appointments, delegate selection, and internal decision-making. Khamala argued that officials had been appointed without elections or adequate member involvement, and that the party had not conducted grassroots elections to establish the branch and county structures from which legitimate delegates could be drawn. He also challenged the process through which Sifuna and other officials had been positioned for party roles, questioning whether it complied with the party’s constitution and the Political Parties Act. The tribunal dismissed the petition, clearing the way for the conference to proceed — but the complaints it raised about procedural regularity did not disappear with the ruling. They remain live questions about the legitimacy of the structure delegates are today being asked to endorse. That tension sits at the centre of a broader story about how Kenyan opposition politics is being remade in the nine months remaining before the August 2027 ballot. The Linda Mwananchi Movement is one of several vehicles being assembled or reconfigured by politicians who sense that the post-Raila Odinga landscape has created an opening that did not exist before. Odinga’s departure from domestic electoral politics removed the singular force that had organised opposition energies for more than two decades, leaving a vacuum that multiple figures are now racing to fill with varying degrees of institutional credibility and popular support. Sifuna’s calculation is distinctive. Where others have sought to inherit Odinga’s mantle by positioning themselves as continuity candidates within the Orange Democratic Movement’s structures, Sifuna has chosen to build a separate vehicle — one that he controls from the top, that bears no inherited obligations to rival factions, and that can be deployed as either an independent presidential platform or a negotiating asset in coalition talks. The Linda Mwananchi Movement, if today’s conference proceeds as planned, gives him that instrument. The question of whether it also gives him a credible path to State House is considerably harder to answer. His networks span both Luo Nyanza and Western Kenya, and his profile as a combative, media-savvy senator has made him one of the opposition’s most recognisable voices. But recognition and organisation are different currencies in Kenyan electoral politics, and the movement’s decision to operate today’s conference without public scrutiny — undisclosed venue, no media, restricted delegate lists — sits awkwardly alongside any claim to represent a new, transparent political culture. Movements that begin by closing their doors invite the question of what they are protecting. The wider opposition landscape into which the Linda Mwananchi Movement is launching remains unsettled. The Ukombozi Alliance, co-chaired by Siaya Governor James Orengo and former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i, is attempting to construct a unified front, while Stephen Kalonzo Musyoka’s Wiper Patriotic Front insists that his presidential ambitions must carry genuine weight in any coalition arithmetic. Rigathi Gachagua’s Democracy for the Citizens Party is simultaneously building its own national structures, with this week’s fresh questions over his formal registration status at the Registrar of Political Parties adding a new complication to his consolidation efforts. TIFA Research polling released this week shows President Ruto’s UDA recovering ground at 25 per cent national support — a figure that underscores how much the opposition’s fragmentation is currently benefiting the incumbent. Against all of that, today’s closed-door conference in an undisclosed location is either a disciplined operational decision by a movement that knows exactly what it is building, or an early warning about the transparency deficits that could limit its appeal when the campaign reaches full intensity. title: Ruto unveils education gains at Mombasa school heads conference
description: The President tells school administrators that 100,000 teachers have been recruited and 23,000 classrooms built as the government accelerates its overhaul of Kenya’s education system. By Jane Njambi President William Ruto yesterday told the Kenya Comprehensive Schools Heads Association Annual General Meeting in Nyali, Mombasa, that his administration has recruited 100,000 teachers, built 23,000 classrooms, and restructured primary and junior schools under single comprehensive management as part of a broad effort to modernise Kenya’s education system. Speaking at the Sheikh Zayed Children Welfare Centre, Ruto announced that a further 20,000 teachers would be hired next month. “We are building an education system that prepares our children for the world they will inherit, equipping them with the knowledge, skills and competence to think creatively, solve problems and turn ideas into practical solutions,” Ruto said. He added that school funding had been increased and was now being disbursed on time — a long-standing complaint among school administrators that his administration says it has resolved through the unified management structure. The address comes nine months before the August 2027 General Election, with education investment forming a central pillar of the government’s public record. Ruto framed the reforms as an investment in human capital, pledging that every teacher would receive the support needed to deliver quality education and every child the opportunity to succeed. The classrooms are built. Whether the learning follows is the measure that matters. author: hilary kimuyu
title: Six dead, five rescued as building collapses along Mombasa Road
description: At least six people were killed and five others rescued alive on Friday when an eight-storey building under construction collapsed along Mombasa Road in Nairobi. The building, near the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) terminus, caved in at about 9.52am while construction workers were on site, with the top slab giving way, according to preliminary reports from Nairobi City County emergency teams. Nairobi County Chief Officer for Disaster Management Bramwell Simiyu confirmed the six deaths as rescuers continued to search the rubble for possible survivors. "Three bodies were retrieved during the initial morning operations, while three more were recovered later from the debris. All six victims were middle-aged men," he said. The five survivors have been pulled out alive and are receiving emergency medical attention. It is not yet clear how many workers were at the site when the building collapsed. The county fire team and the Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) team were deployed to the scene and continue to comb through the debris for anyone who may still be trapped. Authorities have urged motorists and other members of the public using Mombasa Road near the SGR terminus to keep away from the area to allow emergency teams to carry out rescue operations. The collapse again raises concerns about building safety and compliance with construction regulations in Nairobi, where structural failures have repeatedly raised questions about the enforcement and supervision of construction projects.

title: Blow to President RUTO as vocal Mt. Kenya MP dumps UDA for GACHAGUA’s DCP ahead of 2027 elections.
description: Friday, November 13, 2026 - President William Ruto’s United Democratic Alliance (UDA) has suffered another political setback after Runyenjes Member of Parliament Eric Muchangi Karemba defected to former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua’s Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP). Karemba’s move comes barely weeks after announcing his decision not to seek re-election on the UDA ticket, marking another significant shift in the political landscape of the Mt Kenya region. On Friday, November 13, Gachagua confirmed that he had officially welcomed the Runyenjes legislator into DCP following a meeting at his Wamunyoro residence. “This morning at my Wamunyoro residence, I have welcomed the Member of Parliament for Runyenjes, Hon. Eric Muchangi Karemba, to the DCP Party after Decamping from UDA,” Gachagua announced. The DCP leader further revealed that Karemba would team up with Manyatta MP Gitonga Mukunji to strengthen the party's presence across Embu County. Gachagua also announced plans to visit Runyenjes next week, where he intends to formally introduce the legislator to residents under his new political outfit. He said DCP was targeting the Embu governorship, parliamentary seats, and all 20 ward positions. On October 26, Karemba announced that he would not defend his parliamentary seat on a UDA ticket, saying he wanted to consult constituents and other leaders before deciding his political future. His defection adds to a growing list of Mt Kenya politicians abandoning Ruto's ruling party for Gachagua’s DCP. On October 9, Nakuru Senator Tabitha Karanja also ditched UDA, declaring that she would pursue the Nakuru gubernatorial seat on a DCP ticket. The Kenyan DAILY POST.
