title: My culinary arts journey at Kenyatta University: Four years of heat, hustle and growth
description: Esther Wanjiru reflects on four transformative years studying culinary arts at Kenyatta University — the triumphs, the failures and the lessons that forged a professional. By Esther Wanjiru Esther Wanjiru will sit her final examinations in roughly three months, bringing to a close a four-year journey that has been as intense and transformative as the kitchens she has trained in. Pursuing a degree in Culinary Arts at Kenyatta University has not been merely an academic endeavour — it has been a test of endurance, creativity, discipline and self-discovery. This is her story: the hits, the misses and the opportunities that have shaped her into the culinary professional she is becoming. When she first joined the programme, the vision was romantic — beautifully plated dishes, the warm applause of satisfied guests, the glamour so often portrayed in culinary shows. Reality arrived swiftly and without ceremony. The kitchen is not glamorous. It is hot, fast-paced and unforgiving. The opening months came as a genuine shock. Standing for hours on end, handling sharp tools, working under pressure and meeting strict deadlines pushed her far beyond any comfort zone she had previously known. But it was in that discomfort that growth quietly began. Among the biggest hits of the journey has been mastering foundational skills. Knife work, for instance, is not simply about cutting ingredients — it is about precision, safety and efficiency. Learning classical cooking techniques, understanding flavour profiles and appreciating the science behind food fundamentally transformed the way she approaches the craft. There is a particular confidence that comes with knowing not just what to do, but why it works. That shift — from following recipes to genuinely understanding food — stands among her proudest achievements. Exposure has been another significant highlight. Culinary arts extends well beyond the classroom, and through industrial attachments and practical sessions she has worked in real kitchens, engaged with seasoned professionals and experienced the full demands of the hospitality industry at close range. These experiences opened her eyes to the remarkable diversity within the field — hotel kitchens, catering operations, food production facilities and entrepreneurial ventures all revealed themselves as viable and exciting paths. They reinforced a truth that is easy to overlook: culinary arts is not simply about cooking. It is about service, management and innovation in equal measure. The journey has had its misses, too. There were moments of outright failure — dishes that refused to cooperate, assessments that fell short of expectation and days when the pressure felt genuinely overwhelming. One practical examination stands out in memory. Everything that could go wrong did go wrong. Timing collapsed, presentation suffered and she left the kitchen feeling thoroughly defeated. Yet those painful moments became her most instructive teachers. They taught her resilience, humility and the absolute importance of preparation. Failure, it turns out, has a way of building the very qualities that success alone cannot. Financial constraints have also been a persistent reality. Culinary training demands ingredients, equipment and, at times, additional certifications — all of which carry a cost. Balancing academic requirements against financial limitations has never been straightforward. There were moments that demanded creativity not only inside the kitchen but in the management of limited resources. That pressure, difficult as it was, has instilled a resourcefulness she now considers one of her most bankable professional qualities. Time management has emerged as another critical lesson. The programme is demanding, blending theory and practicals in a combination that requires equal and sustained attention. There were days when juggling assignments, kitchen sessions and personal responsibilities felt like trying to manage too many pots on the stove simultaneously. Learning to prioritise, plan methodically and remain disciplined has been essential — not merely for survival but for genuine success. Amidst the challenges, the opportunities have been considerable. Culinary arts rewards passion and creativity in ways that few disciplines can match. She has had the freedom to experiment with different cuisines, fuse unexpected flavours and develop her own distinctive style. The liberty to create — to transform simple, honest ingredients into something meaningful — has been deeply fulfilling. It is in those moments of creation that the original decision to choose this path makes complete and undeniable sense. Networking has been a substantial and sometimes underestimated gain. Engaging with lecturers, professional chefs and fellow students has built connections that reach well beyond the lecture hall or the kitchen. These relationships are not merely social — they are professional networks that will shape the career ahead. Learning from others, exchanging ideas and collaborating under pressure have enriched the experience in ways that no textbook ever could. As the final stretch approaches, the reflection turns not only to what has been learned but to who has been shaped in the process. The discipline is sharper, the resilience is real and the confidence in her abilities has grown steadily. The kitchen has taught patience and meticulous attention to detail. It has demonstrated the value of consistent hard work and the quiet power of showing up, day after day, regardless of how the previous session ended. Looking ahead, the feelings are mixed — genuine excitement tempered by honest anxiety. The transition from student to professional carries its own distinct set of challenges. The industry is competitive and the expectations are high. But the lessons of four years travel with her: the hits that have built confidence, the misses that have strengthened character and the opportunities that have broadened vision. This journey has not been perfect. It has, without question, been worthwhile. Culinary arts has delivered more than a degree — it has given her a sense of purpose and a clearer understanding of who she is. As she prepares to step into the next chapter, she does so with genuine gratitude for the experiences, the lessons and the growth they have produced. The heat of the kitchen has tested her, the hustle has shaped her and the hope keeps her going. This is her story — and it is only just beginning. title: The end of political wholesaling: Why Kenya’s voters are becoming harder to buy, influence and predict
description: Kenya’s political marketplace is shifting as a more demanding electorate challenges the old brokerage model ahead of the 2027 General Election. By Fredrick Chelimo Kenya is becoming a politically dynamic marketplace, its traditional power brokers declining in influence as a more demanding electorate reshapes the rules of engagement ahead of the 2027 General Election. Beneath the familiar rally circuits, party defections, coalition negotiations and declarations of regional loyalty, something fundamental is changing. The traditional political marketplace — where influential personalities claim the ability to deliver entire communities, constituencies or voting blocs in exchange for financial and political reward — is confronting an electorate that is increasingly difficult to predict. As the old saying goes: a political broker may negotiate access to voters, but only the voter can decide who deserves the mandate. This phenomenon, widely described as political wholesaling, has long occupied a central place in Kenyan electoral politics. Political brokers, community influencers, former elected leaders and self-appointed regional kingpins have presented themselves as custodians of political loyalty. Their proposition is straightforward: provide the resources, recognise our influence, and we shall deliver the votes. The arrangement rests, however, on a questionable assumption — that voters are political commodities whose choices can be negotiated by intermediaries on their behalf. The changing political mood suggests otherwise. Recent opinion surveys examining the popularity, likeability and political standing of prominent Kenyan personalities have unsettled sections of the established political class. Familiar names no longer enjoy automatic public acceptance, while relatively new voices are attracting growing attention. More significantly, economic frustrations — unemployment, taxation, healthcare costs and the rising cost of living — are reshaping how citizens evaluate political leadership. The distinction between popularity and electability has consequently become sharper. A politician may command public recognition, draw large crowds and attract favourable social media attention without necessarily holding the confidence of voters at the ballot box. This is where political wholesalers face their greatest challenge. They may organise meetings, negotiate alliances and assemble impressive delegations, but they cannot guarantee that those attending will vote according to instruction. Attendance is not endorsement. Applause is not commitment. A photograph with a political heavyweight is not an electoral contract. Kenya’s experience mirrors developments in other democracies. In Brazil, social programmes such as Bolsa Família demonstrated how practical poverty-reduction interventions could strengthen political confidence beyond traditional patronage networks. India’s Aam Aadmi Party built substantial support through its emphasis on anti-corruption, education and accessible public services. South Korea’s candlelight demonstrations showed how organised citizens could demand accountability beyond the reach of established political elites. Kenya has its own lessons. The 2022 General Election demonstrated that established alliances and presumed ethnic voting patterns could be disrupted. William Ruto’s victory illustrated the possibilities of building a coalition around economic messaging and perceived political exclusion. Ethnicity, party machinery and patronage remain influential nonetheless. The lesson is not that traditional politics has disappeared, but that its ability to guarantee electoral outcomes is diminishing. Three developments explain this transition. First, the economic experience of ordinary Kenyans has become a political scorecard. A farmer wants affordable agricultural inputs, reliable markets and reasonable returns. A young person wants employment and opportunity rather than endless campaign promises. A parent wants affordable education, while a person with a disability expects accessible healthcare, economic participation and respect for constitutional rights. Political rhetoric becomes irrelevant when it cannot respond to these everyday realities. Second, digital communication has weakened the monopoly previously enjoyed by political intermediaries. Citizens can now interrogate statements, compare promises against performance and challenge political narratives almost immediately. Political communication is no longer controlled exclusively by those who claim to speak for entire communities. Online popularity, however, must not be mistaken for genuine electoral support. Third, voters are growing impatient with political blame games. Politicians blame predecessors; predecessors blame successors; and government officials cite inadequate resources. Yet citizens want straightforward answers: What did you promise? What did you accomplish? Where did you fail, and what will you do differently? This presents a particular challenge to former governors, ministers, legislators and senior public officials seeking another term in office. Experience is an advantage only when accompanied by demonstrable results. Previous positions should invite accountability, not permanent political entitlement. For aspiring politicians, the implications are substantial. The successful campaign of tomorrow must be built around credibility, public engagement and measurable commitments rather than expensive delegations and negotiated voting blocs. Candidates must understand their constituencies before presenting manifestos. They must engage farmers, traders, young people, women, professionals, persons with disabilities and other community groups to identify genuine priorities. Their proposals should be realistic, financially explainable and consistent with the constitutional responsibilities of the offices they seek. Political organisations must equally reconsider the role of grassroots representatives. Community leaders should facilitate dialogue, communicate public concerns and strengthen participation — not claim ownership of people’s votes. A campaign that only reports favourable opinions to its candidate is a political liability. Leaders need honest intelligence, not manufactured enthusiasm. Financial transparency, integrity and continuous public accountability must become central to political organisation. Campaign resources should support legitimate mobilisation, research, voter education and genuine public engagement — not inducements designed to compromise electoral choices. The 2027 General Election will test more than political alliances and financial muscle. It will test whether established leaders can reinvent themselves, whether emerging personalities can translate popularity into credible organisation, and whether political parties can offer practical alternatives to the electorate. Public dissatisfaction with an incumbent does not automatically translate into support for the opposition. Equally, popularity among young people does not guarantee national electoral reach. Successful political leadership requires credibility, competence, organisation, policy clarity and the capacity to unite diverse interests. Kenya is not witnessing the death of political brokers. It is witnessing a possible decline in the political value of those who mistake influence for ownership and mobilisation for authority. The modern voter is not demanding a perfect politician — only an honest, accessible and competent leader who understands that public office is a responsibility, not a commercial investment. title: Water problems in the modern world: a global threat to the future of humanity
description: By: Absamatova Iroda Abstract This article discusses the problem of water scarcity, which is becoming increasingly relevant in the modern world, its causes, and its environmental, economic, and social consequences. The rational use of water resources, pollution of freshwater sources, climate change, population growth, and the impact of human activities on water reserves are analyzed. Attention is also paid to the importance of water-related problems in the Central Asian region, particularly in Uzbekistan, the tragedy of the Aral Sea, and environmental responsibility towards future generations. The article substantiates the necessity of saving water, protecting water resources, and strengthening international cooperation. Keywords: Water scarcity, freshwater, environmental problem, climate change, global warming, water resources, Aral Sea, environmental security, sustainable development, water conservation, Central Asia. Introduction Water is the beginning of life, an invaluable gift of nature, and one of the most important conditions for the existence of humanity. Human life cannot be imagined without water. Every day, we use it for drinking, preparing food, maintaining cleanliness, agriculture, industry, and many other fields. However, unfortunately, humanity does not always appreciate the value of this resource, which is essential for its existence. In today’s era of globalization, the world is facing numerous problems. These include climate change, environmental crises, food security, and the depletion of natural resources. Among these problems, water scarcity occupies a special place. This is because water-related problems directly affect not only nature but also human health, the economy, agriculture, social stability, and the future of countries. According to the United Nations, in 2024, 2.2 billion people worldwide were unable to access safely managed drinking water services. This figure shows that the water problem is not limited to certain regions but is a serious issue facing all humanity. Therefore, talking about water today means not simply discussing a natural resource, but thinking about the future of humanity, the future of our children, and the fate of our planet. Main Body Water Scarcity — A Pressing Problem of the Modern World Although a large part of the Earth’s surface is covered with water, most of it consists of salt water. Freshwater reserves suitable for human consumption and daily needs are quite limited. A large part of the available freshwater is also located in glaciers and underground layers. For this reason, usable water resources are becoming increasingly important in meeting the needs of the world’s population. Several factors contribute to the emergence of water scarcity. Firstly, as the world’s population increases, the demand for drinking water and food products also rises. Secondly, large amounts of water are used in industrial enterprises and agriculture. Thirdly, due to climate change, droughts are intensifying in certain regions, and the amount and seasonal distribution of precipitation are changing. In addition, the pollution of water sources by household waste, industrial wastewater, and chemical substances is further deepening the problem. Most regrettably, in some regions, people are forced to travel long distances to find clean drinking water. Climate Change and Its Impact on Water Resources Today, global climate change is recognized as one of the most important causes of water-related problems. Rising temperatures are leading to the melting of glaciers, increased evaporation, and changes in natural phenomena such as droughts and floods. In particular, glaciers in mountainous regions are the main sources of water for many rivers and streams. The shrinking of glaciers may cause changes in river flows and lead to problems with water supply in the future. Water scarcity is not limited only to a shortage of drinking water. It also leads to a decline in agricultural productivity, an increase in food prices, and a deterioration in living conditions in certain regions. Thus, climate change and water-related problems are processes that are closely interconnected. Water Problems and Human Health Water is vital for the human body. Processes such as metabolism, regulation of body temperature, transportation of nutrients, and elimination of harmful substances take place with the participation of water. The lack of clean drinking water and the use of contaminated water pose serious risks to human health. Under such conditions, the likelihood of the spread of intestinal infections, diarrhoea, dysentery, hepatitis A, and other infectious diseases increases. Children, elderly people, and individuals with weakened immune systems are particularly more vulnerable to water-related diseases. From this point of view, the water problem is not only an environmental issue but also an important medical and social issue. Ensuring that every person has access to safe drinking water is necessary for building a healthy society. Water Problems in Central Asia and Uzbekistan Water scarcity is also one of the pressing issues for Central Asian countries. In our region, agriculture, people’s livelihoods, and economic development largely depend on the waters of major rivers such as the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya. Uzbekistan’s geographical location and climatic conditions make the rational use of water resources particularly important. Population growth, the extensive area of irrigated land, water losses during water use, and climate change may create additional pressure on water supplies in the future. In this regard, the tragedy of the Aral Sea is a particular lesson. During the last century, as a result of the improper and excessive use of water resources, a large part of the Aral Sea gradually dried up. Its consequences had a negative impact not only on nature but also on public health, economic activities, and the social life of the region. The environmental situation that emerged in the Aral Sea region clearly demonstrates what consequences human attitudes towards nature can lead to. This historical experience shows the necessity of taking long-term interests into account when using water. title: PUBG MOBILE teams up with Davido as new Flash version launches globally
description: The gaming giant partners with the Afrobeats superstar to broaden access to its Battle Royale platform across Africa and beyond. By Elizabeth Angira PUBG MOBILE has partnered with global Afrobeats superstar Davido in a collaboration that brings together music, gaming and African youth culture, coinciding with the worldwide launch of PUBG MOBILE FLASH, a lighter version of the platform designed to reach a significantly wider audience of smartphone users across the globe. The partnership carries an unusual dimension: Davido is not simply a celebrity endorser. He is a PUBG MOBILE player himself, with a stated passion for squad tactics and close-range combat gameplay. His involvement, the company says, is rooted in genuine affinity with the game rather than contractual association alone — a distinction the brand has been keen to emphasise as it seeks to build credibility with Africa’s discerning gaming community. The collaboration reflects a broader cultural shift across the continent, where mobile gaming has become a defining feature of youth identity. For a generation that plays, creates and connects primarily on mobile devices, the presence of one of Africa’s biggest music stars on the battlegrounds carries direct resonance with how young Africans engage with digital culture today. Gaming is no longer a pastime on the margins — it is a central thread in the social fabric of African youth life, and PUBG MOBILE is positioning itself firmly within that conversation. PUBG MOBILE has recorded more than one billion downloads worldwide, establishing itself as one of the most recognised names in mobile gaming through its Battle Royale format, which centres on immersive shooting gameplay and competitive multiplayer engagement. PUBG MOBILE FLASH builds on that foundation by reducing the initial download size and optimising performance across a wider range of smartphone specifications. Players who were previously unable to run the full version can now access the core Battle Royale experience without compromise to the essential gameplay that has defined the brand’s global reputation. Jeff Tange, PUBG MOBILE’s Marketing Manager, was clear that PUBG MOBILE FLASH is not a simplified or diminished product. “PUBG MOBILE FLASH is a new way to experience the game,” Tange said, noting that players across both versions can connect and compete with one another, preserving the social dimension that underpins the platform’s enduring appeal. He added that the launch reflects the brand’s commitment to expanding access to premium mobile gaming, particularly across African markets where reaching a broader base of smartphone users represents a meaningful and long-term growth opportunity. Alongside the FLASH launch, the company has introduced the 30BG Card Drop campaign, through which players can complete in-game missions, earn draws and collect exclusive Davido, City and Holiday cards for a chance to win prizes. These include concert tickets to Davido’s Oriade show, an Infinix HOT 70 Pro 5G+ handset and limited-edition 30BG merchandise. Players can also win Davido-themed items by downloading the game and participating in associated in-game activities. For Davido, the partnership connects his music platform with an interactive global gaming community, adding a cultural dimension that extends the collaboration well beyond conventional brand endorsement. His involvement builds a bridge between an international gaming phenomenon and Africa’s vibrant entertainment and youth landscape — one that his fanbase, spread across the continent and the diaspora, inhabits daily. PUBG MOBILE said the Davido partnership and the FLASH launch together form part of a sustained push to deepen its presence in African markets. The company has previously invested in server infrastructure, network optimisation, community operations and creator support programmes on the continent. These include the Next Star influencer initiative and the PDP creator programme, both designed to grow local content creation and encourage player participation in shaping game content from the ground up. From Version 4.5 onwards, PUBG MOBILE said it would intensify localisation efforts in Africa by incorporating local artists, music and cultural references directly into the game. Customised songs, music videos, voice packs, outfits and avatar frames are among the tools the company intends to deploy. The stated ambition is for African players to see their own cultural expression genuinely reflected within the game, rather than simply consuming content produced for markets elsewhere. The move signals a maturing approach to the African market — one that goes beyond surface-level representation and attempts to embed local culture into the product itself. Whether that ambition translates into sustained player growth will depend on execution, but the appetite on the continent is not in question. Africa’s gaming audience is young, connected and growing rapidly, and PUBG MOBILE’s decision to anchor its latest global launch to one of the continent’s most recognisable faces suggests it understands where the opportunity lies. Further details of the music collaboration component of the Davido partnership are expected in a subsequent campaign phase. title: Mahlangu turns 91: A legacy of resilience, art and grace in Mpumalanga
description: The Emthambothini artist who defied doubt to build a celebrated craft and a lasting community legacy marks a remarkable birthday. By Themba Emanuel Mashobane Dr. Esther Mahlangu’s hands once worked in silence, overlooked by the very community she called home. In the quiet corners of her village in Emthambothini, Mpumalanga, while critics were loud and recognition slow, she poured her spirit into her art — and refused to let bitterness take root. She turned 91 yesterday, and the celebration was a testament to what perseverance, grace and an unselfish heart can build over a lifetime. Rather than allowing rejection to harden her, she let it fuel her. Piece by piece, her work began to speak a language the world could not ignore. What started as a solitary passion in a small village grew into a celebrated craft known far beyond South Africa’s borders. She rose above the whispers of those who once dismissed her, proving that true talent cannot remain hidden forever. Yet her greatest masterpiece is not the art itself — it is her grace. Despite her international recognition, she carries no pride and holds no grudges against those who once doubted her. With open hands and a generous heart, she continues to pass her skills to others, ensuring the craft endures for generations to come. The fruits of her perseverance are today undeniable. Even her own family, who watched her long and difficult journey, has embraced the art she fought so hard to protect. What was once a misunderstood dream now sustains a household and feeds a community. She did not simply create art. She built a legacy — and paved a road that others now walk with pride. title: The role of artificial intelligence in the modern world
description: By: Zilola Sayfiddinova Alisher Introduction In the twenty-first century, technological development has become one of the most influential factors shaping human civilization. Among the numerous innovations that have transformed modern society, Artificial Intelligence (AI) occupies a particularly important position. It is rapidly changing the way people live, work, communicate, learn, and interact with the world around them. Artificial Intelligence is no longer a concept associated only with science fiction or advanced scientific laboratories; it has become an essential part of everyday life. Artificial Intelligence can be defined as the ability of computer systems and machines to perform tasks that traditionally require human intelligence. These tasks include learning from experience, analyzing information, recognizing images and speech, understanding languages, solving problems, and making decisions. Through technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and computer vision, AI systems are becoming increasingly sophisticated and capable of performing complex operations. Today, artificial intelligence is used in various fields, including education, medicine, science, agriculture, industry, transportation, business, and communication. Its rapid development creates new opportunities for economic growth, scientific discoveries, and social progress. At the same time, it raises important questions concerning employment, privacy, security, ethics, and human responsibility. The purpose of this article is to examine the role of artificial intelligence in the modern world, explore its practical applications in different areas of human activity, identify its major advantages and challenges, and discuss its potential influence on the future of society. Main Part Artificial Intelligence in Education Education is one of the fields in which artificial intelligence has created significant opportunities for improvement and innovation. Traditional educational systems are gradually integrating digital technologies to make the learning process more effective, accessible, and student-centered. AI-powered educational platforms can analyze students’ learning progress, identify their strengths and weaknesses, and provide personalized learning materials. This approach allows students to study at their own pace and receive additional support in areas where they experience difficulties. Intelligent tutoring systems, online learning applications, automated assessment tools, and digital assistants are examples of how artificial intelligence is transforming education. Artificial intelligence also provides valuable opportunities for teachers. Educators can use AI tools to prepare lesson plans, develop educational exercises, create presentations, generate assessment questions, and organize interactive learning activities. These technologies help reduce the time spent on routine tasks and allow teachers to focus more on students’ individual needs, creative thinking, and intellectual development. Moreover, AI-based translation and language-learning applications make foreign language education more accessible. Students can practice pronunciation, improve vocabulary, receive grammatical explanations, and communicate with intelligent virtual assistants. Such opportunities are particularly important in an increasingly interconnected world where multilingual communication has become essential. However, artificial intelligence should not replace teachers or reduce the importance of human interaction in education. Teachers play an irreplaceable role in developing students’ moral values, social skills, creativity, independent thinking, and emotional intelligence. Therefore, the most effective educational approach is to combine modern AI technologies with professional teaching methods and human guidance. The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare Healthcare is another important sector experiencing remarkable changes due to artificial intelligence. Medical professionals and researchers increasingly use AI systems to analyze medical data, identify diseases, improve diagnostic procedures, and support treatment decisions. One of the most valuable applications of AI in medicine is medical image analysis. Intelligent systems can examine X-rays, MRI scans, CT images, and other medical examinations to help specialists identify abnormalities. These technologies can assist in detecting certain diseases at earlier stages, allowing patients to receive timely medical attention. Artificial intelligence also contributes to the development of personalized medicine. By analyzing medical histories, genetic information, and other health-related data, AI systems can help researchers and healthcare professionals understand individual patient needs and explore more suitable treatment approaches. Furthermore, AI technologies are being used in pharmaceutical research, where they can help scientists analyze chemical compounds, identify potential drug candidates, and accelerate certain stages of medicine development. In hospitals, intelligent systems can support patient management, appointment scheduling, and the organization of medical information. Despite these advantages, AI cannot independently replace the professional knowledge, experience, and ethical responsibility of doctors. Medical decisions require careful human evaluation, especially when patients’ lives and well-being are involved. Therefore, artificial intelligence should function as a supportive instrument that improves healthcare services under appropriate professional supervision. Artificial Intelligence in Business and the Economy The influence of artificial intelligence on business and economic development is becoming increasingly significant. Modern companies use AI technologies to improve productivity, reduce operational costs, analyze market trends, and provide better customer services. One of the major advantages of AI in business is its ability to process enormous amounts of information within a short period. Companies can use these analytical capabilities to understand consumer behavior, predict market demands, identify business opportunities, and make more informed decisions. In the banking sector, artificial intelligence helps identify unusual financial transactions, detect potential fraud, and improve customer support services. Chatbots and virtual assistants can answer frequently asked questions and provide information to customers at any time of the day. Manufacturing industries also benefit from AI-powered automation. Intelligent machines and robots can perform repetitive tasks with high precision, monitor production processes, and identify technical problems. This improves efficiency, reduces certain human errors, and contributes to the development of modern industrial systems. However, the expansion of automation also creates challenges for the labor market. Some traditional occupations may change or become less common as machines take over routine tasks. Consequently, employees need to develop new professional skills, improve their digital literacy, and adapt to changing economic conditions. In this context, lifelong learning and professional development are becoming increasingly important. Artificial Intelligence in Science and Research Scientific research has entered a new stage of development with the introduction of artificial intelligence. title: Israel’s post-election crisis: Netanyahu and Eisenkot clash over national unity government as nuclear threat looms
description: Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot trade public accusations over coalition negotiations, exposing deep divisions in Israeli politics ahead of a critical government formation deadline. By David Kimani Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, two of Israel’s most prominent political figures, are engaged in a sharp and increasingly public dispute over the formation of a national unity government, with both men accusing the other of bad faith as the country enters one of its most consequential political periods since the last general election. The confrontation, playing out on social media and in the Knesset, cuts to the heart of Israel’s post-election reckoning — a nation navigating fractured politics, an existential security threat from Iran and a population exhausted by division. The stakes could scarcely be higher. Israel heads into the critical government formation period with no settled coalition, a contested Knesset speakership and a former prime minister who, by Eisenkot’s account, lost the election but refuses to accept its full political consequences. For observers of Israeli politics, the standoff is both familiar and newly dangerous — familiar because Netanyahu has survived every previous political crisis through tactical manoeuvre, dangerous because the geopolitical context in which this one unfolds is unprecedented in its severity. Eisenkot, a former Chief of Staff of the Israel Defence Forces and now leading the charge to form an alternative government, did not mince his words. He dismissed Netanyahu’s public call for immediate coalition negotiations as a calculated distraction. “Netanyahu calls for negotiations after they have already been scheduled,” Eisenkot said in a statement posted to his official social media account. “He claims he wants unity, but disgraces a state ceremony in the Knesset and divides and incites as if there were no tomorrow.” Eisenkot was explicit about his conditions for any power-sharing arrangement under his leadership: acceptance of his stated principles and a complete break with what he described as extremist political partners. Netanyahu, for his part, framed the conversation in dramatically different terms. In his own public statement, he described a recent meeting with Eisenkot in warmer language, invoking years of professional acquaintance stretching back to Eisenkot’s tenure as IDF Chief of Staff. “This meeting only strengthened my understanding of how essential it is to establish a national unity government,” Netanyahu said, arguing that only a broad coalition encompassing all parties committed to Israel as a Jewish state would be capable of confronting the security challenges ahead. He made no reference to preconditions. The centrepiece of Netanyahu’s public argument was Iran. He warned with striking directness that the Iranian regime, which he characterised as one that “did not hesitate to murder many thousands of its own people,” was once again seeking to advance its nuclear programme. “It will use nuclear weapons against us the moment it manages to resume uranium enrichment and the accelerated development of nuclear weapons,” he said, invoking the codenames “Am Kelavi” — meaning Brave People — and “Shaagat Ha’ari” — meaning Lion’s Roar — as examples of past operations that had, in his account, averted immediate threats. A narrow government, or one dependent on parties he characterised as supporters of terrorism, would, he argued, be incapable of meeting that threat. The language of existential danger has long been part of Netanyahu’s political vocabulary, but analysts who follow Israeli politics closely note that the current moment is not merely rhetorical. Iran’s nuclear ambitions remain a live and unresolved threat. Israeli military and intelligence services have repeatedly identified uranium enrichment acceleration as a red line. Whether or not one accepts Netanyahu’s framing of the coalition arithmetic, the underlying security concern he raises is widely shared across the Israeli political spectrum, including by Eisenkot himself. What divides the two men is not the diagnosis but the prescription. Eisenkot contends that a unity government built around Netanyahu and his current allies — particularly those from the Religious Zionism bloc — would not be a government of genuine national reconciliation but rather a continuation of the same political configuration under a different name. His conditions, he has made clear, are not negotiating positions but prerequisites. The Tuesday Knesset vote to appoint Matan Kahana — a former lieutenant colonel, squadron commander and Sayeret Matkal commando — as Knesset speaker represented, in Eisenkot’s framing, an immediate and concrete test of Likud and Religious Zionism’s stated commitment to democratic cooperation. “If they are indeed committed to genuine political partnership, as they claim, they must allow a proper democratic process to take place on schedule,” he said. The Knesset speakership is not a ceremonial matter. Control of the speaker’s chair shapes legislative agendas, determines which motions reach the floor and, in a parliament as finely balanced as Israel’s, can materially affect a government’s ability to function. The contest over that position is therefore not a sideshow — it is a direct proxy battle for the larger coalition struggle being waged in public statements and behind closed doors simultaneously. Netanyahu’s appeal to unity carried an emotional register as well as a strategic one. He invoked the image of ordinary Israelis — naming individual citizens, Elisha Midan alongside Elisaf Peretz, Talik Gvili alongside Shira Shapira — joining forces across their differences in service of a shared national future. It was language designed to reach beyond the political class, to appeal directly to a public that, by most polling measures, is deeply fatigued by years of electoral instability and political polarisation. Israel has held multiple elections in recent years without producing durable governing majorities. The country’s proportional representation system, combined with an increasingly fragmented party landscape, has made coalition-building a prolonged and painful exercise in which ideological distance between potential partners is frequently enormous. The current impasse fits that pattern — but the external environment gives it an urgency that previous formations did not carry to the same degree. What comes next will be determined not by the volume of public statements but by whether the gap between Eisenkot’s conditions and Netanyahu’s position can be bridged in negotiations. title: IsiDonodono wins double awards in a landmark week for isiNdebele literature
description: Themba Emanuel Mashobane’s celebrated poetry collection claimed two prestigious honours in a single day, cementing its place as a trailblazer for South Africa’s marginalised languages. By Themba Emanuel Mashobane IsiDonodono, the award-winning isiNdebele poetry collection by Themba Emanuel Mashobane, claimed two prestigious literary awards on the same day last Friday, 7 November, in what has become a remarkable run of recognition for a book that has now won three awards and received seven nominations since its publication. The first award came at The Book Behind The Awards (TBBA) ceremony held in Howick, KwaZulu-Natal, under the Umngeni Municipality, where IsiDonodono won in the category of Best isiNdebele Book. The second followed the same evening at The Castle of Good Hope in Cape Town, in a ceremony hosted by SHOFAR Books. That two major awards fell on the same date underscored the growing national profile of a collection that began as a manuscript entry and has since travelled the length of the country. The book, which contains 67 poems written in isiNdebele, was previously a winning manuscript at both the ANFASA and DSAC awards in 2025 before being published by ePublishing and Digital Displays. It is structured in the form of a textbook, with Mashobane providing literary analysis and explanatory notes alongside the poems — an approach that makes it both a creative work and a scholarly resource for readers and students of the language. For Mashobane, the awards carry a purpose that extends beyond personal achievement. “I use these awards to promote isiNdebele, which is one of the most disadvantaged languages in South Africa when compared with other indigenous languages,” he said. “Award nominations pave the way for me to promote my book, my genre and to network with writers from different regions and various languages.” His broader concern is access. Mashobane noted that self-published authors are frequently sidelined from both national awards and opportunities enjoyed by those backed by traditional publishing houses. Private awards that partner with established brands, he argued, provide an important platform for independent voices to showcase their work and reach new audiences. He urged emerging writers to pursue such opportunities actively, treating local awards not as validation alone but as a practical tool for market visibility and professional connection. IsiDonodono continues to demonstrate that a language once considered peripheral can, in the right hands, produce work of national distinction. TBBA 2026 WINNER’S . title: Detectives raid a guest house and arrest a fake KDF recruiter who fleeced jobseekers Ksh 1.1 million - Was conducting fake medical tests (PHOTOs)
description: Sunday, November 15, 2026 - Detectives have arrested a man accused of masquerading as a Kenya Defence Forces (KDF) officer and fleecing unsuspecting jobseekers of KSh1.1 million in fake recruitment fees. The suspect, identified as Brian Shem Maboni Achieng, was arrested at Cereda Guesthouse in Shibale Trading Centre, Nambale, Busia County, following credible intelligence received by detectives. According to DCI, officers raided the guesthouse and found the suspect holed up in a room with a 22-year-old woman who had been brought there by her mother in the hope of securing a KDF recruitment slot. Another young woman had similarly been brought to the premises by a parent, with both families hoping to secure their daughters' enlistment into the military. Preliminary investigations indicate that the suspect had been posing as a KDF officer with the purported ability to secure recruitment slots, collecting KSh1.1 million in cash from the victims' parents on different dates between September and November 2026. But what detectives discovered inside the room was even more disturbing. suspect had allegedly drawn blood and urine samples from one of the women under the guise of conducting a KDF medical examination. Among the items recovered were two syringes, one containing a blood sample and another containing clear fluid, a black dual-head stethoscope, an Omron blood pressure machine, surgical spirit and cotton wool. Detectives also seized a laptop, computer mouse and other electronic accessories, as well as white T-shirts bearing the inscriptions CODE 87243 and CODE 624513. Further recoveries included Kenyan and Ugandan national identity cards, a Ugandan driving permit and a VISA card, all bearing the suspect's photograph, alongside two mobile phones. suspect is currently in custody undergoing processing ahead of arraignment, while the recovered items have been detained as exhibits to support ongoing investigations. DCI has cautioned members of the public against falling prey to individuals masquerading as recruitment agents for the disciplined services and demanding money in exchange for enlistment. agency reiterated that KDF recruitment is conducted through officially announced and transparent procedures, not backdoor deals or cash inducements. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Kalenjin man arrested in connection with the murder of a senior police officer after being on the run for nearly 3 years - DCI reveals how detectives finally tracked him down
description: Sunday, November 15, 2026 - Detectives have arrested a murder suspect who had been on the run for nearly two years and nine months following the brutal killing of a senior police officer in Laikipia County. The suspect, identified as Onesmas Kipkoech Tiony, is accused of murdering Inspector Prosper Ojiambo Wandera, who was then the Deputy Officer Commanding Rumuruti Police Station. According to the DCI, the chilling incident happened on February 16, 2024, when Inspector Wandera was found lying in a pool of blood in the Maundu Meri area of Rumuruti Town. senior officer had sustained a deep stab wound on the left side of his chest, pointing to a violent end. suspect reportedly fled the scene and went into hiding, but detectives never abandoned the search for him. Through painstaking investigations, forensic analysis and follow-up on leads, Homicide detectives eventually narrowed down the search and launched a manhunt that culminated in his arrest. On Saturday, November 14, 2026, a coordinated operation involving Homicide detectives, DCI Laikipia West and officers from Rumuruti Police Station led to the raid of the suspect’s hideout and his eventual arrest. During the operation, detectives also recovered a motorcycle believed to have been used by the suspect to flee the scene after the murder. motorcycle has since been secured as an exhibit. suspect is currently in police custody, undergoing processing ahead of his arraignment in court. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Portugal honour Cristiano Ronaldo with special number 7 shirt redesign
description: The Portuguese Football Federation has permanently altered the design of its iconic number 7 shirt in an emotional tribute to one of football’s greatest ever players. By Pascal Okoth Portugal have introduced a special redesign of their iconic number 7 shirt as a permanent tribute to Cristiano Ronaldo, celebrating the extraordinary legacy of a man who transcended football and became the defining symbol of Portuguese sporting greatness across more than two decades of international service. The Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) announced the gesture yesterday, describing it as an effort to immortalise the significance of a number that has become utterly inseparable from Ronaldo’s name, his achievements and his immeasurable contribution to the game in Portugal and beyond. It is a rare honour — the kind reserved not merely for great players, but for those who reshape what a nation believes is possible on a football pitch. Ronaldo’s relationship with the number 7 shirt stretches back to his earliest days representing Portugal, a bond that deepened with every goal, every tournament and every record broken along the way. He retired as Portugal’s all-time leading scorer and the most capped player in the history of the national team, having appeared at multiple World Cups and European Championships and lifted the UEFA European Championship trophy in 2016 — Portugal’s first major international title — in what many consider the crowning achievement of his international career. The number 7 itself carries a mythical weight in football. From the great wingers of the British game to the continental maestros who wore it with flair and purpose, the shirt number has long been associated with brilliance, speed and the capacity to change a match in a moment. For Portugal, however, it means something specific and deeply personal. It means Ronaldo — the boy from Madeira who left home as a teenager, conquered club football at the highest level with Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus, and never stopped returning to pull on the red and green of his country with everything he had. The FPF’s decision to alter the shirt’s design rather than simply retire the number reflects a thoughtful distinction. Retiring a number takes it off the pitch entirely; this tribute keeps the 7 alive in Portuguese football while marking it permanently with the weight of what Ronaldo achieved in wearing it. Future players who pull on that shirt will carry with them a visible reminder of the standard set by the man who wore it before them — a responsibility and an inspiration in equal measure. The tribute has been warmly received across the football world, with supporters, former teammates and football administrators praising the federation for the sensitivity and creativity of the gesture. For Portuguese fans who watched Ronaldo grow from a gifted but raw teenager into the most prolific scorer in the history of international football, the redesign carries genuine emotional resonance. It is not simply a commercial or ceremonial act — it is an acknowledgement that some legacies are too large to be left only to memory and statistics. Ronaldo himself has spoken often about what representing Portugal means to him, describing the national team as a source of immense pride that no club achievement could replicate. That attachment, sustained over a career of extraordinary length and consistency, is precisely what makes the FPF’s tribute feel earned rather than sentimental. The number 7 shirt will continue to be worn by Portugal players in the matches ahead. But it will now carry a design that tells anyone who sees it exactly what that number has meant — not just in the record books, but in the hearts of a nation that watched one of their own become, by any measure, the most remarkable footballer their country has ever produced. For Portugal, the number 7 no longer belongs only to football. It belongs to Cristiano Ronaldo. title: ODM tops KSh 2.26B political parties fund as UDA and Jubilee trail behind
description: The Orange Democratic Movement has received the single largest share of Kenya’s political parties funding, edging out the ruling UDA in the latest allocation covering 47 parties. By Yvonne Wambui The Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) has emerged as the biggest beneficiary of Kenya’s KSh 2.26 billion Political Parties Fund, receiving KSh 801.85 million — the largest single allocation among 47 political parties that participated in the 2022 General Election, according to a report by the Registrar of Political Parties tabled before Parliament yesterday. The figure positions ODM, now led by Oburu Odinga following the death of his younger brother, the late Raila Odinga, ahead of President William Ruto’s ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) and the Jubilee Party in what is one of the most consequential annual distributions of public money to Kenya’s political landscape. The fund exists to support parties in running their operations, maintaining structures and promoting democratic participation — and the scale of the allocations this cycle underscores just how unevenly that support is distributed across the political spectrum. ODM’s total allocation comprises a primary disbursement of KSh 421.22 million, a supplementary allocation of KSh 380 million and a carried-forward balance of KSh 634,896 from the previous financial period. The combination of a primary grant and a supplementary top-up pushed ODM’s total marginally above UDA’s, a gap that is likely to sharpen debate about how the formula rewards electoral performance and parliamentary representation. UDA, which controls the presidency and commands a significant parliamentary bloc, received KSh 788.74 million — placing it second, albeit by a relatively narrow margin. Jubilee Party, now associated with former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i following its dramatic political realignment in recent years, secured KSh 184.89 million, making it the third-largest recipient. Together, the three parties absorbed approximately 79 per cent of the total funds distributed, leaving the remaining 44 parties to share the balance — a concentration of resources that critics argue entrenches the dominance of established political outfits at the expense of newer and smaller formations. Among the mid-tier beneficiaries, Wiper Democratic Movement-Kenya, led by former Vice-President Kalonzo Musyoka, received KSh 98.81 million, reflecting its sustained organisational base in lower Eastern Kenya. The Democratic Action Party-Kenya (DAP-K), associated with Eugene Wamalwa, was allocated KSh 43.20 million. The United Democratic Movement received KSh 36.83 million, Ford-Kenya was allocated KSh 35.33 million, and the Kenya African National Union (KANU) — once the country’s sole legal party and now a shadow of its former self — received KSh 32.89 million. The allocations are determined under the Political Parties Act using a formula that weighs the number of votes a party obtained at the previous general election alongside the number of elected representatives it fields across all levels of government. That formula inherently favours parties with broad national reach and strong parliamentary representation, which explains why ODM and UDA dominate the distribution despite their very different positions — one in government, one navigating a post-Raila future with considerable uncertainty about its long-term political direction. What makes this cycle’s figures particularly noteworthy is the context in which they land. Political parties across the country are actively preparing for future electoral contests, and financial resources at this stage carry outsized strategic importance. Access to party funding determines whether grassroots structures can be maintained, whether local offices remain operational and whether parties can sustain the kind of continuous engagement with voters that translates into electoral strength. For smaller parties scraping by on allocations in the tens of millions, the gap between their resources and those of the top three is not merely financial — it shapes their entire capacity to compete. ODM’s position at the top of the table is also significant given the party’s current moment. The death of Raila Odinga — the towering figure who built ODM into a national force over two decades — has left the party at a crossroads. Oburu Odinga inherits both the leadership and the challenge of holding together a coalition that was, in many respects, built on his brother’s singular political personality. The KSh 801.85 million allocation provides a substantial financial platform from which to attempt that consolidation, but money alone will not resolve the deeper questions of identity and direction that now confront the party. For UDA, the second-place finish in funding despite holding the presidency and a parliamentary majority reflects the technicality of how the formula operates — ODM’s stronger performance in the 2022 vote in certain categories, combined with the supplementary disbursement, nudged it ahead. It is a distinction the ruling party’s strategists will note, though UDA’s proximity to state resources through its position in government gives it advantages that do not appear in the Registrar’s report. The tabling of this report before Parliament also reopens broader questions about accountability. Kenya’s Political Parties Act requires that parties submit audited accounts detailing how public funds are spent, but enforcement of that requirement has historically been inconsistent. With KSh 2.26 billion of taxpayer money now distributed, the scrutiny on how each party accounts for its allocation will inevitably intensify — as it should. Kenyans have a right to know whether these funds are strengthening genuine democratic structures or simply sustaining party bureaucracies with little accountability to ordinary members and voters. The report now sits before Parliament, and the conversation it triggers about equitable distribution, formula reform and financial accountability is one that Kenya’s political class can no longer afford to have only on paper. title: The poll shock, opposition realignment and the gathering storm ahead of 2027
description: A statistical tie between Ruto and Sifuna, a fractured opposition seeking unity and mounting institutional questions are reshaping Kenya’s electoral landscape with 2027 drawing steadily closer. By Fredrick Chelimo “The political fortunes of a nation are rarely determined by the loudest voices in its political arena, but by the silent conversations taking place in the homes, workplaces and communities of ordinary citizens. When those conversations begin to change, even the most established political arrangements must reconsider their foundations.” Kenya’s political landscape is displaying unmistakable signs of a competitive and complicated electoral season as the country moves through the week of November 16–22, 2026. The latest presidential opinion poll, renewed debate over opposition unity, emerging political movements, regional rivalries and growing scrutiny of public institutions have combined to create an atmosphere in which almost every political engagement carries an electoral undertone. The events of the past week are significant precisely because they reveal a shifting relationship between political leadership, public perception and the traditional methods through which electoral support has been built and negotiated. The most consequential development is the TIFA Research survey released on November 12, which placed President William Ruto and Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna at 31 per cent each in preferred presidential choice for 2027. Kalonzo Musyoka registered nine per cent, Fred Matiang’i five per cent and Rigathi Gachagua four per cent, while 15 per cent of respondents remained undecided. Conducted between October 26 and November 5 among 2,036 adults across all 47 counties, the survey has generated considerable political debate. These figures measure stated preference at the time of interviews — they are neither an election result nor a definitive prediction of voting behaviour, and they should be read as such. The reaction from Kenya Kwanza leaders has itself been revealing. Senate Majority Leader Aaron Cheruiyot and other government-aligned politicians have challenged the suggestion that Ruto and Sifuna are operating at comparable levels of public support. Yet opinion polling should not be treated as a political endorsement, nor dismissed simply because its findings are inconvenient. Its real value lies in identifying changing public attitudes, stimulating debate and encouraging political institutions to examine honestly the reasons behind those shifts. Equally, the opposition should resist the temptation to interpret a statistical tie as an electoral victory. The 15 per cent undecided electorate, the constitutional presidential threshold and the practical challenges of coalition-building remain critical variables. What makes the findings particularly interesting is Sifuna’s emergence as a national political personality beyond his traditional parliamentary and ODM constituency. His Linda Mwananchi platform appears to be attracting citizens seeking a different kind of political conversation — one centred on accountability, economic opportunity and generational renewal. However, translating personal popularity into a sustainable political organisation requires considerably more than public enthusiasm. The November 13 delegates’ conference, which proceeded after the Political Parties Disputes Tribunal declined to stop it, focused on organisational restructuring, nomination rules and coalition negotiations. Crucially, delegates deferred key leadership appointments, leaving Sifuna’s formal elevation unresolved. The distinction between a popular political personality and an established political institution will define the movement’s next phase. Opposition unity has simultaneously gained renewed momentum following former President Uhuru Kenyatta’s appeal to opposition principals to subordinate individual ambitions to a common political purpose. Kalonzo Musyoka’s November 14 declaration that he is prepared to sacrifice his presidential ambition in support of a single opposition candidate is a significant development. His insistence that he will remain in the opposition regardless of the outcome of negotiations provides a clearer indication of his publicly stated position — though the gap between public declarations and durable political agreements remains wide and historically familiar in Kenyan politics. The intervention of Opiyo Wandayi, who urged Kenyatta to step back from active political engagement, has introduced another dimension to the debate, raising an important constitutional and democratic question about the continuing role of retired presidents in national political discourse. Retirement from public office does not extinguish citizenship or the freedom to express political opinions, and that distinction matters. At the regional level, the confrontation during the Maa Cultural and Tourism Festival at Sekenani in Narok on November 14 deserves serious reflection. The clash involving rival supporters associated with Governor Patrick Ntutu and Nairobi West MP Gabriel Tongoyo briefly disrupted an occasion intended to celebrate cultural heritage and promote tourism. President Ruto’s presence did not prevent the confrontation, and security officers were forced to intervene. The incident illustrates the growing difficulty of separating cultural institutions from competitive electoral politics — a difficulty that will only intensify as 2027 approaches. The controversy surrounding the Kenya Pipeline Company share transaction adds another layer of institutional concern. Ndindi Nyoro’s questions about the transaction and Treasury Cabinet Secretary John Mbadi’s defence of the sale of a 25 per cent stake to private investors have opened a wider debate about public asset management, transparency and national economic interests. The government maintains the transaction was commercial and above board, but the public deserves access to relevant valuation, ownership and governance arrangements. Trust in public institutions is built through transparency, not assertion. The distribution of KSh 2.26 billion in political party funding offers yet another perspective on the changing environment. ODM received approximately KSh 801.85 million, UDA KSh 788.74 million and Jubilee KSh 184.89 million — the three parties together accounting for approximately 79 per cent of total disbursements. Audit concerns about inadequate records and party offices that existed only on paper raise legitimate questions about whether public resources are genuinely strengthening democratic participation or merely sustaining political bureaucracies. title: No Ronaldo, no party: Denmark deliver 4–1 reality check to Portugal
description: A night planned as a celebration of Cristiano Ronaldo’s legacy turned into a sobering lesson as Denmark dismantled Portugal 4–1 in the UEFA Nations League at Braga. By Andalo Christine Ingutia Portugal’s carefully choreographed tribute to Cristiano Ronaldo was yesterday gate-crashed by a ruthless Denmark side who showed no interest in sentiment, handing the hosts a stunning 4–1 defeat in the UEFA Nations League at the Estádio Municipal de Braga — their heaviest home loss in the competition’s history. The evening had been designed as an emotional farewell to Ronaldo’s international legacy, with Portugal’s players and their mascots taking to the pitch in shirts bearing his iconic number 7, while supporters unveiled a breathtaking stadium display honouring the forward’s extraordinary contribution to Portuguese football. It was a night built for warmth and celebration. Denmark, however, had not read the script. Pierre-Emile Højbjerg broke the deadlock in the 43rd minute, stepping up to convert from the penalty spot after VAR confirmed a handball by Portugal defender Rúben Dias. It was a clinical, composed finish that set the tone for everything that followed — and Portugal never truly recovered. Denmark returned from the break with greater intent and sharper teeth. Rasmus Højlund, one of Europe’s most dangerous young strikers, took centre stage with a devastating seven-minute double that effectively killed the contest. He first volleyed home Mikkel Damsgaard’s cross in the 50th minute, all timing and technique, before firing a low, precise effort past Diogo Costa in the 57th minute to put the visitors firmly in control. The Braga crowd, so electric before kick-off, had fallen into a stunned silence. The evening’s misery was completed in the 75th minute when Joachim Andersen rose highest from a corner to power a header into the net, making it four and emphatically ending any Portuguese hope of a comeback. Bernardo Silva provided a late consolation in the 94th minute, but it was exactly that — a consolation, with no bearing on a result that told an uncomfortable story about where this Portugal side currently stands without the man they had spent the evening honouring. Portugal head coach Jorge Jesus was characteristically blunt when asked whether Ronaldo’s absence had contributed to the defeat. “Missing what? He’s no longer on the national team, so what’s missing? The only thing missing is his presence here to keep me company,” Jesus said. It was a deflection dressed as a quip, but it also contained a pointed challenge to his players — that the Ronaldo era is over and the responsibility of carrying Portugal forward rests entirely with those now in the squad. There is an irony in all of this that is hard to ignore. The night was meant to draw a line under the Ronaldo chapter with grace and gratitude, to send him off with the full-throated affection of a nation he served for more than two decades. Instead, it exposed with unusual clarity the size of the vacuum his retirement has left — not because Portugal lack quality, but because replacing a player of Ronaldo’s psychological force and goalscoring certainty is not something that happens in one match, or one season, or perhaps even one generation. The result, painful as it is, does not alter Portugal’s standing in Group A4. They remain top with 12 points and have already secured their place in the quarter-finals. Denmark move to nine points, keeping alive their own qualification hopes heading into the final round of group fixtures. Portugal travel to Cardiff to face Wales on Tuesday, while Denmark host Norway in Copenhagen. For Denmark, it was a statement — a victory on Portuguese soil that announced their own ambitions loudly and without apology. For Portugal, it was a reality check delivered on the worst possible night. The tributes to Ronaldo were genuine and deserved. But football, as it always does, moved on before the applause had even faded. The post No Ronaldo, no party: Denmark deliver 4–1 reality check to Portugal appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

author: the mt kenya times
title: Modern Uzbekistan, timeless traditions: Preserving national identity in a changing world
description: As Uzbekistan embraces modernisation and global connectivity, one university’s weekly tradition asks a quietly profound question — what does development cost if it erases the culture it was meant to serve? By Odilov Muhammadamin Uzbekistan is developing at a pace and confidence that would have been difficult to imagine a generation ago — new infrastructure, deepening diplomatic ties, expanding international partnerships and a younger generation with opportunities their parents never had. Yet alongside these achievements, a question that refuses to be drowned out by the noise of progress keeps surfacing: how does a nation modernise without losing the very thing that makes it distinctly itself? It is not a uniquely Uzbek dilemma. Every society navigating rapid change faces some version of it. But in Uzbekistan, where culture is not an abstract idea but something woven, literally, into daily life, the stakes feel particularly vivid. Traditional Uzbek clothing represents one of the most immediate and beautiful expressions of that heritage. The richly coloured Atlas and Adras fabrics, the carefully embroidered do’ppi — the traditional skullcap — the elegant chopon robe and the many other elements of national dress have been passed down through generations not as museum pieces, but as living markers of identity, craftsmanship and cultural pride. These garments carry within their patterns and textures a record of who Uzbeks are and where they come from. They are not merely decorative. They are a language. That language has been heard well beyond Central Asia. The late Oscar de la Renta, one of the most celebrated fashion designers of the twentieth century, drew inspiration from Central Asian ikat patterns, incorporating their geometric complexity and colour richness into his international collections. It was a reminder that what is rooted in tradition need not be parochial — that the specific can speak to the universal. In 2017, UNESCO formally recognised the Margilan Crafts Development Centre’s work in safeguarding the traditional production of Atlas and Adras fabrics, lending international weight to what Uzbek artisans have known for centuries. None of this means that global fashion trends are unwelcome. Among young Uzbeks, international styles are popular and their enthusiasm for them is entirely natural. Cultures have always exchanged ideas about how people dress, and that exchange is part of what keeps traditions alive rather than frozen. The question is not whether to engage with the modern world, but how to do so without allowing the pressures of globalisation to quietly hollow out what is most distinctly one’s own. This is precisely the philosophy at the heart of Alfraganus University’s guiding motto: “Zamonaviy ta’lim va sharqona tarbiya uyg’unligi” — the harmony of modern education and Eastern values. The phrase is not merely a slogan. It reflects a genuine institutional commitment to producing graduates who are professionally equipped for a competitive world while remaining grounded in the cultural and moral traditions that give that professional life its meaning. Real education, the university argues, is not limited to academic achievement. It also shapes the kind of person a student becomes — someone who carries their heritage forward with understanding and pride, not embarrassment. That commitment finds a practical and joyful expression every Friday, when Alfraganus University observes Milliy kun — National Dress Day. For more than a year, students have been encouraged to wear elements of Uzbek national clothing to university: an Atlas or Adras outfit, an embroidered do’ppi, garments featuring traditional ornaments. The tradition has become more than a dress code. It is a weekly act of cultural affirmation, a reminder that heritage does not belong only in ceremonial contexts or behind exhibition glass. It can walk into a lecture hall, sit at a desk and open a textbook. Preserving traditional clothing does not demand that every Uzbek wear national dress daily or turn their back on contemporary fashion. It asks something more sustainable and more meaningful — that people understand the significance of what they have inherited, support the artisans who keep those skills alive and ensure that future generations receive that inheritance with its value intact. A nation that moves confidently into the future while remaining anchored in its past is not caught between two worlds. It has found the harder and more rewarding thing: a way to be both. Uzbekistan’s future is modern. Its roots are timeless. The two are not in conflict — not if the choice is made, every Friday and beyond, to carry both forward together. title: Press freedom in Kenya: Free on paper, difficult in practice
description: Kenya’s Constitution promises world-class press protections — the streets tell a different story. By Mathew Kipkemboi Kenya’s 2010 Constitution is, on paper, a journalist’s charter. Article 33 protects expression. Article 34 guarantees media independence. Article 35 grants access to information. Few countries write these protections more boldly into law. Yet Reporters Without Borders ranked Kenya 117th for press freedom in 2025, recovering only modestly to 106th in 2026, with conditions rated “difficult.” The gap between constitutional promise and lived reality is wide. The evidence is not abstract. During the 2024 anti-Finance Bill protests, journalists were tear-gassed, injured and had equipment destroyed. In June 2025, the Communication Authority ordered broadcasters to pull live protest coverage off-air until courts intervened. On October 20 this year, a Royal Media Services investigative journalist was arrested while reporting on fuel price protests. Each incident is not merely an attack on a reporter — it is a direct violation of the Constitution those same officials swore to uphold. This is not a new fight. Since Gutenberg’s press around 1440, the powerful have sought to control what the public knows. Today the tools are surveillance, internet shutdowns and cybercrime laws — but the impulse is identical. The encouraging signs exist. Courts suspended the broadcast shutdown. Criminal defamation was struck down. The system still has teeth. But a press free in law yet battered in practice is not truly free. A public that cannot see clearly cannot govern itself. Kenya wrote that principle beautifully into its Constitution. The task now is making practice match the promise. title: How Bahati fooled Kenya: The million-shilling ‘wedding’ that was really a campaign launch
description: A gospel star, a fake wedding and KSh 10 million — Bahati’s Mathare 2027 debut raises a question that will follow him to the ballot. By Justus Sware Kenyans waited weeks for Bahati and Diana Marua’s white wedding. Hand-delivered invitations, a black-tie dress code, cameras banned, admission pegged at KSh 1 million per guest. On November 6 at the Argyle Grand Hotel in Nairobi, guests arrived expecting vows. They got a podium reading “MP Mathare 2027.” The wedding was never a wedding. It was a campaign launch in a bridal veil. The stunt worked because of its precision. Viral videos of celebrity invitations, deliberate media restrictions and a month-long buildup kept the true nature of the event carefully hidden. On NTV’s Fixing the Nation, Bahati was unapologetic. “I did not say what was to happen,” he said. “They guessed this is a wedding. I used Bahati’s Big Day artistically to get the attention of the nation.” On the money, Bahati claimed total collections reached approximately KSh 10 million — far below the KSh 100 million rumoured — with proceeds directed to his Bahati Cares initiative. Critics were unconvinced. The million-shilling figure was actively promoted, not imagined. Nairobi official Geoffrey Mosiria announced his own free-entry wedding, challenging Bahati to refund the money to Mathare residents. Bahati contested Mathare in 2022 and lost. His 2027 bid leans on a compelling origin story — orphan, gospel star, devoted husband. But he took public affection for that story and monetised it as a political prop. Technically, he never lied. But if he misled the nation about a wedding to win attention, Mathare voters will ask: what else would he do to win a seat?
