author: the mt kenya times
title: Kenya’s 2027 election crisis: Kalonzo takes opposition case to Washington as IEBC independence comes under fire
description: A high-level opposition delegation has carried Kenya’s deepening electoral anxiety to one of the world’s most influential foreign policy institutions, warning that the conditions for a free and fair vote do not yet exist. By David Kimani Wiper Democratic Movement leader Kalonzo Musyoka has taken Kenya’s pre-election tensions to Washington, leading a senior opposition delegation that met the Council on Foreign Relations on Monday to raise urgent concerns about the independence of the electoral commission, the deployment of state resources for political campaigning, and what the opposition describes as a pattern of organised violence against their supporters. The meeting, which Musyoka confirmed on his official X account, included People’s Liberation Party leader Martha Karua, former National Assembly Speaker Justin Muturi, Ford Kenya’s Eugene Wamalwa, and National Assembly Deputy Minority Leader Robert Mbui. The Council on Foreign Relations was represented by its president, Michael Froman. The delegation’s decision to engage one of Washington’s most respected foreign policy institutions — whose membership includes serving and former heads of state, senior diplomats and leading academics — signals that Kenya’s opposition is internationalising its concerns about the 2027 General Election with deliberate urgency, more than eight months before polling day. At the centre of the opposition’s case is the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission. “There can be no free and fair election when the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission is not independent,” Musyoka wrote in his account of the meeting, a formulation that goes to the heart of Kenya’s recurring post-election disputes. The IEBC has been without a full complement of commissioners since the resignations that followed the 2022 election, and the process of reconstituting the commission has itself become politically charged, with opposition parties accusing the government of seeking to install a compliant body ahead of a consequential election. The opposition’s concerns extend well beyond the composition of the commission. Musyoka and his colleagues told the Council that state funds and civil servants are being deployed for public campaigning on behalf of the ruling administration — a practice that, if substantiated, would constitute a direct violation of Kenya’s electoral laws, which prohibit the use of public resources for partisan purposes. The allegation, which the government has not publicly addressed in response to this specific meeting, reflects a broader anxiety about the uneven playing field that has characterised Kenyan elections across multiple cycles. The violence claims are the most serious element of the opposition’s Washington briefing. Musyoka described a pattern of organised attacks on opposition events: supporters stoned and tear-gassed, vehicles attacked, staff seriously injured and, most gravely, police firing live ammunition. “A regime that turns violence on citizens exercising their democratic rights has no business talking about peaceful elections,” he said. These are allegations that carry significant weight internationally, particularly in the context of Kenya’s history with election-related violence. Independent verification of the specific incidents cited was not immediately available, and the government has not responded publicly to this account of the CFR meeting. The delegation also raised what it characterised as the capture of Parliament by the Executive, arguing that the legislature has been reduced to a rubber stamp and can no longer perform its constitutional function of checking executive power. This is not a new criticism — opposition and civil society voices have repeatedly raised concerns about the relationship between the Ruto administration and the National Assembly — but its presentation to an institution of the Council on Foreign Relations’ standing gives it a new international dimension. Kenya’s foreign policy came under separate scrutiny in the Washington meeting. The opposition drew attention to what it described as President William Ruto’s entanglement with the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan — a paramilitary group that has been accused of mass atrocities in the ongoing Sudanese conflict — and argued that this association has compromised Kenya’s historic reputation as a neutral regional mediator. Kenya’s foreign policy positioning on Sudan has drawn scrutiny from regional analysts, though the government has maintained that its engagement is oriented towards peace facilitation. Underlying all of these concerns is the opposition’s characterisation of corruption under the current administration as having reached levels the country has not previously experienced. “Corruption under Ruto has reached levels this country has never seen, and the rule of law is treated as an inconvenience to be ignored,” Musyoka said. These are claims that the government rejects. The administration has pointed to various anti-corruption initiatives and infrastructure programmes as evidence of responsible governance. The political landscape heading into August 2027 is exceptionally complex. Kenya has never held a genuinely peaceful and uncontested election in which the loser accepted the result without significant dispute. The 2007 post-election violence, the contested results of 2017 and the tight margin of 2022 — which produced a Supreme Court petition before Ruto’s victory was confirmed — have embedded deep institutional scepticism about electoral processes across the political spectrum. What distinguishes the current moment is the scale and sophistication of the opposition’s international engagement. The decision to brief the Council on Foreign Relations, an institution whose analysis shapes American foreign policy thinking, is a deliberate signal that Kenya’s opposition intends to hold its concerns before international audiences throughout the campaign period. The United States, as Kenya’s most significant bilateral partner and a major source of investment and diplomatic support, is not an incidental audience. Whether the CFR meeting produces any concrete response — increased international monitoring commitments, diplomatic pressure around IEBC reconstitution, or formal statements on electoral conditions — remains to be seen. What is already clear is that Kenya’s 2027 election has acquired an international dimension that will be difficult to contain within the country’s borders. The ballot, as Musyoka framed it, is where the opposition intends to settle matters. The question is whether, by the time August arrives, the conditions for a credible vote will have been established. title: McCarthy turns his back on Bafana Bafana to fire Kenya’s Afcon charge
description: The Kenya head coach says his heart belongs entirely to the Harambee Stars as he prepares to face his home country in a crucial Afcon 2027 qualifier tomorrow. By Martin Weche Harambee Stars head coach Benni McCarthy has declared that he feels no sentimentality whatsoever about facing South Africa when Kenya host Bafana Bafana at Nyayo Stadium tomorrow evening in a pivotal Africa Cup of Nations 2027 Group C qualifier. The South African-born coach, who remains his country’s all-time leading scorer, was unequivocal in stating where his loyalties lie. “Nothing to do with me. My passport is South Africa, but I have no say in what they do. With all my experience, everything that I know, my heart goes into giving the best to Kenya national team — and the rest will sort itself out,” McCarthy said. It is a remarkable position for a man who, by any measure, is a giant of South African football. McCarthy, 49, scored 31 goals in 80 international appearances for Bafana Bafana — a record that still stands — and was the focal point of the South African attack across two Fifa World Cup campaigns, netting at both the 1998 tournament in France and the 2002 edition in Japan and South Korea. His most iconic moment in a Bafana shirt came at the 1998 Africa Cup of Nations in Burkina Faso, where he scored four goals in a single 13-minute spell against Namibia and announced himself to the world as one of the continent’s most lethal finishers. The Porto striker he was then bears little relation to the man now plotting South Africa’s downfall from the Kenyan dugout — but the competitive fire, those who know him well insist, has not dimmed one degree. Kenya arrive at tomorrow’s match in a position of unique comfort. As co-hosts of Afcon 2027, alongside Uganda and Tanzania, the Harambee Stars are already guaranteed a place at the continental showpiece regardless of their qualifying results. That assurance has not, however, diluted McCarthy’s ambitions for the group stage. With three matches remaining and nine points still available, he has set a clear target. “We’ve got three matches, there’s nine points still at hand. Our goal is to go for all nine points starting tomorrow. It has no sentimental value for me. This is my job and I give everything for the job that I am in and it is with Kenya,” he said. The backdrop to tomorrow’s fixture is Friday’s 2–2 draw in Soweto, a result that left South Africa frustrated after twice allowing Kenya to peg them back. McCarthy knows Pitso Mosimane’s side will arrive at Nyayo carrying a point to prove. “I know they have quality and they believe that they should be on top — and they are on top of the group. So at the end of the day, it depends on them. They play as many games as we do,” he said, his words carrying the measured confidence of a coach who has studied his opponents carefully and found them beatable. Mosimane, himself a figure of enormous stature in African football, faces the peculiar task of overturning a result against a team managed by one of his country’s most celebrated footballers. The tactical contest between two coaches of this calibre gives tomorrow’s tie a dimension that extends well beyond the Group C standings. Elsewhere in the group, Guinea defeated Eritrea 3–1 in Cairo yesterday, a result that tightens the race for qualification. Bafana Bafana currently lead the group, and a defeat in Nairobi would significantly damage their Afcon ambitions. The stakes, then, are entirely asymmetric — South Africa need a result; Kenya want one for pride and momentum. Kick-off at Nyayo Stadium is set for 7pm, and a capacity crowd is expected to create the kind of atmosphere that McCarthy, in his playing days, would have relished as an opponent. Tomorrow evening, it will be working in his favour. South Africa produced McCarthy the footballer. Kenya, he has made clear, will have everything McCarthy the coach has to give. title: Ten-man England silence Madrid as Spain’s 43-game unbeaten run ends
description: Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White put England three goals up before a red card sparked a Spanish fightback that goalkeeper James Trafford ultimately repelled to seal a famous Nations League victory. By Andalo Christine Ingutia England defeated Spain 3–2 in a stunning UEFA Nations League clash at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid yesterday, ending the hosts’ extraordinary 43-match unbeaten run and finishing top of Group A3 despite playing the final half-hour with ten men. Thomas Tuchel’s side produced a performance of genuine attacking quality and hard-won defensive resilience, surging into a commanding three-goal lead before a red card handed Spain the momentum they needed for a tense, nerve-shredding finale. The result, achieved on Spanish soil against a side that had not lost since March 2024, will rank among England’s finest away performances in recent memory. Both nations finished the group stage on 15 points from six matches, but England claimed top spot on goal difference — +13 against Spain’s +8 — confirming their status as the group’s dominant force. England started with intent, pressing Spain high and creating several promising chances before the hosts settled into their characteristic possession-based rhythm and began to push the visitors back. The breakthrough, when it came, arrived at the perfect moment. In the 45th minute, captain Harry Kane was fouled inside the penalty area by Pau Cubarsí, and Kane stepped up to convert the spot-kick himself, sending England into the interval with a deserved lead and the away end in full voice. The second half began where the first had ended. England returned from the dressing room with renewed purpose and doubled their advantage in the 53rd minute when Ezri Konsa rose above the Spanish defence to head home with authority. Four minutes later, the tie appeared all but settled. Ben White completed a beautifully worked move involving Kane and Jude Bellingham to make it 3–0, and England’s travelling supporters allowed themselves to dream of something historic. Then came the moment that turned the evening on its head. In the 63rd minute, Elliot Anderson was shown a straight red card for pulling back Lamine Yamal as the teenage Spanish winger threatened to break clear on goal. Spain sensed their opening almost immediately. Mikel Oyarzabal stepped forward to convert the resulting penalty in the 65th minute, reducing the deficit to 3–1 and setting the stadium alight. The home side pressed with increasing urgency, and their persistence was rewarded in the 75th minute. Yamal delivered a dangerous delivery across the England defence, and substitute Nico Williams arrived at the far post to finish and make it 3–2. With 15 minutes remaining and Spain in full control of the momentum, the outcome suddenly felt far from certain. What followed was a defensive rearguard of genuine character. England’s back line held its shape under wave after wave of Spanish attack, and goalkeeper James Trafford emerged as the night’s most important figure in an England shirt. The 22-year-old produced a string of vital saves as Spain threw everything forward, commanding his area with a composure that belied his relatively limited international experience. The defining moment came deep in stoppage time. With Spain pressing desperately for an equaliser, Trafford produced a crucial double save to deny Fermín López and preserve England’s slender advantage. When the final whistle sounded, the relief and elation on the England bench was unmistakable. For Spain, defeat ends a streak that had come to feel almost permanent. Luis de la Fuente’s side were not without credit — their second-half response demonstrated exactly why they remain European champions — and they progress to the Nations League quarter-finals as group runners-up. But the manner of this defeat, at home, against ten men, will sting. For England, it is a statement. Tuchel’s side showed they can defend a lead under the most intense pressure, score goals from multiple sources, and find a way to win on the grandest stages. The road to the 2027 World Cup just got a little more interesting. The post Ten-man England silence Madrid as Spain’s 43-game unbeaten run ends appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: Gachagua opens DCP’s Nairobi office and vows free nominations ahead of 2027 polls
description: The Democracy for the Citizens Party leader used yesterday’s Nairobi launch to signal grassroots intent, promising smart-card membership, open nominations and no favoured candidates. By James Mwangi Rigathi Gachagua, leader of the Democracy for the Citizens Party, yesterday officially opened the party’s Nairobi County office, using the occasion to announce plans for a smart-card membership system and to pledge that the party’s 2027 nominations would be open, competitive and free of preferential treatment for any aspirant. The launch, held at a party meeting in Nairobi, marked the latest step in DCP’s accelerating effort to build a credible organisational presence in the capital ahead of what is shaping up to be one of Kenya’s most consequential general elections. “The DCP party will hold free and fair nominations, with smart cards for party members to be introduced soon,” Gachagua told those gathered. “There are no special individuals or favoured aspirants. I encourage all aspirants across the country to put their best foot forward and strengthen their grassroots networks ahead of the nominations in March.” The opening of a dedicated Nairobi County office carries significance beyond the symbolic. Nairobi is Kenya’s most populous county and its most politically volatile, a battleground where no single party has historically commanded undisputed loyalty and where the urban vote has repeatedly proven decisive in shaping national outcomes. For DCP, which has built its strongest foundations in Mount Kenya and Maasailand, establishing a visible institutional footprint in the capital represents a deliberate signal of national ambition. Gachagua was direct about what the new office represents. “Today, I was honoured to officially open our new DCP party office for Nairobi County,” he said. “This office is a statement of our commitment to serving Kenyans and strengthening our grassroots presence across the county and the country. We must continue listening to the people and acting on their wishes, as enshrined in Chapter One of the Constitution of Kenya: all sovereign power belongs to the people.” His remarks on party growth carried the confidence of a leader who believes the political tide is running in his direction. “Our party is the party of the moment and the future. We are growing every single day as we work to earn the mandate of the great people of Kenya,” he said, closing with a phrase that has become something of a DCP rallying call: “Green is wealth. Green is the future.” The timing of the Nairobi launch is not incidental. With the IEBC’s published electoral calendar placing party primary nominations between 17 March and 10 April 2027, and membership list submissions required by 16 March, the window for organisational preparation is narrowing faster than many in the political class appear to have fully absorbed. Gachagua’s announcement of a smart-card membership system — a move that would give DCP a verifiable, digitalised record of its membership base — suggests the party is thinking carefully about the administrative requirements of a credible nomination process, not merely the political theatre of rallies and launches. DCP has grown rapidly since its establishment. The party currently has three elected Members of County Assembly and one Member of Parliament among its ranks, and has attracted figures of political weight from both the Mount Kenya and Maasailand regions. It is widely regarded as one of the most consequential new political forces heading into 2027, with Gachagua himself described by analysts as a potential kingmaker whose endorsement could prove structurally decisive for any presidential candidate seeking a majority. The question of whether Gachagua will seek the presidency himself or transfer his support to another candidate — including DCP Secretary-General John Methu, whose name he has previously floated — remains publicly unresolved. Yesterday’s event offered no fresh clarity on that front. What it did offer was a portrait of a party leader investing seriously in the machinery of political organisation: offices, membership systems, open nominations and a constitutional framing of popular sovereignty that speaks to voters wary of elite deal-making. Whether DCP can translate that organisational investment into electoral dominance across a city as complex and competitive as Nairobi will be one of the defining tests of the party’s national credibility in the months ahead. title: Later: The quiet procrastination of a day off and the book that waited until evening
description: A day off, a book within reach and the small, familiar voice that keeps saying there is still time — until there almost isn’t. By Munavvar Tlewbaeva Procrastination rarely announces itself — it arrives quietly, dressed as good intention, and spends the day rearranging the furniture of your plans until evening falls and you realise the thing you most wanted to do is still exactly where you left it that morning. That was the shape of one particular day off: a book on the table, work that needed finishing, and the easy promise made to oneself that one would follow the other. It had seemed so simple when the day began. Wake up, finish the outstanding work — there was not much of it — and then settle in with the book that had been waiting. That was all. No grand ambitions, no complicated schedule. Just a few hours of quiet reading on a day that belonged, for once, entirely to oneself. Work came first. That much was reasonable. Hands busy, thoughts wandering, the morning moved forward in the way mornings do when you are half-present. At some point, almost without deciding to, the phone appeared and Chingiz Aitmatov’s The First Teacher began to play — an audiobook, a voice in the background, something to fill the silence while the hands kept moving. At first it was barely there, a murmur beneath the thoughts. Then a sentence caught the attention. Then another. The pace of work slowed imperceptibly, not enough to notice, just enough for the story to find its way in. There is something particular about listening to a great writer while doing something ordinary. The words arrive without effort, without the conscious act of sitting down and opening a page, and perhaps because of that they carry a different kind of weight. Aitmatov’s Central Asian plains and the fierce simplicity of his characters settled over the room like afternoon light. The work continued. The listening deepened. And still the book on the table went untouched. This is the texture of so many days — not dramatic, not marked by any visible failure, but quietly shaped by the gap between what we intended and what we actually did. The tea gets drunk. The window gets glanced at. The list of things still to do gets mentally revised and silently carried forward. From the outside, nothing has changed. From the inside, the day is slowly becoming something other than what was planned. By the time the work was done — most of it, at least — the afternoon had given way to early evening. The recording was still playing. The book lay where it had been since morning, two steps away, untouched. Not because there had been no time. Not because anything had prevented it. Simply because the moment had never quite felt right, and the moment that never quite feels right has a way of persisting until the light outside changes colour. It would be easy, at this point, to reach for self-reproach. But that impulse deserves a little scrutiny. People do not always leave things undone because they are careless or idle. Sometimes they are genuinely tired. Sometimes the small reserves of energy that remain after work and obligation are not quite enough to begin something new, even something deeply wanted. And sometimes — perhaps most honestly — there is the assumption of tomorrow: the quiet, largely unexamined belief that the time will come, that the book will be read, that the moment will arrive when everything feels right for it. That assumption has a long history of being wrong. The recording reached its end. The street outside had grown dark and quieter. The day off was nearly over. The book was still on the table. It took no great act of will to pick it up. It never does. It was two steps away. The cover opened. The first page appeared. The first line was read. Then a pause. The clock on the wall. Not too late — not quite. Outside, tomorrow was waiting, as it always seems to be. The book lay open. The first line had been read. Whether the second followed is, perhaps, beside the point. Munavvar Tlewbaeva is a fourth-year student at the Chimbay Faculty of Karakalpak State University, Uzbekistan. title: Interswitch and UBA Kenya launch Verve card partnership
description: The deal gives UBA Kenya customers access to more than 2,000 ATMs and payment points under Africa’s homegrown card scheme, as local payment infrastructure edges closer to the mainstream. By Grace Wanja Interswitch has partnered with United Bank for Africa Kenya to issue Verve payment cards to the bank’s customers, expanding the reach of the pan-African domestic card scheme across Kenya’s growing retail and digital payments market. The agreement will give UBA Kenya customers access to cash withdrawals and everyday payments across a network of more than 2,000 Interswitch-connected ATMs, participating merchants and other payment acceptance points — a meaningful extension of the scheme’s footprint in a market long dominated by international card brands. The partnership is the latest signal that Africa’s financial technology sector is maturing in ways that extend beyond mobile money. Verve, Interswitch’s domestic payment card scheme, was built specifically for African markets rather than adapted from frameworks designed elsewhere, and its expansion into Kenya through a banking partnership of this kind represents a deliberate push to demonstrate that locally developed payment infrastructure can serve customers as effectively as global alternatives — and in some respects more efficiently. For UBA Kenya customers, the practical benefit is straightforward: a card that works across a wide network of acceptance points, issued by their own bank, settled in local currency for eligible domestic transactions. That last detail matters more than it might initially appear. When a Kenyan cardholder uses an internationally affiliated card for a domestic transaction, the payment may still be routed through overseas processing infrastructure, triggering foreign exchange conversions that add cost and complexity to what is, in economic terms, a purely local exchange. Verve’s domestic settlement capability removes that friction, keeping Kenyan shillings circulating within Kenyan infrastructure rather than passing through international systems unnecessarily. Geoffrey Njuguna, Managing Director of Interswitch Kenya, framed the UBA partnership as a step in a longer journey to establish Verve as a credible and competitive force in the Kenyan market. “Our partnership with UBA Kenya is an important step in growing Verve’s presence in Kenya and demonstrating the value a domestic card scheme can bring to the market,” he said. “Verve is designed for African markets, combining a cost-effective proposition for financial institutions with convenient everyday payments for customers.” Njuguna was also direct about the systemic argument for domestic card schemes, moving beyond the customer convenience narrative to make a structural case. “The value of Verve goes beyond issuing a card. A strong domestic scheme can support a more efficient payments ecosystem, including local-currency settlement for eligible domestic transactions that can help reduce unnecessary foreign exchange conversion and currency exposure,” he said. It is a point that resonates at a moment when African central banks and finance ministries are increasingly focused on reducing dollar dependency in domestic economic activity and strengthening the foundations of local financial infrastructure. UBA Kenya Executive Director Joseph Adedotun echoed the accessibility argument from the bank’s perspective, positioning the Verve card issuance as consistent with UBA’s broader mission of making banking simpler and more reachable for Kenyan customers. “Payments are an integral part of everyday life, and our priority at UBA is to make banking simpler, more accessible and convenient for our customers,” Adedotun said. “By introducing Verve cards to our customers, we are extending access to a wider network of ATMs and payment acceptance points, making it easier for them to transact wherever they are.” His remarks pointed to a distinction that the partnership’s architects are keen to emphasise. Verve is not, in their framing, a compromised substitute for an international card — a second-best option for customers who cannot access global schemes. It is a product designed around the specific realities of African markets: the merchant infrastructure that exists here, the currency dynamics that apply here, the customer behaviours that have developed here. “As Verve acceptance continues to grow across merchants, ATMs and digital payment channels, UBA Kenya customers will have a reliable option for everyday transactions — one designed specifically around the Kenyan market, rather than adapted for it,” Adedotun said. That distinction between designed-for and adapted-for carries real weight in the payments industry. International card schemes were built to serve North American and European consumer markets, and their infrastructure, pricing models and processing logic reflect those origins. When those schemes enter African markets, the adaptation is imperfect: costs that make sense in high-income markets can be disproportionate in lower-margin African retail environments, and processing architectures optimised for developed-market infrastructure may not perform optimally across Africa’s diverse connectivity landscape. A scheme built from the ground up for African conditions starts from different assumptions — and potentially arrives at better outcomes for the financial institutions and customers it serves. Interswitch has indicated that Verve’s development will continue beyond the current card issuance partnership, with planned innovations including tokenisation, contactless technology and enhanced online payment acceptance. These additions would extend the scheme’s capabilities into the digital and e-commerce channels that are growing rapidly across Kenya and the wider East African region, where smartphone penetration and internet connectivity are expanding the population of consumers who transact online. A domestic card scheme that works seamlessly across physical merchant terminals, ATM networks and digital payment environments would represent a genuinely competitive offering — not merely for cost-conscious financial institutions but for the end customers whose trust ultimately determines whether any payment product succeeds or fails. Kenya’s payments market has undergone remarkable transformation over the past two decades, driven primarily by the mobile money revolution that made M-Pesa a global case study in financial inclusion. Card payments have played a secondary role in that story, but the infrastructure supporting them has grown steadily, and the population of Kenyans with bank accounts and smartphones capable of supporting digital card payments has expanded significantly. Interswitch and UBA Kenya are betting that the moment for a domestically rooted card scheme is arriving. title: Naivas tops Kenya’s supermarket rankings in 2026 Superbrands survey
description: The homegrown retailer has been named Kenya’s number one supermarket brand and sixth strongest brand overall, as surging profits and expanding store networks cement its dominance of the country’s retail sector. By Grace Nduta Naivas Supermarket has been ranked Kenya’s number one supermarket brand and sixth strongest brand across all sectors in the 2026 Superbrands East Africa rankings, a consumer-driven assessment that places the homegrown retailer at the pinnacle of a fiercely competitive market and signals the depth of trust it has built with Kenyan shoppers over more than three decades of operation. The ranking, based on consumer research conducted by Kantar, assessed brands on reputation, reliability and distinction — criteria that speak directly to the relationship between a retailer and the households it serves every day. For Naivas, the recognition arrives at a moment of exceptional commercial momentum. The retailer posted a net profit of KSh3.37B for the year ended June 2026, a 41.7 per cent increase from KSh2.38B the previous year, while sales grew by 11 per cent to KSh123.66B, according to IBL Group’s 2026 Integrated Report. These are not the numbers of a business coasting on brand equity — they are the figures of a company that is investing in growth, winning customers and converting footfall into financial performance at a rate that is outpacing many of its competitors. Naivas Chief Executive Officer Andreas von Paleske was measured in his response to the award, using it to acknowledge the people he said had earned it. “This recognition belongs to the millions of customers who choose Naivas every day, as well as our colleagues and partners who work tirelessly to serve them,” he said. “Being ranked Kenya’s number one supermarket brand and sixth among the country’s strongest brands is an honour, but more importantly, it is a responsibility to keep earning that trust through quality, reliability and a consistently strong customer experience.” That framing — recognition as obligation rather than reward — reflects the particular dynamic of consumer retail, where brand strength is not an asset that can be banked and held. It must be replenished continuously, in every transaction, in every store, on every shelf. A supermarket brand is built in the accumulated experience of millions of shopping trips: the product that was in stock when a customer needed it, the queue that moved efficiently, the price that felt fair, the store that was clean and well managed. Naivas has, according to Kantar’s research, earned higher marks on those dimensions than any of its competitors in the Kenyan market. The Superbrands East Africa ranking covers the 2026–2028 period, with the formal presentation of the recognition certificate scheduled to take place at Naivas’ headquarters in Nairobi. Superbrands is an independent authority on branding that has operated across more than 90 countries, and its East Africa ranking has become one of the more closely watched indicators of brand health in the region. Inclusion among the top brands in any sector carries commercial significance — it influences supplier negotiations, shapes consumer choice and signals to investors that a business has the kind of intangible asset that is difficult to replicate quickly. For Naivas, whose origins lie in a single shop in Rongai in 1990, the journey to the top of Kenya’s supermarket rankings is a story of consistent expansion and adaptation in a retail environment that has changed dramatically over that period. The company has navigated the entry and exit of international retailers, the disruption of informal trade, the volatility of consumer purchasing power and the growing challenge of e-commerce — and emerged from each of these pressures with its market position strengthened rather than diminished. The retail sector in which Naivas operates remains intensely competitive. Kenyan supermarkets compete on pricing, product range, store location, convenience and the quality of private-label offerings. Household purchasing power — shaped by the cost of living, employment conditions and the overall performance of the economy — remains the most important external variable in the sector, with consumers making precise calculations about where to spend constrained budgets. The retailer that wins in this environment is the one that most consistently delivers value that shoppers trust. Naivas has responded to those competitive pressures with an aggressive store expansion programme that has extended its network across Nairobi and into counties beyond the capital, bringing organised retail to communities that previously had limited access to it. That geographic spread has broadened the brand’s reach beyond its urban heartland and introduced it to a new generation of shoppers for whom Naivas is not a challenger but a fixture — the supermarket that has always been there. The 11 per cent revenue growth recorded in the year to June 2026 is particularly significant in the context of an economy in which consumer spending has been under pressure. It suggests that Naivas is not merely retaining its existing customer base but actively expanding it, a feat that requires both competitive pricing and the kind of consistent operational execution that builds loyalty over time. The 41.7 per cent jump in net profit adds a further dimension: the business is not only growing its top line but managing its costs and margins with increasing discipline. For Kenya’s retail sector, the Naivas ranking is a data point in a broader story about the emergence of homegrown brands capable of competing at the highest level on quality, service and consumer trust. In a market where international brand names once carried an almost automatic premium, the ascent of a Kenyan-founded, Kenyan-operated supermarket to the top of the national rankings represents a meaningful shift in how consumers evaluate and reward the businesses that serve them. The Superbrands certificate to be presented at Naivas’ Nairobi headquarters will be a formal acknowledgement of what Kenyan shoppers have already voted on with their feet, their loyalty cards and their spending. title: Ruto demands global finance reform as Africa’s $100B food import bill lays bare a continent’s missed potential
description: to convert their continent’s extraordinary agricultural resources into food security, regional prosperity and freedom from dependency. By Grace Nduta President William Ruto yesterday called for sweeping reforms to the international financial architecture, arguing that Africa’s annual food import bill of more than $100 billion represented not an inevitability but a failure of investment, political will and access to affordable capital that the continent’s legislators had both the power and the obligation to reverse. Speaking at the opening of the Third Global Parliamentary Summit Against Hunger and Malnutrition at Parliament Buildings in Nairobi, Ruto delivered a pointed challenge to delegates from across the continent: a land mass with the soil, the sun, the water and the people to feed the world should not be writing cheques to import the food it is capable of producing. The argument Ruto made was not new in its broad contours — African leaders have spoken of the continent’s agricultural potential for decades — but the specificity and urgency with which he pressed it yesterday suggested a president determined to move the conversation from aspiration to accountability. Africa, he said, did not merely have an agricultural opportunity. It had an agricultural obligation, and the gap between that obligation and current reality was a measure of collective failure. “Our continent spends more than $100 billion annually importing food, loses a substantial share of its harvest after production and directs only a small fraction of commercial lending to agriculture,” Ruto told delegates. “We cannot continue to import what we have the capacity to produce, export raw agricultural commodities while importing processed products, or leave our young people without opportunity in a continent endowed with such extraordinary productive capacity.” The diagnosis he offered was precise. Africa’s agricultural potential, he said, was being strangled by inadequate irrigation, limited access to affordable credit, poor storage facilities, low processing capacity and fragmented markets that prevent farmers from accessing buyers at scale. These are structural failures, not natural ones — and structural failures, he argued, yield to structural solutions, beginning in the legislative chambers where the delegates before him held power. At the centre of his prescription was the African Continental Free Trade Area, which Ruto described as the most consequential institutional opportunity the continent currently possesses for transforming its agricultural economy. The AfCFTA, he said, offered a framework for building an integrated agricultural market of genuine scale — one in which the logic of raw commodity export is replaced by a logic of continental value addition. “Through the African Continental Free Trade Area, we have an opportunity to build an integrated agricultural market in which African farmers feed African consumers, African enterprises process African produce, and African trade creates African prosperity,” he said. He urged parliamentarians to use their legislative authority to dismantle unnecessary trade barriers, harmonise regulatory frameworks, facilitate cross-border investment and build the infrastructure that connects smallholder farmers to regional markets. Ruto also invoked the Kampala Declaration, the continental agri-food framework that entered into force in January this year, which sets targets of increasing agricultural output by 45 per cent by 2035, reducing post-harvest losses by half, tripling intra-African agri-food trade and mobilising $100B in investment. The ambition of those targets, he acknowledged, was not in question. What was in question was whether parliamentarians would translate them into budgets, laws and accountability mechanisms that made them real. His challenge to delegates was unambiguous. “Declarations do not appropriate money. Parliaments do. The Kampala Declaration will succeed or fail not only in summit halls, but in the laws you enact, the budgets you approve and the accountability you demand long after these meetings have ended.” The domestic agricultural argument was accompanied by a broader critique of the international financial system that Ruto has made a recurring theme of his presidency. Africa’s ability to invest in agriculture, infrastructure and climate resilience, he argued, was being directly constrained by the high cost of borrowing, unfair assessments of sovereign risk and growing debt-servicing obligations that crowded out productive expenditure. As evidence of the structural imbalance he described, he cited the fact that despite the continent’s significant renewable energy potential, Africa attracted less than three per cent of global energy investment — a figure that, in his framing, illustrated not Africa’s unattractiveness as a destination for capital but the persistent distortions of a financial architecture designed by and for wealthier nations. “This is why reform of the international financial architecture is essential to the fight against hunger and climate change,” he said. “We need multilateral development banks that lend more and lend longer, fairer assessments of sovereign risk, affordable development and climate finance, and instruments that mobilise private investment at scale.” The demand is one that Kenya has pressed in various international forums, from the Summit for a New Global Financing Pact in Paris to the United Nations General Assembly, and Ruto deployed it here with the authority of a leader who has made it a signature diplomatic cause. Yet he was equally insistent that external reform alone was insufficient. Africa, he said, could not credibly demand fairer access to international capital while failing to mobilise its own. He called on governments to strengthen domestic development finance institutions, channel domestic savings towards productive sectors and build the internal investment capacity that would reduce structural dependence on external financing. “Africa seeks not charity, but fair access to capital and the opportunity to turn its vast resources into shared prosperity,” he said. The closing note he struck was one of conditional optimism, grounded not in what Africa had been given but in what it had chosen to do or not do with what it already possessed. “Africa has the resources. Africa has the people. Africa has the potential. What we must now demonstrate is the political will to turn that potential into production, production into prosperity, and prosperity into freedom from hunger.” The continent has heard that call before. description: A bid to block the implementation of the Nairobi Senator’s National Delegates Conference resolutions has collapsed, freeing the path for The Equitable Party’s transformation into the Linda Mwananchi Movement. By James Mwangi Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna yesterday secured a significant legal victory when the High Court declined to block the implementation of resolutions passed at his party’s National Delegates Conference last Friday, clearing the way for The Equitable Party to be formally rebranded as the Linda Mwananchi Movement ahead of the 2027 General Election. The ruling removes what had been an immediate legal obstacle to one of the more visible political repositioning exercises currently under way in Kenya’s rapidly shifting pre-election landscape. Sifuna announced the outcome on his official X account, characterising the case as politically motivated. “The case by Ruto’s minions seeking to block the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties from implementing decisions of the Friday NDC has collapsed,” he wrote. The Senator did not name the petitioners directly in his post but described them as individuals aligned with President William Ruto — an allegation that the government has not publicly addressed. The dispute centred on resolutions adopted at the party’s National Delegates Conference held on 13 November 2026, through which delegates approved the transition from The Equitable Party to the Linda Mwananchi Movement. The rebrand is not merely cosmetic. The Linda Mwananchi Movement has been positioned by Sifuna as the institutional vehicle for his presidential ambitions in 2027, and the name itself — which translates broadly as “the movement of ordinary citizens” — carries a deliberate populist message aimed at urban and working-class voters, particularly in Nairobi where Sifuna holds his Senate seat and commands a significant political following. Following the court’s refusal to grant the blocking order, Sifuna moved quickly to signal that the rebrand would proceed without delay. “It’s full steam ahead for now. We know Kasongo will not give up, but every hurdle he puts in our way, we shall surmount,” he said, in a reference that indicated the legal contest may not be entirely concluded. The name Kasongo, cited by Sifuna in his post, appears to be associated with the party challenging the NDC resolutions, though the precise identity and standing of the petitioners in the case were not set out in detail in Sifuna’s public statement. He also took a moment to acknowledge the lawyers who had represented the party’s interests. “Salute to our overworked legal team. Msichoke, tutapumzika State House” — a Swahili phrase meaning, in substance: do not tire, we will rest at State House — a line that doubles as both gratitude and a declaration of presidential intent. The legal skirmish, though resolved in Sifuna’s favour for now, illustrates the increasingly combative environment in which Kenya’s opposition parties are operating as the August 2027 election approaches. Legal challenges to party resolutions, NDC processes and registration decisions have become a recurring feature of the political calendar, with rival factions and, in some cases, actors alleged to have government connections, using the courts and the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties as terrain for pre-election warfare. The pattern reflects a broader reality: that in Kenya’s current political moment, the battle for 2027 is being fought not only at rallies and in coalition negotiations, but in courtrooms and before regulatory bodies. For Sifuna, the successful defence of his NDC resolutions matters for reasons that go beyond the immediate rebrand. The Linda Mwananchi Movement needs to demonstrate organisational credibility — a functioning party structure, a verifiable membership base and a clear programmatic identity — if it is to compete seriously in a presidential field that is becoming more crowded by the month. The IEBC’s published electoral timelines place party primary nominations between 17 March and 10 April 2027, with presidential candidate registration opening on 29 May. That calendar leaves limited room for protracted legal distractions. Sifuna has built a national profile that extends well beyond his Nairobi base, with networks across both Luo Nyanza and Western Kenya giving him reach into regions that will be fiercely contested. His pitch — grounded in economic populism, anti-establishment rhetoric and the politics of ordinary Kenyan livelihoods — is calibrated for a moment when the cost of living remains the dominant concern of voters across the country. Whether the Linda Mwananchi Movement can translate that pitch, and Sifuna’s considerable personal political capital, into a credible presidential campaign will depend in large part on the organisational work of the coming months. Yesterday’s court outcome removes one obstacle. Many more lie ahead. The road to State House, as Sifuna himself might say, has never been without its hurdles. title: Trouble for former KTN host REGINA RE’s daughter as DPP approves murder charges against her - She is suspected of stabbing her grandmother over 20 times
description: Tuesday, November 17, 2026 - Former television actress and KTN host Regina Wambui Gitao, popularly known as Regina Re, is facing fresh trouble after the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) approved murder charges against her daughter over the killing of her 86-year-old grandmother. The DPP has approved murder charges against Thandie Malaika Wanjiku Gitao, who is accused of killing her grandmother, Dorita Lasinder Macharia. Thandie will be charged with murder contrary to Section 203 as read with Section 204 of the Penal Code. Her mother, Regina Re, and brother, Alton Jimmy Macharia, will also face charges of being accessories after the fact to murder. They are accused of interfering with the crime scene to conceal evidence and cover up Thandie's involvement in the killing. A post-mortem examination conducted on November 3, 2026, established that Dorita died from severe blood loss following multiple sharp-force injuries, including cuts to the face and neck, stab wounds and injuries that severed the external jugular veins. The cause of death was recorded as excessive blood loss resulting from a stab wound to the neck that caused vascular injury. Investigators also recovered clothing belonging to Thandie and the deceased, bloodstained towels and carpet samples, which were submitted to the Government Chemist for forensic analysis. The three appeared before Magistrate Beryl Akinyi, where they sought release to attend Dorita's burial scheduled for Wednesday, November 18. However, the prosecution opposed their release, citing the risk of them absconding court proceedings given the gravity of the offences. The court declined to release them and ordered that they remain in custody at Gigiri Police Station pending plea-taking. Meanwhile, Immanuel Munyeki, who had also been held in connection with the murder investigations, was released on November 12 after the prosecution informed the court that investigators had found no evidence linking him to the killing. The three are expected to appear before the Kibera Chief Magistrate's Court on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, for plea taking. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: “The Old Witch is Dead. We Can Now Have Money”- Details emerge on how former KTN host REGINA RE celebrated after her daughter brutally murdered her mother
description: Wednesday, November 18, 2026 - Chilling details have emerged surrounding the murder of 86-year-old Dorita Lasinder Macharia, whose granddaughter, Thandie Malaika Wanjiku Gitao, is accused of killing her. According to reports, Thandie's mother, Regina Re, was over the moon following the cold-blooded murder. The prosecution reportedly heard that Regina celebrated after her mother died, allegedly saying, "The old witch is dead. We can now have money." Further reports indicate that Regina had separated from her husband and pursued life as an independent woman while building her career in the entertainment and media industry. However, her television fame eventually faded, and claims have emerged that she was struggling financially and living in a bedsitter along Thika Road. Meanwhile, Thandie reportedly lived with her grandmother in a rented two-bedroom apartment, while her brother occupied a separate servant's quarter (SQ) next to the apartment. The brother has also been mentioned in the investigations, with allegations that he was found cleaning blood from the scene after receiving instructions from Regina. It is also alleged that Regina frequently fought with her elderly mother whenever she visited. As previously reported, a post-mortem examination established that the 86-year-old died from severe blood loss following multiple sharp-force injuries, including stab wounds to the neck. Thandie is facing murder charges, while Regina and her son, Alton Jimmy Macharia, are accused of being accessories after the fact to murder over alleged attempts to interfere with the crime scene. The three have denied the charges, and the case is expected to proceed in court. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Xi says China-Vietnam top-level exchanges inject positive energy into regional peace, development
description: Source: Xinhua, Editor: huaxia SHENZHEN, (Xinhua) — General Secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday met with General Secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam Central Committee and Vietnamese President To Lam in Shenzhen. In recent years, the top leaders of the two parties and the two countries have maintained close exchanges and reached important consensus on building a higher-level China-Vietnam community with a shared future that carries strategic significance, Xi said. This has helped advance bilateral relations and injected positive energy into regional peace and development, Xi added. The Vietnamese leader is in Shenzhen to attend the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting, scheduled for Nov. 18-19. During the meeting, Xi expressed willingness to deepen experience sharing with Vietnam, firmly support each other, and strengthen exchanges on self-supervision and self-governance of the parties, so as to ensure continuous progress in both countries’ socialist causes and national development. “As comrades and brothers, China and Vietnam must stand together and weather the storms,” Xi said. Xi also underscored the importance of enhancing mutual trust and solidarity, deepening all-round cooperation, jointly safeguarding peace and stability, and advancing shared development and prosperity. The two sides should properly manage maritime differences and steadily advance maritime cooperation, Xi said. Xi called on China and Vietnam to strengthen coordination within frameworks such as the United Nations, China-ASEAN cooperation and Lancang-Mekong cooperation, and to fulfill their duties as successive hosts of APEC in 2026 and 2027, respectively. Noting that the Vietnamese side views China as its most important strategic support, Lam said that, amid the current complex international situation, his country stands ready to strengthen solidarity and cooperation with China to support the development of both countries. Lam also pledged to work with China to safeguard maritime stability. As the next APEC host, Vietnam will build on the outcomes of APEC “China Year” and continue efforts to advance Asia-Pacific cooperation, the Vietnamese leader added. ■ The post Xi says China-Vietnam top-level exchanges inject positive energy into regional peace, development appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: APEC CEO Summit 2026 kicks off in Shenzhen with focus on regional cooperation, future prosperity
description: Source: Xinhua, Editor: huaxia SHENZHEN, Nov. (Xinhua) — The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO Summit 2026 opened Tuesday in Shenzhen, south China’s Guangdong Province, bringing together business and political leaders from across the Asia-Pacific and beyond to discuss regional economic cooperation and future development. Under the theme “To Prosper and Win the Future Together,” the two-day event has attracted more than 2,000 representatives from 21 APEC economies and 13 non-APEC economies, including Britain, France, Germany and Switzerland. Participants include representatives from 115 Fortune Global 500 companies, as well as heads of several international organizations and representatives of business associations from Russia, the United States and other economies. U.S. companies make up the largest group among participating companies from economies other than China, accounting for nearly 20 percent of the total. As an important part of the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders’ Week, the summit is expected to launch a Shenzhen initiative this year, marking the first time in the summit’s 30-year history that an outcome document will be issued in the form of an initiative. In his welcome address, Ren Hongbin, chairman of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade and chair of the APEC CEO Summit 2026, expressed the hope that the dialogue will spark new ideas and forge broad consensus, injecting fresh momentum into the Asia-Pacific community and global growth. Attendees at the summit are discussing the new landscape of the Asia-Pacific economy and opportunities for cooperation. Key topics include crafting a new blueprint for connectivity, building an open and inclusive AI innovation ecosystem, and setting a new paradigm for sustainable development in the Asia-Pacific. Other sessions will focus on advancing the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, exploring new paths for digital economy cooperation, the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area and Asia-Pacific development opportunities, and promoting synergized digital and green transformation. An important event in the APEC calendar, the APEC CEO Summit has been held annually since 1996, serving as the highest-level platform for APEC economy leaders and business representatives to discuss open cooperation and advance regional economic development. As the host of APEC in 2026, China will hold the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen from Nov. 18 to 19. This year’s gathering, under the theme “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together,” will focus on three priority areas identified by China — openness, innovation, and cooperation. These priorities are “particularly relevant today,” according to Antonio Basilio, director of the secretariat of the APEC Business Advisory Council, a mechanism that allows the regional business community to participate in APEC cooperation and submit policy recommendations to APEC economy leaders. Basilio expects all sides to hold constructive dialogues during the APEC meeting, and enable businesses to conduct trade and investment activities under more coherent, transparent and predictable rules. Working together with other APEC member economies, China has hosted more than 300 APEC meetings and events this year, drawing a cumulative attendance of over 10,000 participants. In the economic and trade field, China and other APEC economies have reached nearly 50 practical outcomes. ■ The post APEC CEO Summit 2026 kicks off in Shenzhen with focus on regional cooperation, future prosperity appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: Uzbekistan youth and reproductive health: What a new study reveals
description: A survey of 65 students in Termez exposes critical gaps in gynecological awareness and the urgent need for structured preventive education By Mahmudova E’zoza Abstract Reproductive health constitutes an essential component of individual physical, mental and social well-being. This study aims to provide an initial assessment of respondents’ self-reported awareness of reproductive health issues and to establish the vital role of preventive education, based on a survey administered via Telegram channels. A total of 65 respondents participated. Their demographic profile, regional distribution and educational status were systematically recorded. Approximately 65 per cent of participants considered themselves knowledgeable regarding the survey topics, while the remainder indicated either basic familiarity or an insufficient grasp of the subject. Because findings rely on self-evaluation and a non-probabilistic convenience sample recruited through a digital messaging platform, they cannot be generalised to reflect the objective knowledge level of the broader population. Nonetheless, this research highlights a clear need for systematically structured preventive health education and validated information interventions going forward. Keywords: reproductive health, health literacy, preventive education, survey, awareness, university students, healthy lifestyle. Introduction Reproductive health extends well beyond the mere absence of disease or infirmity within the reproductive system. It encompasses a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being in all matters relating to the reproductive system, its functions and the life processes connected to it. The World Health Organisation identifies reproductive health as a critical pillar of overall human development, placing particular emphasis on equitable access to professional healthcare services and scientifically sound medical information. Awareness in reproductive and gynaecological health involves a working understanding of menstrual cycle physiology, the distinction between normal and pathological reproductive signs, the clinical symptoms of anaemia, the prevention of sexually transmitted infections, cervical cancer screening and prophylaxis, and the importance of timely clinical consultation. Such educational guidance must be delivered in a framework that is age-appropriate, evidence-based and genuinely accessible to the people it is meant to serve. Health literacy, however, is not simply a matter of having heard or read about a medical topic. Functional health literacy requires that individuals understand clinical information, assess its scientific credibility and translate it into sound, informed personal health decisions. A person’s subjective sense of being well-informed does not automatically equate to objective medical competence or practical disease-prevention behaviour — a distinction this study keeps firmly in view. In contemporary public health research, digital platforms — specifically Telegram messaging channels — offer efficient tools for collecting exploratory data across diverse age groups and regions. The voluntary nature of participation, educational background and prior exposure to medical disciplines, however, introduce methodological considerations that require careful acknowledgement. Study aim The primary objective of this investigation is to provide a preliminary descriptive assessment of respondents’ self-perceived awareness of reproductive and gynaecological health, based on a cross-sectional survey administered via Telegram channels, and to establish both the theoretical and practical case for targeted preventive health education. Materials and methods A total of 65 participants were recruited through educational and community Telegram channels. The dataset was analysed according to demographic age categories, geographic origin, educational status and subjective self-ratings of knowledge across core reproductive health domains. The study was designed as a preliminary descriptive survey, with relative percentage distributions calculated against the total sample size of 65. Approximately 65 per cent of participants reported sufficient awareness of the topics presented, while the remainder reported either superficial familiarity or an outright deficit in reliable information. Because convenience sampling via a digital messaging platform was used, the findings cannot be extrapolated to represent the objective knowledge levels of the entire population of Surkhandarya Region or Uzbekistan as a whole. Domain-specific competencies were not evaluated through standardised clinical testing; the data reflect participants’ subjective self-assessments only. Results Age distribution The predominant age bracket was 18 to 21 years, accounting for 47 respondents, or 72.3 per cent of the total. Respondents under 18 years and those aged 40 to 50 each represented 6.2 per cent (four respondents apiece), while the 25 to 39 age group accounted for 15.4 per cent, or ten respondents. The findings therefore largely reflect the perspectives and academic environments of young people and university students. Geographic distribution The majority of participants were based in Termez City, accounting for 58.5 per cent of respondents (38 individuals). Other districts across Surkhandarya Region contributed 27.7 per cent (18 respondents), Tashkent City 12.3 per cent (eight respondents) and Navoiy Region 1.5 per cent (one respondent). While this demonstrates a reasonable geographical spread, non-random sampling prevents regional comparisons or generalised epidemiological extrapolations. Educational profile Approximately 59 participants — representing 90.8 per cent of the cohort — were active university students, with around 50 of those enrolled in medical academic disciplines. This concentration of medical students is a significant factor in interpreting the findings. Individuals undergoing medical training naturally carry higher baseline exposure to biological and anatomical concepts than non-medical or non-student populations, which bears directly on how the awareness figures should be read. Self-assessed reproductive health awareness Approximately 65 per cent of respondents identified themselves as knowledgeable about the reproductive health topics covered in the survey. The remaining proportion acknowledged having only rudimentary familiarity or a meaningful shortage of reliable information. Critically, this 65 per cent figure represents subjective self-perception rather than objectively verified clinical accuracy or demonstrated readiness to manage reproductive health challenges in real-world situations. Discussion The findings reveal that even within a cohort composed predominantly of university students — many of them from medical faculties — a notable proportion continue to experience informational gaps or rely on only basic insights. This underlines the need for systematic, validated and accessible reproductive health education delivered well beyond the walls of medical schools. The World Health Organisation defines health literacy as the composite cognitive and social skills that determine an individual’s motivation and ability to access, understand, evaluate and apply health information. Binary self-reports of being either “knowledgeable” or “not knowledgeable” are therefore insufficient to capture true behavioural readiness. title: Entertainment’s grip on Kenya’s youth
description: Digital platforms are reshaping how young Kenyans consume content — with consequences that cut both ways By Caren Nekesa Entertainment in Kenya is no longer a pastime. For a generation raised on smartphones and streaming, it is the air they breathe. With young people constituting over 75 per cent of Kenya’s population, they are the country’s dominant consumers of entertainment content. Digital platforms have fundamentally transformed how that content is accessed, shared and internalised — faster, cheaper and in greater volume than any previous generation experienced. The benefits are real. Entertainment provides stress relief and emotional regulation at a time when young Kenyans face mounting academic and economic pressure. It builds social bonds, fosters cultural identity and, increasingly, generates livelihoods. The creative economy — music, comedy, film, digital content creation — is producing genuine employment opportunities for young people locked out of formal job markets. But the risks are equally real and deserve honest scrutiny. Excessive screen time eats into academic performance and personal development. Relentless exposure to idealised lifestyles on social media feeds anxiety, depression and corrosive self-doubt. Some content actively promotes drug abuse and normalises violence, reaching young audiences with little filtering or critical media education to push back against it. The challenge for Kenya’s youth is not to retreat from entertainment but to engage with it deliberately. Balance is not a vague aspiration — it is a discipline, and one that schools, families and content creators all share responsibility for building. Entertainment can empower a generation. Unchecked, it can quietly diminish one. The post Entertainment’s grip on Kenya’s youth appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: Let students write: The case for authentic authorship in school drama
description: Kenya’s school drama festival must put learners back in the creative driving seat By Ashford Kimani The requirement that all competitive drama and film entries in Kenya’s school festivals be authored by students is not only timely — it is necessary. It is a call to restore the soul of a platform originally conceived as an educational space for nurturing creativity, originality and authentic student voice. Without this shift, the festival risks becoming an arena where adult brilliance is paraded through borrowed youthful voices, defeating its very purpose. At its core, drama and film in schools are not merely about performance. They are about process — the intellectual and emotional journey of a learner who must conceptualise ideas, structure narratives, experiment with language and ultimately present a piece that reflects their own understanding of the world. When students are sidelined in authorship, that process is disrupted. What remains is performance without ownership, expression without authenticity. Across many stages today, the imprint of adult authorship is difficult to ignore. Themes are often too layered, language too refined and ideological positions too sophisticated to genuinely belong to the learners performing them. Such pieces may win awards, but they raise a fundamental question: whose voice are we actually celebrating? When a student delivers lines crafted by an adult, they are not expressing their own reality — they are echoing borrowed thoughts. That reduces the learner to a vessel rather than a creator. The consequences reach further than the stage. Creativity cannot be taught through substitution. Writing skills cannot be developed through imitation alone. When teachers or external scriptwriters take over the authorship process, learners are denied the opportunity to struggle, to draft, to fail and to improve — the very experiences that build intellectual resilience and artistic confidence. First, the development of critical competencies is undermined. Then comes a subtler but equally damaging effect: an uneven playing field. Schools with access to highly skilled adult writers produce more polished pieces, overshadowing institutions that attempt to remain faithful to student authorship. The competition shifts from a test of student creativity to a contest of adult expertise, demoralising genuine student effort and entrenching a culture of dependency. Perhaps most critically, the practice distorts the purpose of education itself. Education is not about perfection; it is about growth. A flawed but authentic student-written script carries far more educational value than a technically immaculate piece authored by an adult. The former reflects learning in progress. The latter reflects learning outsourced. Advocating for student authorship does not mean excluding teachers from the process. On the contrary, it demands more of them, not less — but in a different capacity. Teachers must transition from scriptwriters to facilitators of creativity. Their role becomes guiding learners through idea generation, helping structure narratives, refining language and providing constructive feedback. That is the essence of effective pedagogy: supporting without overshadowing, guiding without dictating. This conviction is personal as well as professional. While in Form Two, Ashford Kimani authored a Kiswahili shairi. It was not perfect, but it was his own. It reflected his thoughts, his linguistic ability and his interpretation of the themes he had engaged with. With teacher guidance, he refined it and performed it with confidence. The experience was transformative — not simply because of the poem itself, but because it taught him that his voice mattered. That is precisely the kind of empowerment the festival should seek to cultivate in every learner who walks onto a competitive stage. For the student-authorship policy to succeed, it must be backed by practical enforcement. Declaring that items should be student-authored is not sufficient on its own. Schools could be required to submit drafts showing the evolution of a script from initial concept to final product. Learners could be asked to defend their work before adjudicators, explaining their creative choices and thematic intentions. Such measures would not only verify authenticity but also deepen the learning experience considerably. Teacher training workshops should be prioritised alongside enforcement. Many educators default to writing scripts themselves not out of any intent to circumvent policy, but because they lack practical strategies for facilitating student writing at a competitive level. Equipping teachers with mentorship skills would bridge that gap and bring practice into genuine alignment with policy intent. Ultimately, the debate is not about denying students access to quality work. It is about redefining what quality means within an educational context. True quality, in this setting, lies not in linguistic perfection or dramatic complexity but in authenticity, originality and learner growth. A student-written piece may lack the polish of an adult-authored script, but it carries something far more valuable: the imprint of a young mind in the process of becoming. If Kenya’s school drama and film festival is to remain committed to its educational mandate, it must be bold enough to prioritise authenticity over spectacle. It must create an environment where learners are not just performers but creators — where their voices are not borrowed but owned. Let students write. Let them stumble through drafts, wrestle with ideas and discover the power of their own expression. In doing so, the festival will not only preserve its integrity but fulfil the deeper purpose it was always meant to serve: nurturing thinkers, creators and confident individuals ready to engage with the world in their own voice. title: Are Kenya’s university graduates ready for the job market?
description: Degrees are multiplying but employability is not keeping pace — and the gap is widening. By Charles Wafula Kenya produces thousands of university graduates every year. Too many of them leave campus underprepared for what awaits them. The disconnect between classroom learning and workplace expectations is well documented and stubbornly persistent. Employers consistently flag deficits in communication, teamwork, problem-solving and digital literacy among fresh graduates — skills that academic syllabuses still treat as secondary to theoretical knowledge. The result is a generation credentialled on paper but underpowered in practice. The labour market compounds the problem. Employment opportunities have not grown at anything close to the rate of graduate output, forcing many young professionals into roles unrelated to their fields of study or into prolonged unemployment. Internship experience, which most employers now treat as a baseline requirement, remains inaccessible or poorly structured for a significant proportion of students. The solutions are not complicated. Universities must embed practical, industry-linked training into curricula rather than offering it as an afterthought. Employers should invest in structured graduate programmes rather than demanding experience that the system does not provide. Government must create conditions — through policy, incentives and direct support — that make youth employment a business priority, not a corporate social responsibility gesture. Students, too, carry responsibility. Waiting for institutions to act is a luxury that Kenya’s job market does not allow. Skills development, entrepreneurial thinking and practical exposure must begin long before graduation day. A degree should be a launchpad, not a waiting room. Kenya cannot afford to keep producing graduates the economy is not equipped to absorb. The post Are Kenya’s university graduates ready for the job market? appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.
