description: Relebohile Mofokeng scored twice in the second half to hand South Africa a 2-1 victory over Kenya at Nyayo National Stadium. By Andalo Christine Ingutia Harambee Stars suffered a 2-1 defeat to South Africa in their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations Group D qualifier at Nyayo National Stadium in Nairobi on Tuesday, with Orlando Pirates forward Relebohile Mofokeng stealing the show with a second-half brace that proved the difference between two evenly matched sides. Playing in front of a passionate home crowd, Kenya started with purpose and defensive discipline, pressing forward in the opening exchanges and looking determined to register their first win of the qualifying campaign. South Africa, however, were organised and patient at the back, absorbing the early pressure and gradually imposing themselves on the contest. The first half was tight and physical. Kenyan defender Rooney Onyango picked up a yellow card in the 27th minute as the tempo rose, but neither side could find a breakthrough before the break. Both goalkeepers were largely untroubled, and the match headed into the interval goalless. Bafana Bafana returned from the dressing room with sharper attacking intent, and their greater urgency in the second half began to tell. The breakthrough came in the 68th minute when Mofokeng punished a defensive error inside Kenya’s penalty area to put the visitors ahead. It was a moment of clinical opportunism from the 20-year-old, and it changed the shape of the contest entirely. Kenya responded by pushing men forward in search of an equaliser, opening up space that South Africa were only too willing to exploit on the counter. Harambee Stars created chances but struggled to test the visitors’ goalkeeper with any real conviction, and the longer the game went on, the more vulnerable they looked at the back. The tie appeared settled in the 86th minute when Mofokeng struck again, completing his brace and extending Bafana Bafana’s lead to 2-0. It was a composed, well-taken finish that underlined why the youngster is regarded as one of the most exciting attackers on the continent. Kenya, to their credit, refused to capitulate. Two minutes later, substitute Ryan Ogam pulled one back after a sharp assist from Adam Wilson, sending a ripple of renewed energy through the stands and setting up a tense final few minutes. The home faithful roared their side forward, but South Africa held firm to secure all three points. The 2-1 result gives Bafana Bafana a 4-3 aggregate advantage across the two November fixtures, following the sides’ 2-2 draw in Johannesburg on Friday, 13 November. More significantly, the victory lifts South Africa to the top of Group D with 10 points from four matches, moving one point clear of second-placed Guinea. Kenya remain third in the group with just two points and are still searching for a first qualifying win. However, the result carries limited consequence for Harambee Stars in terms of tournament participation — Kenya have already secured automatic qualification for the 2027 AFCON finals as co-hosts alongside Uganda and Tanzania. For coach Benni McCarthy, though, the performance will be a source of frustration. Conceding twice from individual errors and failing to convert home advantage into points are habits that will need correcting before the continental tournament begins. With the final qualifying fixtures scheduled for March 2027, Kenya have time to sharpen their game — but McCarthy will know that the standard required at AFCON will be considerably higher than what was on display yesterday. South Africa, by contrast, travel home with momentum, a place at the top of their group and confirmation that Mofokeng, in the right conditions, is capable of deciding matches on his own. title: Blow to Ruto as three Mt Kenya MPs abandon UDA for Gachagua’s DCP
description: Three sitting MPs cross to the former deputy president’s party, deepening the battle for Mt Kenya ahead of 2027. By Yvonne Wambui President William Ruto suffered a significant political setback in the Mt Kenya region yesterday after three Members of Parliament abandoned his United Democratic Alliance and joined former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua’s Democracy for the Citizens Party, sharpening what is fast becoming one of Kenya’s most consequential political rivalries ahead of the 2027 General Election. The three legislators who announced their departure from UDA are Gabriel Kagombe, MP for Gatundu South, Wachira Karani, MP for Laikipia West, and Rahab Mukami, the Nyeri Woman Representative. Their decision to cross to Gachagua’s DCP signals growing fractures within the ruling party’s Mt Kenya base — a region that was central to Ruto’s victory in the 2022 General Election and remains critical to his re-election prospects. The timing is pointed. With under a year to polling day, political leaders across the country are making calculated decisions about where to place their allegiances, and Mt Kenya is shaping up as the most closely watched battleground. For Ruto, the defections raise uncomfortable questions about his grip on a bloc that delivered for him four years ago. For Gachagua, the gains could not have come at a better moment. The former deputy president, who was removed from office following a parliamentary impeachment in 2024, has been methodically constructing his political base through DCP. Attracting three sitting MPs — each with an established constituency — provides the party with credibility, visibility and momentum it has been working to build. Kagombe’s Gatundu South constituency carries particular symbolic weight, sitting at the heart of the late President Jomo Kenyatta’s political legacy and deep within Mt Kenya’s political core. Karani’s Laikipia West and Mukami’s Nyeri county seat add geographic spread to the DCP’s expanding footprint, strengthening the party’s claim to represent a cross-section of the region rather than a narrow faction. The defections are also a reflection of a broader pattern emerging in Kenyan politics. As 2027 approaches, elected leaders are increasingly willing to reconsider party affiliations when the political calculus shifts. Loyalty, in this environment, is transactional — and the three MPs’ move suggests that for some in Mt Kenya, the calculation has already changed. UDA still controls a significant number of elected representatives in the region, and the ruling party retains the considerable advantages of incumbency — state resources, patronage networks and the institutional weight of government. However, losing sitting MPs publicly, in a region of this strategic importance, is not easily dismissed as routine political noise. The more pressing question for the ruling party is whether these three departures are an isolated event or the visible tip of a wider discontent. Within UDA’s Mt Kenya caucus, there will be MPs watching the reaction closely, weighing their own futures and calculating their options. If the party does not move quickly to stabilise its position in the region, further movement cannot be ruled out. Gachagua, for his part, has shown he understands the importance of momentum. Each high-profile addition to DCP changes the conversation — transforming the party in public perception from a vehicle of personal grievance into a credible political force capable of winning seats, attracting talent and presenting a genuine electoral challenge. Yesterday’s announcement was a carefully staged demonstration of exactly that. The contest unfolding in Mt Kenya is about more than two political heavyweights settling a personal score. It is about the future shape of Kenyan politics — about whether the dominant coalition that brought Ruto to power in 2022 holds together or fractures under the pressure of competing ambitions and unmet expectations. Mt Kenya’s voters have shown in previous election cycles that they are neither passive nor monolithic. They respond to leadership, to perceived benefit and to the confidence that their region will have genuine influence in government. If Gachagua succeeds in persuading enough of them that DCP offers a more credible path to that influence, the electoral arithmetic for 2027 could shift in ways that matter. Whether yesterday’s defections mark the beginning of a sustained political migration or represent the outer limit of DCP’s current appeal in the region remains an open question. What is no longer in question is the seriousness of the challenge Gachagua is mounting — and the pressure that challenge is placing on a president who cannot afford to take his home region for granted. The battle for Mt Kenya has begun in earnest. The next twelve months will determine who wins it. title: Nairobi senator Edwin Sifuna met Canada’s top diplomat in Kenya
description: A closed-door meeting at the Canadian High Commission signals growing foreign interest in Kenya’s political trajectory ahead of 2027. By Anne Njeri Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, leader of the Linda Mwananichi Movement, met Canadian High Commissioner Joshua Tabah, Deputy High Commissioner Julanar Green, and First Secretary for Political Affairs Siobhan Kerr at the Canadian High Commission in Nairobi yesterday, in a closed-door engagement that underlines the deepening diplomatic interest in Kenya’s rapidly evolving political landscape ahead of the August 2027 general election. The meeting comes at a charged moment. With political realignments accelerating, coalition negotiations intensifying and the electoral commission under scrutiny over technology procurement, Western missions in Nairobi are paying close attention to how Kenya’s democratic institutions hold up under pressure. Sifuna, one of the opposition’s most prominent voices in the Senate, is well placed to offer foreign diplomats an unfiltered reading of the political temperature. Canada, which has consistently supported democratic governance and electoral integrity across East Africa, has a direct interest in ensuring Kenya’s 2027 transition is credible and peaceful. No statement was issued following the meeting. The post Nairobi senator Edwin Sifuna met Canada’s top diplomat in Kenya appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

author: the mt kenya times
title: Gachagua brands Ruto’s ‘Usawa ni Sawa’ a cover for ethnic appointments
description: The DCP leader’s latest broadside over senior public service jobs cuts to the heart of one of the most combustible issues heading into the 2027 election. By David Kimani Democracy for the Citizens Party leader Rigathi Gachagua yesterday attacked President William Ruto’s “Usawa ni Sawa” campaign, accusing the government of using an equality slogan to mask a pattern of ethnically skewed appointments at the highest levels of Kenya’s public service. Gachagua’s remarks came shortly after the Teachers Service Commission named Cheptumo Ayabei as its new Secretary and Chief Executive Officer. In a sarcastic post on X, the former Deputy President linked Ayabei’s appointment to other recent selections — Ronoh Kibet as KenGen Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, and Lydia Sitienei Chelagat’s nomination as Data Commissioner, which is awaiting parliamentary approval. All three appointees are from the Kalenjin community. “To start with, Ruto cannot tell anybody about Usawa. He’s a con. He’s deceptive,” Gachagua said. The remarks were pointed in their target. “Usawa ni Sawa, Mbele Pamoja” — equality is fair, forward together — is Ruto’s rebranded campaign message for 2027, a deliberate pivot from the bottom-up “hustler nation” rhetoric that carried him to State House in 2022. For Gachagua, the slogan is not a governing philosophy. It is a political instrument designed, in his telling, to neutralise Mt Kenya’s legitimate grievances while systematically concentrating economic and institutional power elsewhere. The allegation is not new, but its persistence gives it weight. Gachagua, who was impeached in October 2024 after facing charges that included accusations of promoting ethnic divisions, has repeatedly accused his former boss of favouring members of his community in public appointments. Government allies have defended the selections, maintaining that the individuals were picked on merit through competitive recruitment processes. That defence is the standard response — and it is the response that Gachagua is methodically working to undermine. His strategy is accumulation. Each appointment, taken in isolation, can be explained away. Assembled into a pattern and placed before a Mt Kenya electorate already primed to see economic grievance in institutional decisions, they become a political narrative with real electoral traction. Mt Kenya delivered approximately 2.9 million votes for Ruto in 2022 — roughly 41 per cent of his national tally of 7.1 million. The region has long been Kenya’s most influential political kingmaker, having produced three presidents. Ruto cannot afford to lose it, and Gachagua knows it. The “41 vs 1” charge — the accusation that Ruto is reviving the politics of isolating one community against the rest of the country — is the most incendiary weapon in Gachagua’s arsenal. It resurrects the darkest chapter of Kenya’s pre-2007 political rhetoric, and its deployment ahead of 2027 is a calculated escalation. Whether it reflects genuine grievance, political strategy or both, it will resonate in every household, church and market in central Kenya. Ruto’s “Usawa ni Sawa” message was designed precisely to defuse this kind of attack — to reframe his presidency as one of national inclusion rather than ethnic patronage. Yesterday’s exchange suggests that reframing has not taken hold where it matters most. The battle for Mt Kenya’s 7.4 million voters has entered its most dangerous phase. title: Why Ruto’s State of the Nation address today carries more weight than any before it
description: With the 2027 election closing in and Kenyans demanding answers on the cost of living, President Ruto faces Parliament today in the most politically charged address of his first term. By David Kimani President William Ruto will today deliver his State of the Nation Address to a joint sitting of the National Assembly and Senate at Parliament Buildings in Nairobi, in what is shaping up to be the most consequential speech of his presidency — one that will be heard not only as a constitutional obligation but as the opening salvo of a re-election campaign that has already begun in everything but name. Parliament confirmed the address in a formal notice issued yesterday, 17 November 2026, citing the constitutional requirement under Article 132 of the Constitution of Kenya, which obliges the president to address a special sitting of Parliament once every year. The provision requires Ruto to report on measures taken and progress achieved in realising the national values and principles of governance enshrined under Article 10, as well as to submit reports on Kenya’s progress in meeting its international obligations. Speaker of the National Assembly Moses Wetang’ula also highlighted Article 247, which separately requires the president to provide Parliament with an annual report on the state of national security — making today’s address a dual-purpose constitutional exercise with both domestic and strategic dimensions. On paper, it is routine. In practice, nothing about today’s address is routine. Kenya is nine months from a general election. The political temperature is rising by the week. Coalitions are forming and fracturing simultaneously. Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, impeached and ousted barely a year ago, is building a rival political base in the Mt Kenya region with a speed that has unsettled the ruling Kenya Kwanza administration. The opposition, fragmented but vocal, is sharpening its critique of the government’s economic record. And ordinary Kenyans — the ones who voted in August 2022 with specific, urgent expectations — are waiting to hear whether this administration has delivered on the promises that brought it to power. That is the real audience for today’s address. Not the lawmakers seated in the chamber. Not the diplomats in the gallery. Not the political commentators parsing every sentence for tactical meaning. The real audience is the Kenyan voter who is paying more for unga, struggling to find work for their children and wondering whether the bottom-up economic model — the centrepiece of Ruto’s 2022 campaign — was a governing philosophy or a campaign slogan. Ruto is expected to address the cost of living, employment, economic growth, healthcare reforms, education, agriculture and infrastructure development. These are not abstract policy categories. They are the daily lived realities of millions of Kenyans, and the gap between what was promised and what has been delivered will be measured not in percentage points or GDP figures but in the price of cooking oil, the availability of fertiliser and the accessibility of affordable credit for small traders and farmers. The Kenya Kwanza administration came to power on an explicitly pro-poor, pro-hustler platform. Its economic transformation agenda was built around expanding opportunities for those at the bottom of the economic pyramid — the mama mboga, the boda boda operator, the small-scale farmer, the informal trader. Three years into the administration, the question being asked in markets, churches and barber shops across the country is a simple one: has the hustler nation actually improved the lives of hustlers? The honest answer is mixed, and Ruto will need to navigate that complexity carefully today. There have been genuine achievements. Infrastructure investment has continued at scale, with significant road projects, the expansion of affordable housing and progress on universal health coverage. The government’s agricultural interventions — subsidised fertiliser, improved seed programmes and expanded irrigation — have produced measurable results in certain counties. Digital financial services and government-to-person payment systems have improved the efficiency of some social transfers. But the challenges have been equally real and, in many cases, more visible than the achievements. The cost of living has remained stubbornly high. Youth unemployment persists at levels that represent both an economic crisis and a political risk. The tax burden introduced through successive finance bills — including the controversial 2023 Finance Act, elements of which were struck down by the courts following deadly protests — left a residue of public anger that has not fully dissipated. The government’s relationship with young Kenyans, in particular, was tested severely in mid-2024 and has required sustained effort to repair. It is against this backdrop that today’s address takes on its full political weight. Ruto is not merely reporting to Parliament. He is making an argument to the electorate — constructing a narrative of progress, resilience and forward momentum that he will carry into the 2027 campaign. The challenge is that the narrative must be credible. In an era of social media scrutiny, real-time fact-checking and an energised civil society, a presidential address that glosses over failure or overstates achievement will be dismantled within hours of delivery. The security dimension of today’s address adds another layer of complexity. Under Article 247, Ruto is required to report on the state of national security — a provision that will draw attention to the security situation in several parts of the country, including the ongoing challenges in parts of the Rift Valley and the broader question of how the government is addressing the conditions that generate insecurity in the first place. Security, in Kenya’s political context, is never a purely technical matter. It is deeply intertwined with land, ethnicity, resource allocation and the perception of whether the state is equally present and equally protective across all communities. Parliament will subsequently have the opportunity to debate the address and assess the government’s progress. That debate, in the current political climate, will be lively. title: Nairobi’s KSh86.9B debt crisis: How stalled projects and unpaid bills are strangling county suppliers
description: Parliament is now proposing a national government bailout as Nairobi’s mounting obligations threaten to choke businesses and derail devolution’s economic promise. By Grace Wanja Nairobi County accounts for more than half of Kenya’s KSh172.5B in county pending bills, with KSh86.9B owed to suppliers and 57 stalled projects making it the worst performer among all 47 counties, according to a new Parliamentary Budget Office report. The figures, covering the period to June 2026, lay bare the scale of a fiscal crisis that has been building quietly beneath the surface of devolution for years — one that is now threatening to undermine business confidence, destabilise suppliers and contractors, and raise serious questions about financial governance at the county level as Kenya heads into a general election in which devolution’s record will be a central point of contest. Of the KSh172.5B total stock of pending bills held across all counties, KSh71.7B had remained unpaid for more than three years as of June 2026. That figure alone — obligations outstanding for over three years — speaks to a structural problem that goes beyond cashflow difficulties or delayed disbursements from the national government. It points to a pattern of spending commitments that counties have been unable or unwilling to honour, with suppliers and contractors bearing the cost. Nairobi’s position within that picture is in a category of its own. The county owes KSh49.1B of the total pending bills stock — more than half of the national county figure — with nearly a third of that accumulated in the 2025/26 financial year alone, amounting to KSh46.7B. A further KSh30.6B is aged between one and two years, and KSh22.9B between three and four years. The layering of these figures tells a story not of a single crisis but of accumulated defaults across successive financial years, each one compounding the last. The human dimension of these numbers is easily lost in the aggregation. Behind every unpaid bill is a business — a construction firm, a medical supplier, a road contractor, a cleaning company — that delivered a service or completed a project on the expectation of payment. Many of these are small and medium enterprises for which delayed government payments do not merely affect profitability; they threaten survival. Staff go unpaid. Bank loans fall into default. Supply chains freeze. The Parliamentary Budget Office is explicit on this point, noting that Nairobi’s level of pending bills creates a significant risk for businesses and economic activity in the county and beyond. The proposed remedy is as notable as the diagnosis. Parliament is suggesting the introduction of a matching financing arrangement between the national government and Nairobi County — either a one-for-two model, in which the national government contributes one shilling for every two settled by the county, or a one-for-one arrangement under which the national government matches every shilling the county pays. Under the more generous version, the national government would effectively absorb half of Nairobi’s outstanding obligations. The Budget Office argues that clearing the bills by 2030 would improve liquidity for suppliers and strengthen business confidence across the broader Nairobi economy. The proposal is pragmatic but politically loaded. It amounts to an acknowledgement that Nairobi County, the seat of Kenya’s capital and economic engine, cannot clear its own debts without central government intervention. That is a significant admission, and one that will not be lost on the county’s political leadership as the 2027 election approaches. County governance — and the question of whether devolution has delivered value for money — is increasingly a live electoral issue, and Nairobi’s pending bills crisis hands critics a substantial line of attack. The stalled projects data sharpens the concern further. Nairobi leads all counties with 57 incomplete projects, followed by Kakamega at 26, Baringo at 23, Machakos at 22 and Kilifi at 10. The Parliamentary Budget Office is insisting that viable stalled projects be completed before new ones are initiated — a recommendation grounded in straightforward economic logic. A project that is 70 per cent complete generates no economic return until it is finished. Beginning a new project while the existing one sits idle doubles the waste and compounds the inefficiency. What the report ultimately captures is a governance gap that devolution, now in its second decade, has not closed. The constitutional promise of county governments was accountability, proximity and responsiveness. Pending bills that sit unpaid for three years and construction sites that lie dormant for want of political will represent a failure of all three. With the 2027 election nine months away, every county governor will face voters who can point to a half-built hospital, an unpaid contractor or a development promise that never materialised. In Nairobi, there are 57 of them. That is not a statistic. It is a ballot paper. title: Oburu meets Ruto at State House as ODM sets its price for 2027 support
description: With Raila gone and elections nine months away, ODM is negotiating hard — and its message to UDA is blunt: nothing is for free. By James Mwangi Orange Democratic Movement leader Oburu Oginga held talks with President William Ruto at State House in Nairobi yesterday, as the two parties moved to consolidate their working relationship ahead of the August 2027 general election — with ODM making clear it expects a formal power-sharing agreement in return for its support. The meeting comes at a delicate moment for ODM. The party is navigating a politically sensitive transition following the death of its longtime leader Raila Odinga in October 2025, with Oburu — Raila’s elder brother — now steering its negotiations with the ruling United Democratic Alliance. The broad-based arrangement between the two parties was initiated in March 2025, when Ruto and Raila signed a ten-point cooperation framework covering governance, national unity, devolution, anti-corruption efforts and the rule of law. With Raila gone, the question of whether that framework survives — and on what terms — is one of the defining political questions of the pre-election period. Senior ODM officials were unambiguous on Tuesday about where the party stands. National Chairperson Gladys Wanga, Deputy Party Leader Simba Arati and Director of Elections Junet Mohamed said any arrangement with UDA must be anchored in a formal agreement, not goodwill. The party had already prepared its conditions, they said, and would negotiate from a position of political strength. Junet was the most direct. “ODM is not an NGO. It is a political party that has been formed to capture and exercise political power. That is why the party leader has said, what do we want? Power,” he declared. He acknowledged that Ruto had delivered development projects in ODM strongholds but was explicit that projects alone would not satisfy the party’s ambitions. “We will form the government together with UDA and we will negotiate with UDA. Nothing is for free. Our support for UDA must count for something and we must share power,” he said. Junet drew a sharp boundary around ODM’s traditional strongholds, identifying Nyanza, Western, Nairobi, North Eastern and the Coast as areas where the party would tolerate no interference from coalition partners. “We will defend those strongholds to death. And we will not spare anybody who comes to interfere with the strongholds of ODM,” he warned — a signal directed as much at smaller parties within the broad-based arrangement as at any external challenger. His framing of ODM’s position in government was equally pointed. “We are in a broad-based government by right, we are not vagrants. We did not go for a walk. We went to form a government with UDA,” he said, firmly rejecting any suggestion that the party’s presence at the table was a concession rather than a negotiated entitlement. The stakes of these negotiations are substantial. ODM controls significant voting blocs in regions that Kenya Kwanza did not carry convincingly in 2022. Nyanza in particular delivered heavily against Ruto in the last election. If ODM delivers those votes to the incumbent in 2027 — and delivers them actively rather than passively — the electoral arithmetic shifts meaningfully in Ruto’s favour in what is already shaping up as a fiercely competitive race. The complication for Ruto is that ODM’s demands are structural rather than transactional. The party is not asking for a single ministerial appointment or a targeted development fund. It is asking for a defined seat at the governing table — shared authority, clear roles and a political roadmap that commits UDA to genuine partnership. Whether UDA is prepared to offer terms on that scale, without compromising its own internal coalition dynamics, is the central question the two parties must resolve before the campaign season begins in earnest. There are pressures on both sides. Within ODM, divisions over the party’s political direction since Raila’s death have not fully settled. The leadership is pushing for a structured pre-election agreement, but not every faction is convinced that alignment with Ruto represents the right path. Managing that internal debate while simultaneously negotiating with UDA requires considerable political skill. For Ruto, the calculation is different but no less demanding. Absorbing ODM’s support without alienating existing Kenya Kwanza partners — many of whom regard ODM’s strongholds as territory to be contested, not conceded — is a balancing act that leaves little room for error. On 13 November, Ruto hosted leaders from both parties at State House, where they agreed to strengthen their structures and coordinate their political machinery, particularly in Nairobi. Yesterday’s meeting with Oburu continued that conversation at the highest level. But ODM’s public statements on Tuesday made plain that the talking phase has a deadline. Kenya’s 2027 election will not be won in August. It is being won or lost in rooms like these. title: Ruto hosts Western Kenya leaders at State House ahead of regional development tour
description: The president’s pre-visit briefing signals that Western Kenya is firmly on the 2027 electoral map — and the government wants its development record heard. By Jane Njeri President William Ruto met government officials, governors and Members of Parliament from Western Kenya at State House in Nairobi yesterday, ahead of a development tour of the region scheduled for later this week. The meeting covered progress in agriculture, infrastructure and industrial investment across Busia, Kakamega, Vihiga and Bungoma counties. Ruto pointed to reforms in the sugar sector as a tangible marker of delivery, saying revived public factories had improved both farmer incomes and worker pay. “Farmers are producing more and earning more while workers are paid every month,” he said. The government also highlighted ongoing investment in roads, affordable housing, healthcare, industrial parks and an economic processing zone — a package framed as evidence of transformation rather than promise. The visit comes as Western Kenya assumes growing significance in Kenya’s pre-election calculations. With ODM negotiating its terms for supporting Ruto’s re-election bid and opposition formations actively courting the region’s vote, the president’s tour carries clear political weight alongside its development optics. Delivery, not dialogue, will determine which argument lands. title: Maraga and Karua back single opposition candidate as 2027 race sharpens
description: Senior opposition figures insist unity is achievable — but cracks are already visible over who should carry the ticket. By Grace Wanja Former Chief Justice David Maraga and People’s Liberation Party leader Martha Karua yesterday declared their commitment to fielding a single presidential candidate against President William Ruto in the 2027 general election, while their host Caleb Amisi openly backed Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna for the opposition ticket — exposing the fault lines the two leaders were trying to paper over. Speaking at a gathering hosted by People’s Renaissance Movement leader Amisi in Kitale, Trans Nzoia County, Maraga and Karua sought to reassure supporters that the opposition would settle its differences and present a united front ahead of the August 2027 polls. Both leaders accused the Kenya Kwanza administration of presiding over declining governance standards and deepening corruption, framing the election as a battle between an exhausted public and an administration they argue has failed to deliver. “Kenyans are tired, and if we want to remove Kasongo we must field one candidate — we will not fight each other, we must agree so the work gets done,” Karua said, using the opposition’s coded reference for Ruto. Her message was clear: personal ambition must yield to collective purpose, or the opposition risks handing Ruto a second term by default. Maraga was equally direct about what is at stake. “Next year’s vote is between the people and Kasongo. Do not worry — we will agree,” he said, before delivering a stark warning about the consequences of another five years under the current administration. “If Kasongo comes back there will be no Kenya, no country. Kenya will end as a country. I will finish corruption so we can have medicine in our hospitals,” he declared — a remark that blended genuine alarm about governance with an unmistakable personal pitch. Karua, who has built her political identity around anti-corruption advocacy, did not shy from staking her own claim even as she preached consensus. “Kenya is in this mess because of corruption. The person to clean it up is not someone else — it is Mama Martha Karua,” she said, leaving little ambiguity about her own presidential ambitions. That both she and Maraga called for unity while simultaneously positioning themselves as the natural flagbearer captures the central paradox of opposition politics in Kenya at this moment: everyone agrees a single candidate is necessary, but agreement on who that candidate should be remains elusive. The unity message was further complicated by Amisi himself. The People’s Renaissance Movement leader broke ranks with the evening’s dominant theme, openly endorsing Linda Mwananchi Movement leader Edwin Sifuna for the presidential ticket. “We want Edwin Sifuna to be given the ticket — and we as PM must also be at that decision-making table, or we will break the table,” Amisi warned, signalling that smaller parties within the opposition coalition intend to be active participants in the selection process, not passive bystanders. His remarks illustrated the structural challenge facing the opposition as it heads into the most consequential phase of its pre-election planning. The coalition is not short of presidential material — it is short of a mechanism for choosing between it. Without a credible, agreed process for settling on a flagbearer, the calls for unity risk remaining precisely that: calls, rather than commitments. Ruto, watching from State House, will have noted the evening’s contradictions with interest. Nine months from polling day, the opposition’s arithmetic remains dangerously unsettled. title: TSC stands firm on Ayabei appointment as Gachagua’s tribalism claims are rejected
description: The commission says 27 years of institutional experience made Cheptumo Ayabei the best candidate — but the row has exposed the raw nerves of Kenya’s pre-election politics. By Jane Njeri The Teachers Service Commission yesterday rejected former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua’s allegations that the appointment of Cheptumo Ayabei as its new Secretary and Chief Executive Officer was driven by ethnic considerations, defending the selection as the outcome of a transparent, competitive and legally compliant recruitment process. TSC Chairman Dr Jamleck Muturi John confirmed in a statement dated 17 November 2026 that Ayabei emerged as the best candidate among five shortlisted applicants interviewed on 16 November 2026, following a recruitment exercise that attracted 124 applicants. The commission published the names of all applicants and shortlisted candidates in newspapers and on its official website, Muturi said, in line with its commitment to transparency and accountability. “We are mandated to recruit the CEO of TSC. We follow procedures. On July 1, 2025, the seat fell vacant. We commenced the process in May 2025 and advertised the position on social media, newspapers and our website,” Muturi explained. He added that the process was briefly interrupted by a court-issued restraining order, before resuming on 28 September 2026 following a judicial instruction to proceed. Five candidates were shortlisted from over 140 applicants, with interviews conducted on 16 November 2026. “Cheptumo was the best and was appointed CEO. He had a sterling career at TSC, where he joined as a finance officer before rising to Director of Finance and Accounts,” the commission stated. Ayabei brings more than 27 years of experience at TSC, having joined the institution in 1999. He is also notable as the first person with a disability to head the commission, and hails from Baringo County. Gachagua’s response was swift and scathing. The DCP leader claimed on social media that “TSC gave the job to a number-four candidate who scored less than 70 per cent,” framing the appointment as the latest evidence of what he describes as a systematic pattern of ethnic favouritism under President William Ruto’s administration. He linked Ayabei’s appointment to two other recent selections — Ronoh Kibet as KenGen Managing Director and Lydia Sitienei Chelagat’s nomination as Data Commissioner — all involving individuals from the Kalenjin community, arguing that the cumulative picture undermines Ruto’s “Usawa ni Sawa” equality campaign. Opposition figures and members of the public questioned whether Ayabei was the most deserving candidate and alleged possible political influence by President Ruto — claims the TSC has rejected as unfounded. The commission did not directly address Gachagua’s specific claim about scores, but maintained that its interview and selection process followed established legal and procedural requirements under the Constitution and the Teachers Service Commission Act, 2012. The row is about more than a single appointment. It is the latest episode in a deepening political contest over the distribution of public service positions ahead of the August 2027 general election — a contest in which every senior appointment is being read through an ethnic and political lens by an electorate primed to scrutinise the composition of the state. Ruto’s “Usawa ni Sawa, Mbele Pamoja” — equality is fair, forward together — is the president’s rebranded campaign message for 2027, a deliberate pivot from the bottom-up “hustler nation” narrative of 2022. Gachagua has accused Ruto of using the slogan to deflect criticism over uneven development and alleged disparities in public appointments, saying bluntly: “To start with, Ruto cannot tell anybody about Usawa. He’s a con. He’s deceptive.” The TSC, for its part, is an institution that manages the employment, compensation and discipline of Kenya’s more than 350,000 public school teachers — arguably the largest single professional workforce in the country. Its CEO wields significant institutional influence. That the appointment has become a flashpoint in the ethnic arithmetic of pre-election politics says as much about the temperature of Kenya’s current political environment as it does about the specific merits of the recruitment process. In a pointed response on social media, presidential digital advisor Dennis Itumbi framed the appointment as proof that Ruto is “practically implementing Usawa ni Sawa,” citing Ayabei’s selection as evidence of merit-based recruitment across communities. That the government felt compelled to respond through its own digital machinery underscores how politically loaded the moment has become. Ayabei himself has been largely silent publicly. His record speaks through the institution — he first applied for the TSC CEO position in 2015, was shortlisted among four candidates and lost to Nancy Macharia. He did not give up, and a decade later, the job is his. Whether that story of persistence and institutional loyalty is enough to settle the political noise is another matter entirely. In Kenya’s current climate, no appointment arrives without a political price tag attached. title: Economics: The key to a better future
description: By: Shonazarov Shohjaxon Economics plays a significant role in our daily lives and the development of every country. It is the study of how individuals, businesses, and governments use limited resources to meet people’s needs and wants. Economics is not only about money; it is also about improving living standards and creating opportunities for future generations. One of the main goals of economic development is to improve people’s quality of life. When a country’s economy grows, businesses expand, new jobs are created, and people’s incomes increase. For example, when governments invest in education, healthcare, technology, and infrastructure, society becomes more developed and productive. Another important factor is international trade. Countries exchange goods and services to develop their economies and build strong relationships. This allows businesses to reach new markets, attract foreign investment, and create more employment opportunities. Moreover, modern technology helps companies produce products more efficiently and reduce production costs. However, economic growth also brings certain challenges. Inflation, unemployment, poverty, and income inequality are serious problems that many countries face today. Governments must develop effective economic policies to control inflation, support small businesses, and provide equal opportunities for citizens. A balanced economy should create wealth while ensuring that its benefits reach different groups of society. In addition, sustainable economic development is becoming increasingly important. Countries should use natural resources responsibly, protect the environment, and invest in renewable energy. Economic progress should not destroy the environment for future generations. In conclusion, economics is the foundation of a strong and successful society. A healthy economy creates opportunities, reduces poverty, and improves people’s lives. True economic success is not measured only by money, but also by people’s happiness, well-being, and quality of life. title: Rodri delivers brutal Champions League reality check: ‘Our chances of winning are zero’
description: Manchester City midfielder Rodri warns Barcelona they are nowhere near UEFA Champions League contenders and must raise their level significantly before dreaming of European glory By Pascal Okoth Rodri has delivered a strikingly candid assessment of Barcelona’s chances of winning the UEFA Champions League, insisting the club’s current level falls well short of what is required to be considered genuine contenders for European football’s most coveted prize. The Spain international made no attempt to soften his words. “Our chances of winning the Champions League are zero,” he said, in comments that have since reverberated across European football. It was a remarkable statement — not because it came from an opponent, but because it reflected the kind of honest self-appraisal that is rarely heard from within a dressing room carrying the weight of expectation that surrounds Barcelona. Rodri’s assessment cuts to the heart of a tension that has followed the Catalan club throughout the season. Despite the considerable excitement around their performances in certain matches, he believes there remains a significant gap between where Barcelona are and where they need to be when the Champions League enters its most demanding phase. “We need to raise our level and maintain it over time, so that by March and April, we have real chances of competing for titles,” he said. “And then we’ll have to raise it even further if we want to win everything.” Those months — March and April — are where Champions League campaigns are truly decided. The knockout rounds separate the genuinely elite from the merely talented, demanding consistency, tactical discipline, mental strength and the ability to perform under sustained pressure. Rodri’s point is clear: promising performances in November count for little if they cannot be replicated when the stakes are highest. He also challenged the very idea of discussing favourites before trophies have actually been delivered. “There’s no point talking about whether we’re favourites or not,” he said. “For me, until we win those titles, especially the Champions League, we cannot consider ourselves favourites.” It is a position grounded in results rather than reputation — and one that implicitly acknowledges the distance between Barcelona’s historical standing and their current European reality. That reality is worth examining. Barcelona last lifted the Champions League trophy in 2015, when they defeated Juventus 3–1 in the final in Berlin under Luis Enrique. In the eleven years since, their European campaigns have been defined more by painful eliminations than deep runs. The 4–0 collapse against Paris Saint-Germain in 2017, the astonishing 4–0 reverse at Liverpool in 2019 and a bruising 8–2 defeat to Bayern Munich in 2020 all left lasting marks on the club’s continental reputation. More recent campaigns have brought improvement in patches, but not the sustained excellence that Champions League success demands. Rodri’s comments, then, are not merely a talking point — they are a diagnosis. Barcelona, he suggests, must address their defensive vulnerabilities, sharpen their decision-making in key moments and develop the collective resilience that separates clubs who dream of winning the Champions League from those who actually do. There is no shortage of quality within the squad. Players of genuine international calibre populate the roster, and the club’s financial recovery has allowed significant investment in recent years. But individual talent and institutional prestige, as Rodri rightly notes, do not automatically translate into European success. The Champions League is littered with examples of star-laden squads that fell short when it mattered most. What Barcelona require, in his view, is a sustained elevation of their collective standards — not a single impressive performance or a run of three or four victories, but a consistent, identifiable level of output maintained across months of competition. For the club’s supporters, Rodri’s words will sting. Barcelona’s fans have waited more than a decade to see their team reclaim European football’s ultimate prize, and patience has worn thin through years of near-misses and embarrassments. But there is also something refreshing in the candour. It strips away the noise of expectation and forces an honest conversation about where this squad genuinely stands. The coming months will provide the clearest answer yet. Barcelona’s performance between now and the end of the season will determine whether Rodri’s assessment proves prophetic — or whether the club finds the consistency and character to prove him wrong. For now, his message is unambiguous: reputation is not enough. The Champions League must be earned. title: Sex before marriage: Have we abandoned our values in the name of modernity?
description: A generation navigating sexual freedom without moral anchors risks confusing liberation with the quiet erosion of values that once held communities together By Jackline Kathure There was a time when sex was sacred, intimacy belonged to marriage, and abstinence was respected rather than ridiculed. That time feels distant now — and the distance deserves honest examination. Traditional African societies understood sex as carrying cultural, moral and social weight beyond physical pleasure. Marriage provided its proper foundation. Discipline and responsibility were public expectations, not private eccentricities. That framework had real failures — forced marriages, silenced abuse, gender inequality — but its emphasis on commitment and boundaries served a purpose worth remembering. Today’s reality looks markedly different. Universities are grappling with rising rates of unintended pregnancies, sexually transmitted infections and the emotional wreckage of relationships built on pressure rather than affection. Reproductive health services are increasingly visible across student neighbourhoods — necessary, but symptomatic of deeper questions going unasked about prevention, education and personal responsibility. Most troubling is the creeping belief that sex is compulsory proof of love. Some young people face partners who present physical intimacy as the ultimate test of commitment. But genuine love accommodates boundaries, patience and personal conviction. If someone makes sex a condition for staying, the real question is whether they value you — or simply what they can take from you. Abstinence, meanwhile, is increasingly mocked. That is not progress — it is simply pressure wearing a modern mask. This conversation must never become a vehicle for shaming those who have made different choices. Dignity belongs to everyone. Freedom without responsibility is not liberation. It is a different kind of trap. title: Kenya warns against using children to solicit donations in online fundraisers
description: The State Department for Children Services cautions organisations and individuals that exposing minors in digital fundraising campaigns risks exploitation, abuse and irreversible harm to their dignity By Yvonne Wambui Kenya’s State Department for Children Services has issued a stern warning to organisations and individuals against using children’s photographs, videos and personal stories to solicit donations through online fundraising campaigns, citing serious concerns over the protection of children’s rights, privacy and dignity. The warning comes as social media platforms become an increasingly popular vehicle for raising money on behalf of vulnerable children and families facing financial hardship. Many Kenyans have turned to online fundraising to seek assistance with medical bills, school fees, food and other basic needs — a trend that, while driven by genuine goodwill, has raised uncomfortable questions about how children are being portrayed in the process. The department cautioned that exposing minors to public scrutiny in the name of financial assistance could leave them vulnerable to exploitation, abuse and other forms of harm. The Principal Secretary for Children Services urged organisations, well-wishers and individuals to find responsible ways of supporting children in need without placing their private lives on public display. At the centre of the concern are fundraising campaigns that rely on emotionally charged photographs, videos and personal accounts of children’s suffering to attract sympathy and encourage public contributions. Though such campaigns may succeed in raising significant funds, the exposure carries consequences that can outlast the financial benefit. Images and personal details shared online do not simply disappear once a fundraising target has been met — they can remain accessible indefinitely, beyond the control of the families or organisations that originally posted them. Children are particularly vulnerable in this regard. They may not fully appreciate the long-term implications of having their photographs and personal struggles circulated on social media, nor are they in a position to give meaningful, informed consent to such exposure. The department stressed that children should not be treated as instruments for attracting public sympathy or generating financial contributions. Their welfare, safety and best interests must remain the overriding priority in every charitable activity. The warning also reflects the broader challenge of protecting children’s rights in a digital environment where information travels instantly and widely. Once a photograph or personal detail is uploaded, controlling its distribution becomes virtually impossible, increasing the risk of misuse by those with harmful intentions. Charitable organisations have been called upon to adopt ethical fundraising practices that safeguard the identities and personal information of minors. The department encouraged organisations to explore alternative approaches to communicating the needs of vulnerable children — approaches that convey urgency and generate support without unnecessarily exposing private lives to public consumption. The issue equally raises important questions about the responsibilities of parents, guardians and institutions when sharing children’s information online. Good intentions, the government maintains, do not justify practices that compromise children’s fundamental rights. The desire to secure financial assistance, however sincere, cannot override a child’s right to dignity and protection. Online fundraising has undeniably become a lifeline for many struggling Kenyan families, particularly those confronting costly medical treatments or urgent school-related needs. The government does not dispute its value. What it insists upon is that such assistance be delivered in a manner consistent with the rights and dignity of the children it is intended to help. As digital fundraising continues to grow in popularity across Kenya, the message from government is unequivocal: supporting vulnerable children and protecting them are not competing obligations — they are one and the same. title: Kenyans still pay the same for diesel even as global prices fall 6.1%
description: Kenya’s diesel import costs rose 6.7% in October despite a drop in world prices, with KCh 4.6B in government support preventing a pump-price increase — but analysts warn the relief may be temporary By Grace Wanja Kenya’s diesel pump price has held steady despite a 6.1% fall in global oil prices, with the government deploying KSh 4.6 billion from the Petroleum Development Levy Fund to absorb a sharp rise in the country’s actual import costs — a measure that has spared motorists and commuters an immediate price shock but raised serious questions about how long the cushion can hold. Analysis by EBC Financial Group reveals the apparent contradiction sitting at the heart of Kenya’s fuel pricing: while the world price of diesel fell in October, the landed cost — what Kenya actually paid to bring diesel into the country — rose 6.7%, climbing from USD 1,065.38 to USD 1,137.09 per cubic metre. The gap between global market movements and what Kenyan consumers eventually pay at the pump is not accidental. It is the product of cargo timing, shipping costs, insurance charges and the averaging methodology used by the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority, which bases its pump-price calculations on cargoes unloaded at Mombasa port up to the ninth of each month. Diesel bought weeks earlier at higher prices therefore continues to shape what consumers pay long after international markets have moved on. David Precious, Senior Market Analyst at EBC Financial Group, explained the disconnect plainly. “A fall in the world price does not mean Kenya’s diesel costs fall at the same time,” he said. “Kenya pays for the diesel that actually arrives, and that diesel was bought earlier. Cargo timing, shipping and insurance can all widen the gap between the world price and what Kenya pays.” The exchange rate contributed little to the October increase. The Kenyan shilling depreciated by just 0.2% against the dollar during the period, moving from KSh 129.91 to KSh 130.17, ruling out currency movement as a meaningful factor in the rising import bill. The global supply picture adds further complexity. The International Energy Agency reported on 13 November that overall oil supply is recovering and expected to exceed demand in the fourth quarter. Diesel, however, occupies a different position within that market. European diesel prices fell 11% from their early-October peak but remain 77% above pre-war levels, and the IEA has indicated that diesel could remain in short supply into 2027. A broad recovery in crude oil production does not automatically translate into cheaper refined diesel for importing nations such as Kenya. To prevent the rising import cost from reaching drivers and passengers, EPRA kept the maximum pump price unchanged at KSh 227.76 per litre in Nairobi until 14 December, drawing on the Petroleum Development Levy Fund to cover a potential increase of KSh 10.54 per litre. The fund, built from a levy of approximately KSh 5.40 on every litre of petrol and diesel sold, collects around KSh 2.4 billion monthly. This month’s deployment of KSh 4.6 billion — nearly double the fund’s regular monthly intake — signals the scale of intervention required to hold the line. Treasury Cabinet Secretary John Mbadi had indicated in early November that the fund was withheld in October in anticipation of rising European energy demand as the continent entered winter. Its deployment this month has provided immediate relief, but the arithmetic of that decision carries its own risks. A fund collecting KSh 2.4 billion a month cannot sustain KSh 4.6 billion monthly disbursements indefinitely without additional support or a reduction in import costs. A second layer of relief comes through tax policy. The Tax Laws Amendment Act 2026, signed into law on 16 October, maintains value added tax on fuel at 8% rather than the standard 16%, for a 90-day period from 14 October, with the possibility of a further 90-day extension. The Central Bank of Kenya acknowledged at its October meeting that these combined interventions were easing inflationary pressure across the economy. That pressure remains significant. Annual inflation rose to 7.3% in October from 6.8% in September, sitting just below the CBK’s upper threshold of 7.5%. Over the past year, diesel prices have risen 32.5%, transport costs 17.1% and food prices 10.2% — a chain of increases that has already reshaped household budgets across the country. In May, a single EPRA review pushed diesel up KSh 46.29 per litre to KSh 242.92 in Nairobi, prompting matatu owners to announce a 50% fare increase that illustrated precisely how rapidly fuel costs ripple outward into the daily lives of ordinary Kenyans. The timing of the next decisions makes December a particularly consequential month. The CBK’s Monetary Policy Committee meets on 9 December, five days before EPRA’s current pricing period expires and a new import cost assessment takes effect. The CBK will therefore set its interest rate position without knowing whether the diesel import costs driving inflationary pressure are easing or continuing to climb. Precious offered a measured but pointed warning. “Holding the pump price steady has a cost of its own: KSh 4.6 billion this month, against the roughly KSh 2.4 billion a month that the fund is reported to collect,” he said. “If support at this scale continues, the fund may need topping up. And if import costs stay high while support is reduced, the pump price may rise in one larger step instead of gradually.” For Kenyans, the relief at the pump is real but conditional. Diesel moves the lorries carrying food to market and the matatus carrying workers to their jobs. Keeping its price stable matters enormously. What matters equally is whether the government can sustain that stability — or whether December’s review will deliver in a single announcement the increase that October and November managed to avoid. title: Greenland Girls School shows Kenya how to rescue young mothers from the education crisis
description: One school’s decision to combine childcare with classroom learning offers a transformative model for how Kenya can turn its teenage pregnancy crisis into an opportunity for intergenerational change By Ashford Kimani Greenland Girls School tells a story that is equal parts inspiring and unsettling — inspiring because it proves what becomes possible when an education system chooses compassion over exclusion, and unsettling because it lays bare how many young girls are still falling through the cracks of a system that, in theory, exists to protect them. Teenage pregnancy remains one of the most persistent disruptors of girls’ education in Kenya. Thousands of girls are pushed out of school every year — not always because policy demands it, but because society quietly enforces it. Shame, stigma, poverty and the absence of support converge to make returning to school feel impossible. The result is a silent crisis: young mothers whose academic journeys end abruptly and whose futures are permanently altered before they have had a fair chance to begin. What makes Greenland remarkable is its refusal to accept that outcome as inevitable. The school reimagines education in a way that acknowledges reality rather than denying it. By allowing young mothers to continue learning while providing childcare within the school environment, it removes the single greatest barrier to re-entry: who looks after the child while the mother is in class. That question, so simple to articulate and so devastating when left unanswered, has ended the educational dreams of countless girls across Kenya. This is not merely an administrative adjustment — it is a philosophical shift. Conventional schooling models are rigid by design, expecting learners to conform to pre-existing structures regardless of their circumstances. Greenland inverts that logic entirely. It reshapes the structure to fit the learner, and in doing so, restores dignity to girls who have too long been defined by misfortune rather than potential. The impact extends well beyond the individual. When a teenage mother is given a genuine second chance at education, she regains agency over her own life. She becomes economically empowered. She alters the trajectory of her child’s future. Education, in this context, is not merely personal advancement — it is intergenerational intervention, breaking cycles that would otherwise repeat themselves across decades. Yet the existence of such a school also raises uncomfortable questions. Why should this model be the exception rather than the rule? Kenya already has a re-entry policy allowing girls to return to school after giving birth. On paper, the policy is progressive. In practice, it is inconsistently implemented and routinely undermined by entrenched cultural attitudes that no policy document has yet managed to shift. Many schools remain ill-equipped or simply unwilling to accommodate teenage mothers. There are no childcare facilities, no counselling systems and often no institutional willingness to try. Even where doors are technically open, the environment can be quietly hostile. A young mother may face ridicule from peers, judgement from teachers and sustained pressure from her community to abandon her education altogether. Technically re-enrolled but practically unsupported, she is set up to fail a second time. This is where the deeper lesson of Greenland lies. Creating a safe space matters, but it is not sufficient on its own. What these learners need is an enabling ecosystem — academic instruction alongside psychosocial support, mentorship and practical life skills. They need an environment that consistently communicates a message too rarely delivered: motherhood does not cancel potential. For educators and school leaders, this presents both a challenge and an opportunity. The challenge is an honest reckoning with institutional bias. It is easy to invoke discipline and moral standards; it is considerably harder to practise restorative education. The opportunity, however, is genuinely transformative. Schools that adopt more inclusive approaches do not lower their standards — they expand their definition of who deserves the chance to meet them. Discipline should never be confused with exclusion. The purpose of education is not to filter out those who stumble but to guide them back onto the path. Teenage mothers are not disruptions to the system. They are evidence that the system must evolve. The broader societal dimension cannot be ignored either. Preventing teenage pregnancy must remain a priority, requiring comprehensive sexuality education, meaningful community engagement and stronger protection against gender-based violence. Prevention and support, however, must advance together. Focusing on one while neglecting the other produces an incomplete and ultimately inadequate response. The Greenland model offers a clear way forward. It demonstrates that with intentional design, genuine empathy and institutional commitment, a point of crisis can become a point of recovery. It challenges policymakers to move beyond declarations and invest in the structures that make re-entry not merely permissible but genuinely feasible. The true measure of an education system is not how well it serves the privileged. It is how effectively it rescues the vulnerable. Greenland Girls School has chosen, quietly and deliberately, to be measured by that standard. title: Alcoholism among Kenyan youths: A growing social and public health crisis
description: With over a million young Kenyans trapped in alcohol dependency, the country faces a generational emergency that unemployment, illicit brews and silence are quietly making worse By Charles Waruingi Over one million Kenyans aged 18 to 35 are struggling with alcoholism, with Central and Western regions bearing the heaviest burden. The scale of the crisis demands more than concern — it demands action. Unemployment is the most powerful accelerant. Young people who cannot find work despite completing their education face prolonged frustration and idleness. Alcohol becomes an escape. Cheap illicit brews — particularly chang’aa — deepen the trap. Unregulated, often laced with toxic substances and priced within reach of the poorest, these drinks are destroying lives in low-income communities across the country. Peer pressure and popular culture have normalised what should alarm us. Music, celebrity culture and social media increasingly portray excessive drinking as glamorous. For impressionable young people already searching for belonging, the message lands hard. Untreated mental health struggles complete the cycle. Depression, anxiety and trauma push young people toward alcohol as self-medication. But alcohol does not heal — it compounds. Dependency deepens. The original wound remains. The consequences reach far beyond individual drinkers. Families fracture. Children are neglected. Productivity collapses. Contaminated brews cause blindness, organ failure and death. Road accidents and violence claim lives that could have been saved. Reversing this requires three urgent responses: strict enforcement against illegal brewing and irresponsible alcohol advertising; accessible, affordable rehabilitation and mental health services in every county; and meaningful youth employment through vocational training, entrepreneurship and internship programmes. Kenya cannot afford to lose this generation to a preventable crisis. The bottle should never be the only door left open. title: Martha Karua backs book exposing Kenya’s constitutional gap as 2027 elections loom
description: Senior politician Martha Karua endorses Marilyn Muthoni Kamuru’s new book “Unconstitutional,” reigniting debate over Kenya’s unmet constitutional promises ahead of a defining election year By James Mwangi Martha Karua attended the launch of Marilyn Muthoni Kamuru’s new book, Unconstitutional, on Tuesday, lending her political weight to a publication that challenges Kenya’s failure to fully implement its 2010 Constitution. Karua, one of Kenya’s most prominent voices on constitutional governance and the rule of law, described the launch as an important moment for national reflection. “We gave ourselves a progressive Constitution in 2010, yet so many of its promises remain works in progress,” she said. “From accountability and access to justice to the two-thirds gender principle, there is still a considerable gap between what we agreed as a country and what we actually practise.” The timing is charged. With Kenya’s August 2027 General Election drawing nearer, questions about constitutional fidelity, institutional accountability and gender representation are moving from academic debate into live political contest. The two-thirds gender rule — never implemented despite a 2010 constitutional deadline — remains one of the most visible symbols of that gap between promise and practice. Kamuru’s book arrives as opposition formations sharpen their governance critiques and voters begin measuring incumbents against constitutional benchmarks. “Well done, Marilyn, for keeping these important conversations alive,” Karua added. Some conversations refuse to wait. The post Martha Karua backs book exposing Kenya’s constitutional gap as 2027 elections loom appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

author: the mt kenya times
title: Sifuna’s sisters rally at LMHQ as Linda Mwananchi Movement builds its 2027 momentum
description: A family show of solidarity at movement headquarters signals the personal bonds driving Kenya’s most watched emerging political force ahead of next year’s elections By James Mwangi Edwin Sifuna’s sisters visited the Linda Mwananchi Movement headquarters yesterday, in a show of personal solidarity that the Nairobi Senator said he would never take for granted. Sifuna acknowledged the visit publicly, expressing heartfelt gratitude to his sisters for their commitment to the movement he leads. “I see your efforts, deeply appreciate your commitment and will never take your love and support for granted,” he said. The visit, modest in form but pointed in timing, comes as the Linda Mwananchi Movement accelerates its national expansion ahead of Kenya’s August 2027 General Election. With county offices being established across all 47 counties, a diaspora tour underway in the United States and high-profile political figures joining its ranks, the movement is methodically converting grassroots energy into organised political infrastructure. Family solidarity has long carried symbolic weight in Kenyan politics, where personal networks and community trust frequently determine electoral outcomes. Sifuna’s public acknowledgement of his sisters’ support reflects a deliberate effort to humanise a movement that has otherwise trained its messaging on constitutional accountability, democratic governance and youth empowerment. As Kenya’s political temperature rises ahead of 2027, even the smallest gestures are being read for meaning. title: Edwin Sifuna’s Linda Mwananchi Movement expands its influence
description: With county offices, diaspora outreach and high-profile recruits, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna is building a national political machine with 2027 firmly in its sights By Job Mwavuwa Edwin Sifuna’s Linda Mwananchi Movement is rapidly positioning itself as a serious political force, intensifying grassroots mobilisation across Kenya’s 47 counties as the 2027 General Election draws closer. The movement, rebranded from The Equitable Party, centres its identity on constitutionalism, accountability and people-driven governance. Since its launch on 30 October, it has moved swiftly to convert ambition into structure — announcing county offices, recruiting members and claiming representation in 38 counties. Its roster of allies is growing in stature. Former Meru Governor Kawira Mwangaza, Vihiga Senator Godfrey Osotsi, Mavoko MP Patrick Makau and former Law Society of Kenya President Faith Odhiambo have all associated with the movement, lending it cross-regional credibility. Engagements with opposition figures Rigathi Gachagua and Kalonzo Musyoka have attracted attention, though no formal alliances have been announced. The movement is also looking beyond Kenya’s borders. A diaspora tour running from 21 November to 7 December will take Sifuna through New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Washington DC, Texas, Seattle and California, with town hall meetings and community engagements planned throughout. Diaspora support — financial and political — could prove significant heading into a contested election cycle. Sifuna has placed youth squarely at the movement’s centre. During a November engagement in Laikipia, he warned young Kenyans against backing President William Ruto’s re-election, arguing it would foreclose their own path to leadership. The movement is no longer just noise. It is building walls. The post Edwin Sifuna’s Linda Mwananchi Movement expands its influence appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

author: the mt kenya times
title: Challenges university students are facing
description: Kenya’s campus generation is battling poverty, mental health crises and a jobless horizon — and silence is not helping anyone By Kelvin Simiyu Kenya’s university students are struggling — and the pressure is mounting from every direction. Fees remain the heaviest burden. Many students come from families that cannot cover tuition, accommodation and food simultaneously. The Higher Education Loans Board offers a lifeline, but disbursements arrive late and rarely stretch far enough. Students who should be focused on learning are instead consumed by financial anxiety. The emotional toll compounds the financial one. Far from home, under relentless academic pressure and navigating unfamiliar social environments, many students battle loneliness, depression and stress in silence. Without accessible counselling, some turn to alcohol, drugs or destructive peer groups simply to cope. Infrastructure gaps widen the disadvantage. Unreliable internet access and scarce laptops lock out students from digital learning at a time when education increasingly depends on connectivity. Then comes graduation — and the grim arithmetic of a job market that cannot absorb thousands of new graduates annually. Many leave campus qualified but unemployed, their sacrifices yielding uncertainty rather than opportunity. The solutions exist: expanded scholarships, reliable HELB disbursements, affordable hostels, robust counselling services and genuine private-sector investment in youth employment. A student who succeeds does not succeed alone. Neither does one who fails. The post Challenges university students are facing appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.
