author: the mt kenya times
title: Sifuna calls Ruto’s State of the Nation a ‘state of imagination’
description: Linda Mwananchi Movement leader Edwin Sifuna boycotts President Ruto’s fourth parliamentary address, accusing him of substituting constitutional obligations for a development catalogue while human rights abuses go unanswered By John Kamau Edwin Sifuna, leader of the Linda Mwananchi Movement and Nairobi Senator, has dismissed President William Ruto’s fourth State of the Nation Address as a “State of Imagination,” accusing the President of violating the constitutional purpose of the annual parliamentary report by substituting genuine governance accountability with a showcase of roads, markets and infrastructure projects. Sifuna, who said he has boycotted the annual address since his election to the Senate, delivered his critique on Wednesday as Ruto spoke before a joint sitting of the National Assembly and the Senate — a platform the opposition leader described as one the President uses to make inflated claims while sidestepping the most pressing questions of democratic governance. With barely eight months remaining before Kenya’s 10 August 2027 General Election, the exchange illustrated with unusual clarity the fault lines along which the coming campaign will be fought. At the heart of Sifuna’s objection is a constitutional argument. Article 132(1)(c) of the Constitution requires the President to report annually to Parliament on the steps taken and progress achieved in realising the national values and principles of governance enshrined in Article 10 — values that include the rule of law, human rights, democracy, equality, human dignity, social justice and public participation. It is a precise and demanding obligation, and one that Sifuna argues Ruto has consistently failed to meet. “The Constitution of Kenya, in Article 132, states that when the President comes to Parliament, he does only two things. You have to tell the country steps taken and progress achieved in the realisation of the values under Article 10,” Sifuna said. “You tell us what steps you have taken as a government to ensure there is respect for human rights, that there is the rule of law, and that there is democracy in this country, as well as what progress has been achieved.” The distinction he draws is not merely procedural. It reflects a fundamentally different understanding of what presidential accountability should look like. For Ruto, Wednesday’s address was an opportunity to present his Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda in its most favourable light — improved exchange rates, reduced inflation, lower commercial lending rates, expanded foreign exchange reserves, 23,000 new classrooms, 100,000 teachers recruited and a northern highway corridor stretching 750 kilometres from Isiolo to Mandera. For Sifuna, none of that answers the question the Constitution actually asks. “You know the values under Article 10: human rights, the rule of law, equality, freedom of citizens and public participation. We are talking about sustainable development — you don’t tell us about roads,” he said, in remarks that distilled the opposition’s broader critique of an administration it accuses of prioritising visible hardware over invisible but essential democratic software. The reference to Albert Ojwang gave Sifuna’s argument its most human and politically charged dimension. Ojwang, a teacher and blogger from Homa Bay, died in police custody in June 2025 — one of hundreds of Kenyans whose deaths in circumstances involving security forces have remained incompletely investigated and sparsely prosecuted. Sifuna invoked Ojwang directly, arguing that the President’s pride in building a market in Homa Bay rang hollow against the unresolved question of accountability for a constituent who died in state custody. “He will go there to tell you, ‘Oh, we built a market over there in Homa Bay,’ while forgetting he killed Albert Ojwang from Homa Bay,” Sifuna said. The Independent Policing Oversight Authority has documented 127 deaths across three major protest periods since 2024. Missing Voices, a rights monitoring alliance, recorded 24 police-related killings in May 2026 alone. Ruto, in his address, acknowledged these events, pledged KSh 2 billion in compensation and called for continued investigations and prosecutions. Critics, including Sifuna, argue that acknowledgement without sustained prosecutorial consequence is insufficient — and that the State of the Nation address is precisely the moment to account for it in constitutional terms. Sifuna used the occasion to offer what amounted to a campaign preview, outlining what he described as his governance priorities should he assume the presidency after August 2027. The pitch was deliberately framed in constitutional language. “When we take the helm next year, when I go to Parliament as the President of this nation, my job will be to explain the steps our government has chosen or taken to ensure there is respect for human rights, there is democracy in our country, there is freedom for citizens and there is the rule of law,” he said. It is a carefully constructed contrast — positioning himself not against specific policies but against what he characterises as a fundamental misunderstanding of presidential responsibility. Whether that contrast resonates with voters whose immediate concerns centre on the cost of maize flour, school fees and matatu fares remains the central political question his movement must answer. The Linda Mwananchi Movement has been accelerating its national infrastructure over recent weeks, establishing county offices across all 47 counties, attracting defecting legislators and embarking on a diaspora tour of the United States. Its political argument is sharpening in parallel: that Kenya’s crisis is not merely economic but constitutional, rooted in an executive that has forgotten what the law actually requires of it. Ruto’s camp will contest that framing vigorously. The President’s address cited tangible improvements across multiple sectors, and his political strategists will argue that voters judge governments on what they can see and touch — classrooms, roads, hospital registrations — rather than on the precise interpretation of Article 132. That argument has carried incumbents through difficult elections before. But with eight months remaining and a cost-of-living crisis that has not fully abated, neither side can afford complacency. title: Ruto’s State of the Nation: Billions promised
description: President William Ruto used his fourth address to Parliament to announce KSh 61.8B in debt settlements, healthcare gains and a major northern road — while firing an unmistakable political shot at Rigathi Gachagua ahead of 2027 By David Kimani President William Ruto delivered his fourth State of the Nation Address to Parliament on Wednesday, announcing the settlement of KSh 61.8 billion in long-outstanding government obligations, pledging police accountability reforms and issuing a pointed, if unnamed, rebuke of former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua’s campaign to consolidate the Mt Kenya region behind his Democracy for the Citizens Party ahead of the 10 August 2027 General Election. The address, delivered to a joint sitting of the National Assembly and the Senate in Nairobi, covered ground ranging from university and hospital debts to highway expansion, healthcare registration and examination integrity — but it was the political undercurrent that gave the speech its sharpest edge. With Kenya’s electoral clock ticking toward August 2027, Ruto used the constitutional platform of Parliament to frame the coming contest on his terms: a debate about policy, delivery and evidence, not personality and regional loyalty. “No community should be reduced to a voting bloc. No region should be asked to surrender its judgement to a personality,” he told lawmakers, in remarks whose target, while unnamed, was unmistakable. Gachagua has spent recent weeks describing Mt Kenya as DCP territory, warning residents against incumbent legislators allied to the ruling United Democratic Alliance and declaring a political “transfer window” open until 31 December. On Tuesday, one day before Ruto’s address, Gachagua received three sitting MPs at his Wamunyoro residence — Gatundu South’s Gabriel Kagombe, Nyeri Woman Representative Rahab Mukami and Laikipia West’s Wachira Karani — and declared DCP “the party of the moment and the future.” Ruto’s response was measured but deliberate. He called on all political actors — beginning with his own administration — to submit to a standard of evidence-based accountability. “Those who offer alternatives must explain their proposals. All of us must respect the people’s right to question, scrutinise and choose,” he said, challenging rivals to articulate how they would lower electricity costs, finance infrastructure, expand employment and improve healthcare. It was a calculated pivot: shifting the 2027 conversation from the grievance politics that Gachagua has cultivated toward a terrain where an incumbent with a delivery record believes he holds the advantage. On financial settlements, Ruto announced the approval of KSh 18 billion owed to public and private universities and KSh 16 billion owed to hospitals under the now-defunct National Hospital Insurance Fund. Both payments, he said, were undergoing processing at the National Treasury and would be disbursed within weeks. He also announced the settlement of 28,726 verified pending bills amounting to KSh 27.8 billion, covering claims dating back to 2005. “These payments are undergoing the due process at the National Treasury for payment in the coming weeks,” he said, arguing that the disbursements would restore cash flow to businesses, protect jobs and ease financial pressure across multiple sectors. In education, the President cited the recruitment of 100,000 teachers over four years against a shortage of 116,000 when his administration assumed office, with a further 20,000 to be recruited. He said the government had constructed 23,000 classrooms, was equipping 1,600 laboratories and had increased the annual education budget from KSh 521 billion in 2022/23 to KSh 784 billion currently. Notably, he revealed that for the first time in 65 years, Kenya’s national examination papers had been printed locally — a quiet but symbolically significant assertion of institutional capacity. Some 3.6 million candidates were sitting the KPSEA, KJSEA and KCSE examinations, he added, in conditions described as calm and orderly. Healthcare figures dominated a significant portion of the address. Ruto said 33.7 million Kenyans had registered with the Social Health Authority, compared to approximately eight million under NHIF in 2022. He cited 53,465 patients receiving cancer treatment, 24,468 undergoing dialysis and 89 who had received kidney transplants under the scheme. “Through SHA, cover treatment costs are being financed on behalf of citizens, reducing the amounts that families would otherwise have to raise from either their savings, borrow from relatives, or obtain through sale of their assets,” he said. He acknowledged the troubled transition from NHIF to SHA but maintained that the long-term objective remained the progressive removal of catastrophic medical expenses from household budgets. On infrastructure, Ruto confirmed that plans to dual the Nairobi–Mombasa Highway — approximately 460 kilometres — had reached an advanced stage, with the Kenya National Highways Authority estimating costs at around KSh 300 billion. He said the project would proceed without new taxes or additional public debt, though the proposed toll-road model has drawn scrutiny from the Motorists Association of Kenya, which has called for full public disclosure of the financing structure. Ruto also announced the Northern Kenya Gateway Corridor, a 750-kilometre road linking Isiolo, Wajir and Mandera — a project he acknowledged had attracted widespread mockery when first proposed. “Some have lived their entire lives without a single tarmacked road reaching their communities. Their entire lives,” he said, invoking the equity imperative that has become a recurring theme of his administration. The most consequential passage of the address, however, may prove to be his remarks on police accountability — a subject that has shadowed his presidency since the June 2024 anti-Finance Bill protests. The Independent Policing Oversight Authority has documented 127 deaths across three major protest periods, while Missing Voices recorded 24 police-related killings in May 2026 alone. Ruto acknowledged the pain of those events, confirmed a KSh 2 billion compensation allocation and said KSh 1.2 billion had already been paid to 1,476 verified beneficiaries. He was unequivocal that compensation did not replace criminal accountability. “Investigations must continue, and prosecutions must follow for violations of the law, wherever the evidence warrants,” he said. His pledge to strengthen de-escalation procedures, oversight mechanisms and professional standards within the police service will be measured against a record that rights organisations have consistently found wanting. title: Nairobi health revenue triples to KSh 2.6B as digital reforms and SHA transform county hospitals
description: Governor Johnson Sakaja credits Social Health Authority reimbursements and digital accountability for a revenue surge that is restocking medicine shelves, upgrading diagnostics and funding community health workers across the capital By Jane Njoki Nairobi County has tripled revenue from its public health facilities from KSh 800 million to KSh 2.6 billion following digital reforms and improved reimbursements under the Social Health Authority, Governor Johnson Sakaja announced yesterday, as the county sets its sights on KSh 4 billion in health facility revenue before the end of the current financial year. Sakaja made the disclosure at the Third Annual Nairobi Health Scientific Conference, where he credited the revenue growth to a combination of SHA integration, Facility Improvement Financing, enhanced claims management and strengthened accountability at the facility level. The figures represent one of the most striking illustrations yet of how the transition from the defunct National Hospital Insurance Fund to SHA is reshaping the financial architecture of Kenya’s public health system — at least in the country’s most populous county. The numbers at individual facility level are even more arresting. Riruta Health Centre, which previously generated approximately KSh 100,000 annually, now records around KSh 6 million every month — a transformation so dramatic it strains the imagination of anyone familiar with the chronic underfunding that has long defined Kenya’s lower-tier public health infrastructure. Westlands Health Centre has similarly surged from roughly KSh 200,000 to KSh 6 million monthly, while Pangani Health Centre now generates approximately KSh 1 million each month. These are not marginal improvements — they represent a structural shift in what community-level facilities can afford to do for the patients who walk through their doors. “When we came into office, our county health facilities were generating approximately KSh 800 million annually,” Sakaja told delegates. “These resources help us procure medicines, support healthcare workers and improve our facilities to ensure better service delivery to Nairobi residents.” The additional income, he said, has enabled public hospitals to procure medicines, strengthen diagnostic services, maintain equipment and fund community outreach programmes — the unglamorous but essential work that determines whether a health system actually reaches the people it is meant to serve. SHA registration figures for Nairobi are equally significant. The county has enrolled three million residents under the scheme, representing more than 60 per cent of the city’s population. “SHA has been working well in Nairobi, enabling us to serve more residents through the reimbursement of claims for services provided,” Sakaja said. National Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, who also addressed the conference, placed that figure in a slightly broader context, noting that Nairobi’s three million registrations represent approximately 69 per cent of the county’s population. “This is commendable and demonstrates Nairobi’s commitment to primary health care,” Duale said. Sakaja was careful, however, to frame the revenue growth within a clear philosophical boundary. The reforms, he emphasised, were not designed to commercialise public hospitals or to introduce market logic into facilities whose fundamental purpose is service to those least able to pay. The intent, rather, is to ensure that facilities have the resources they need to deliver care at the standard residents deserve — a distinction that matters enormously in a city where the gap between the healthcare experience of the wealthy and the poor remains one of the starkest expressions of urban inequality. Duale used the occasion to commend Nairobi specifically for two achievements that set it apart from other counties. The first is the Nairobi County Cancer Centre, which he described as the first public cancer facility of its kind in the city — a significant development in a country where cancer treatment has historically been accessible only to those with private insurance or significant personal means. The second is Nairobi’s status as the county with the highest number of Community Health Workers and the only county in Kenya currently paying them stipends. That latter detail is quietly consequential: community health workers are the capillary system of any primary health care model, and the chronic failure to compensate them has long been one of the structural weaknesses undermining community-level healthcare delivery across the country. The county has established 782 Community Health Units supported by 7,820 Community Health Promoters conducting household visits, supporting expectant mothers, promoting immunisation, undertaking disease surveillance and linking families to health services. Sakaja said the county was also strengthening digital community health systems to improve household-level data collection and referrals, and introducing AI-assisted digital X-ray screening for tuberculosis — a disease that continues to exact a heavy toll in Nairobi’s densely populated informal settlements. Health, Wellness and Nutrition CEC Suzanne Silantoi reported that 99 per cent of county health facilities had been digitised and integrated into the SHA system, enabling them to submit claims and receive reimbursements with a speed and reliability that the NHIF era rarely delivered. Chief Officer for Medical Services Maryam Dahir added that emergency response capacity had been strengthened, with residents able to access assistance through the 1508 hotline. Her closing remark carried the weight of a standard that the county’s leadership would do well to remember as election season approaches. “We will be judged not by the discussions we hold, but by the improvements we deliver in service to the people of Nairobi,” Dahir said. The three-day conference, held under the theme One Health in Action: Building Resilient, Climate-Smart and Equitable Health Systems for Universal Health Coverage, brought together healthcare professionals, researchers, policymakers and development partners to examine how urban health systems can be made more resilient, more equitable and more responsive to the compounding pressures of climate change, population growth and emerging disease. For Nairobi’s residents — particularly the millions living in areas where a functioning health centre was, until recently, more aspiration than reality — the revenue figures are welcome. But numbers on a conference slide are not the same as medicines on a shelf, a nurse who answers at night or a referral that actually works. title: Nyeri Catholic Archbishop threatens to sack officials who let politicians into the pulpit
description: between church and state, warning that any official who hands a politician a microphone will be dismissed immediately By Jane Njambi Nyeri Catholic Archbishop Anthony Muheria has threatened to dismiss priests, catechists, coordinators and church secretaries who allow politicians to address congregations, issuing one of the starkest warnings yet from Kenya’s Catholic leadership as political pressure on places of worship intensifies ahead of the 10 August 2027 General Election. Muheria delivered the directive as the Catholic Church escalates its campaign to keep politicians from converting Sunday services into campaign rallies — a practice that reached uncomfortable levels during the 2022 election cycle and shows every sign of repeating itself as Kenya enters another charged electoral season. With barely eight months to polling day, the pews have become some of the most coveted real estate in Kenyan politics, offering candidates direct access to organised, attentive and community-rooted audiences that no roadside rally can replicate. The Archbishop was unambiguous about the consequences for those who facilitate such access. “Whoever allows a leader — anyone among you who allows anybody to speak in the church — will be fired immediately,” he declared. He extended the warning explicitly to administrative staff, making clear that arranging an opportunity for a politician to address worshippers was itself a dismissible offence. “If you are a coordinator, a secretary, and you are the one who arranged this thing, know that once it reaches me, you have lost your job and we will have an election to get another secretary,” he said. The language was deliberate and pointed — the word “election” applied not to the national contest for public office but to the internal process of replacing a church official who had compromised the sanctity of the institution. It was a sharp piece of rhetorical symmetry, and it conveyed Muheria’s message with unmistakable clarity: the Church will govern itself by its own standards, regardless of the political weather outside its doors. His frustration with the 2022 experience was evident. That election period saw politicians engage in heated and at times undignified confrontations inside churches, with congregations pressed into service as audiences for attacks on opponents and displays of political rivalry. Muheria cited those scenes as precisely what the current directive is designed to prevent. “Let us keep politics out of here, so that we can have respect in our churches,” he said. He went further, drawing a sharp and deliberately colourful line between the spaces he considers appropriate for political contest and those he does not. “Let them go to bars, those dens. Let them go there into the fields — there is where they can fight, let them pull each other in the mud. But the church is God’s,” Muheria stated. The image was vivid and intentional: politics, in his framing, belongs to the rough and contested public square, not to the consecrated space where communities gather in a different spirit entirely. Muheria’s directive follows a formal position adopted by the Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops, which has barred politicians from delivering political addresses in churches across the country. The bishops argued that politicians have no shortage of alternative platforms — television, radio, public barazas, roadside rallies — through which to advance their agendas and seek support. What they do not have, the bishops maintained, is a right to the church’s platform, its congregation or its moral authority. That authority is precisely what makes churches so attractive to Kenyan politicians. In a country where community trust in formal institutions has been eroded by years of broken promises and governance failures, the church retains a credibility that political parties and government agencies have largely forfeited. A politician who can stand before a congregation — or better still, be seen to receive the implicit endorsement of a priest or bishop — gains something that money and advertising cannot easily manufacture. The Catholic Church’s directive is, at its core, a refusal to allow that credibility to be borrowed for electoral purposes. The timing carries additional significance. Kenya’s political landscape is shifting rapidly as the 2027 election approaches. Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua is consolidating opposition in the Mt Kenya region through his Democracy for the Citizens Party. The Linda Mwananchi Movement is expanding its national footprint. President William Ruto is defending his record against a cost-of-living narrative that has tested public patience. In that environment, every platform matters — and the Catholic Church, with its reach into rural and urban communities across the country, represents one of the most significant platforms of all. By drawing its boundary now, eight months before polling day, the Church is sending a message that it intends to be a moral voice in the 2027 election rather than a political prop. Whether that boundary holds as campaign pressure mounts will be one of the quieter but consequential tests of institutional integrity in the months ahead. The church, Muheria has made clear, is God’s. The mud is available elsewhere. title: Forex scammer KENYAN PRINCE defrauds a gullible fan Ksh 100,000 to trade for them - Claims he lost the money in two days and shamelessly asks for more
description: Thursday, November 19, 2026 - Controversial forex trader Raymond Omosa, popularly known as Kenyan Prince, has been exposed on social media after a fan accused him of swindling KSh100,000 under the guise of trading on their behalf. The complainant approached Kenyan Prince seeking guidance on forex trading and account management, hoping to make money through his expertise. However, things took a different turn after the fan sent him KSh100,000 to trade on their behalf. According to the complaint, Prince went silent after receiving the money, leaving the fan anxious and wondering whether he had executed the trades as agreed. When the fan followed up to establish whether the money had been invested, Kenyan Prince asked for more money instead of providing a clear account of what had happened to the initial amount. After a lengthy back-and-forth exchange, Raymond admitted that he had lost the entire KSh100,000 in just two days and urged the fan to deposit more money so they could try again. “Fund, we try again,” he reportedly told the disappointed fan. Kenyan Prince has been using hired luxury cars and a carefully curated social media lifestyle to attract gullible victims who are tempted to entrust him with their money. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Popular Kikuyu gospel singer REGINA Wa ANGANIWE’s ex-husband, Bishop BERNARD MUTHOGA, demands to be in their children's lives after the woman he married failed to bear children - Has been absent for 8 years
description: Thursday, November 19, 2026 - A family dispute has erupted after popular Kikuyu gospel singer Regina Wa Anganiwe’s ex-husband, Bishop Bernard Muthoga, expressed a desire to reconnect with their children, whom he has been absent from for the past eight years. Muthoga reportedly walked out of his marriage to Regina and moved on with another woman, leaving the singer to raise their children single-handedly. However, eight years down the line, the bishop is said to be seeking a place in the lives of the children he abandoned after his new marriage failed to give him children. Regina, however, has moved on with her life and taken steps to distance the children from their father's identity. At some point, the gospel singer went as far as changing the children's names, dropping their father's surname and replacing it with her own. Their marriage ended in a highly publicised and contentious divorce around 2018, with the former couple remaining embroiled in several legal disputes since their separation. One of the most bitter disputes emerged following Muthoga's remarriage and centred on the grave of their late daughter, who had died from a brain tumour 12 years earlier. The dispute escalated after Muthoga questioned the child's paternity and threatened to flatten her grave. Regina subsequently obtained a court order in October 2022 allowing her to exhume her daughter's remains and rebury them on private land. Now, with Muthoga reportedly seeking to reconnect with the children after years of absence, the latest development threatens to reopen old wounds in a family whose differences have played out publicly for years. The Kenyan DAILY POST

title: WILBRODA’s ex-lover and baby daddy, USTADH KIMATHI, goes on a ranting spree and reveals how she blocked his access to their son after separation - Huyu Mwanamke Ni Kisirani
description: Friday, November 20, 2026 - Former Papa Shirandula actress Wilbroda’s ex-lover and baby daddy, Ustadh Kimathi, has gone on a ranting spree, divulging details of their failed relationship. In a lengthy Facebook post, Kimathi opened up about their separation and accused the celebrated actress of blocking his access to their son following their breakup. He shared his frustrations publicly, revisiting some of the challenges he claims to have faced in trying to maintain a relationship with his child after things fell apart between the two. Read his full post below: There’s this video on TikTok making rounds, and while I have laughed through the parts like I have for the last almost 17 years, the number of forwards compels me to say this: This interview is from about seven years ago, and I remember responding to it at the time with a rather strongly worded letter, through my lawyer. There are, however, a few things I think need to be clarified, even though I know society has a way of sympathizing with the woman in such cases and condemning us (men) unheard. First, I was never married to Wilbroda, contrary to the popular narrative of many years. She moved from her home in Rongai into my house, where we both lived together, and some of her family members moved in. My house lacked nothing and was big enough to accommodate family with two extra DSQs. And I never had issues because I come from a big family myself, until I came to see subsequent interviews years later where she lamented allowing them in, but that’s on her because nobody amongst her siblings wronged or has ever wronged me to that extent. Today, I still consider them family regardless. Before that arrangement, we had not been living together. We would osciallate between my house and hers when she was pregnant with our son. I paid for all the bills and accompanied her to all clinics throughout her journey, despite the fact that “her pregnancy hated” some of the clothes and colognes I wore. (story for another day). When we realized we couldn’t stay together, I just mentioned the reasons, and the answers were very unencouraging. In fact, I had contemplated moving out myself, but I kept on thinking she would struggle considering she didn’t have a good salary. This went on until I returned from an assignment in Tanzania to find my house partially emptied. The last item being undone was the bed in the master bedroom. Anyway, there is a much longer history behind our separation, one that I have consciously chosen not to discuss publicly for close to 17 years now. That silence has neither been an admission of wrongdoing, nor should it be mistaken for an inability to defend myself. I just fear a clash with numbers online. When you fight “big people,” you risk fighting their numbers. Other than that, I have my reasons for keeping certain things private, and they are not trivial; remember I have children, some of whom are adolescents soon to become young adults. But all I want many who have castigated me in my silence to understand is that there are experiences that leave a man with very little appetite for public explanations. Perhaps one day I will elaborate on my side of that story, maybe. But not necessarily to settle scores. I might do it because I know I represent the many men out here who have endured circumstances they never found the courage or an appropriate platform to articulate. Plus, I also cared about the dignity of friends, family, and all of whom this would tamper with. However, it is important to note that immediately after the separation, there were sustained attempts to frustrate my access to my son. Some of those attempts involved her then-boyfriend and the organisation he was associated with at the time, The CRADLE Children’s Foundation. I did not take those matters lightly. I sought legal representation and pursued the appropriate avenues to protect my relationship with my son. The verdict on my relationship and involvement is well known to those who have cared to follow and chronicle it. I don’t do anything for show; I do it to the best of my ability and from my bottomless heart. For the avoidance of doubt, my son has never lacked my support. I have consistently played my part in his upbringing and welfare. The recent disagreement over school fees arose after his mother unilaterally moved him from Mang’u to his current school. I disagreed with the decision and, for reasons I believe were legitimate, declined to finance that particular arrangement. The above disagreement should not be casually rewritten into a story of an absent or financially irresponsible father. If anything, any concerned individual should look at it as a problem they’d love to have in their own family, a situation where either parent can afford their wants. My son has capable parents so this should not worry anybody, and on that front, I think ours are good problems. There is, however, another misconception I have found rather amusing over the years, and it is the impression that I was the financially weaker party in that relationship. The truth is, I have never felt the need to compete over who had more money, but facts matter. I may have come from a difficult childhood, but I never spent my post-college years endlessly looking for my footing financially. I have never earned anything less than a six or seven-figure cheque since leaving college. God has been gracious in ways I will never take for granted. I met my son’s mother while I was working for an international organization that not only paid me well, but also on time. She was in acting which never paid any dignifying wages in this country at the time, unless they just started. Her radio career came along while we were together. Later, I remember advising her to consider the Swahili side of radio when an opening arose and she was faced with the choice to stay or leave the English evening drive show, because I genuinely believed that was where her authentic audience and natural connection with listeners lay. I mention this not to claim credit for anyone’s career, but to put into perspective how independently we were both, with both of us finding our feet professionally. So, I was already working and earning good money before that relationship, and I continued doing so long after it ended. Perhaps the simplest question to ask those who insist on portraying me as financially dependent is this: if I was as incapable as some would have people believe, how did I maintain the same neighbourhood, house, and standard of living for eight straight years after the separation, until I relocated? I was not living off anybody’s generosity. Regarding the allegation of my violent conduct, I am sure there’s no documented report on the same, save for invoking the name of Charles Bukeko (May his soul rest), a man with whom we shared a very cordial relationship and would share loud laughters and lengthy stories in our mother tongue “Olusamia,” whenever we bumped into each other long after all this had happened. The closest we have to debunk this same story is herself saying in subsequent interviews that she was never even “touched,” we simply couldn’t agree on principles that make up a relationship and/or family union. There is also the suggestion that I was physically present when they were moving out or that I subsequently begged for a reconciliation. Neither is true. I have never looked back or pursued a return to that relationship. Those who know me will attest that whenever I have made a physical appearance in circumstances involving my son, it has been shared openly and in solidarity with him, as any responsible father should be. My presence should therefore never be repackaged as evidence of a romantic pursuit because I am yet to even start, especially with him turning into a young adult and needing counsel. Sincerely, not many men would stay quiet for all those years despite interviews all over the place touching on them; I have deliberately remained measured about this entire subject for reasons a sane man will see in my writing so far. I have a family, children, friendships, and important relationships in my present life that deserve respect and peace. They did not create the circumstances of nearly two decades ago, and they should not have to live in the shadow of a dispute I have chosen not to publicise. I am equally conscious that my growing children deserve to mature into their adulthood without being recruited into the grievances of adults they may not agree with even now, but choose silence until the right time. But restraint should not be confused with surrender, and silence should not be interpreted as confirmation of every story told in one’s absence. Sometimes a man chooses not to respond because there are bigger things to protect than his ego. I have been comfortable and remain so, carrying that burden, even when it has meant allowing myself to become the convenient virtual punching bag. And honestly, can we finally allow this chapter to rest? I appreciate that we are living through difficult times, and I understand the pressures of raking social media numbers, propping public relevance and opportunities alive. But must a relationship that ended almost 17 years ago (before it even started) continually be resurrected? I am not the only man here; the world has millions of women and us to boot Surely there is enough life ahead of us for everyone to move on without repeatedly revisiting relationships that belong to another season of our lives. Seasons even you have, only that we have not cared enough to dig in. As I conclude, I mention, like Baks [Pun intended], that I have no intention of entertaining the endless politics of how many women I have dated, how many relationships I have had, or who occupies what position in my life today. I am a grown black, bearded Samia (Luhya) man, and my private life is not a public referendum. I have dated women, as many adults have, I can marry whoever I want, but I have only ever been married once, and I was never married to Wilbroda. So, respectfully, if you have never been married to me, please do not appoint yourself an authority on my marital history. There is a difference between having known someone, having shared a relationship with someone, and having been their spouse. Those distinctions matter, and I would appreciate them being respected. I hope this clarifies the 16 years of silence, ama mnataka Mic Cheque with Chaxy, Mariah, and Mwass ndio hii story iishe? The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: GTA 6 Made $3.79 Billion on Day One - IGN Daily Fix
description: In today's Daily Fix:As if anyone expected anything different, GTA 6 now has the biggest launch in entertainment history with a staggering $3.79 billion in sales in its first 24 hours. This includes more than 30 million pre-sale copies sold. And keep in mind, the PC version has yet to drop. Although GTA 6's launch dwarfs even the biggest movie releases, it's not a true 1:1 comparison as the game sells for about $80 a copy ($100 if you buy the ultimate edition), and your average movie ticket is nowhere near that expensive. In related news, prior to the launch of GTA 6, gamers spent 14% less this October than last year, despite heavy hitters like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 and the Ocarina of Time remake dropping in the same month. This is likely due to the GTA 6 effect, and gamers wanting to save their time and money for that game instead. And finally, Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey film helped boost sales of Ubisoft's Assassin's Creed Odyssey game. AC Odyssey, which was released in 2018, saw a spike in sales after the blockbuster movie debuted in July.

description: Saturday, November 21, 2026 - The man who was threatened with a gun by Narok Senator Ledama Ole Kina during a dramatic confrontation over unpaid dues has broken his silence. Ledama was involved in an altercation with a man identified as Zack Rotiken, who confronted him over unpaid dues and attempted to repossess the legislator’s vehicle using auctioneers. The confrontation nearly turned physical, with the vocal senator threatening to pull out his gun and shoot the man as tensions escalated. Zack has now spoken out, insisting that he will not be intimidated into abandoning his pursuit of the money he claims he is owed. Taking to social media, he pleaded with the senator to pay him, claiming that he had endured years of frustration while seeking his dues. “Nothing will stop me from asking for what I worked for. Nimekuvumilia sana six years, Hon. Ledama Ole Kina. Please pay me my money,” he wrote. The senator is reportedly facing auctioneers following a court ruling over the wrongful dismissal of Rotiken and failure to pay his salary and benefits. According to reports, Ledama lost an appeal against the ruling and was ordered to pay Rotiken KSh1.2 million. Auctioneers are now pursuing Ledama’s assets to recover the money. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Senator LEDAMA OLE KINA breaks silence after he was captured on camera threatening to shoot a man - “Nitakupiga Risasi Ya Kichwa”( Full Statement)
description: Sunday, November 22, 2026 - Today, I am trending over allegations that I threatened to shoot an intruder, a narrative being aggressively pushed by desperate political opponents and fake social media outlets, led by Paran TV, which is widely linked to Ole Lenku. In a reckless and senseless bid to score cheap political points, they have chosen to sensationalize the incident and peddle outright lies to the public that my personal car was being auctioned. As a law-abiding citizen and public servant, let me put the facts on the record while these characters enjoy their fleeting moment of attention. In 2017, a Senate staff member assigned to my office was dismissed for absconding from duty. Years later, a Labour Court issued ex parte orders authorizing the attachment of my personal property in connection with that dispute. Let me be clear: the Senate of the Republic of Kenya is a constitutional institution, not Ledama Olekina’s private estate. Staff salaries and employment obligations are funded by the public purse through the Parliamentary Service Commission, not from an individual Senator’s pocket. What happened next is deeply troubling. Individuals purporting to be court-appointed auctioneers trespassed onto the premises of a private company in which I am a shareholder and seized the keys to a delivery truck. When confronted, they claimed they were acting to recover KSh 365,000 allegedly owed to a former Narok Senate office employee, one Rotiken, over a claim of unfair termination. No personal vehicle of mine was ever under auction. This incident raises urgent questions about judicial overreach: •On what legal basis can a Labour Court treat a Senator’s personal assets or those of a separate private company as fair game for an employment claim involving a public institution? •Where is the legal boundary between an institutional liability and an individual officeholder? Is a private company owned by several people now personal property of an individual? I will not sit back and allow court processes or cheap propaganda to be weaponized as a licence to invade private property, defame my name, and intimidate citizens. Let me be equally clear: anyone who trespasses onto private property should be ready to face the consequences. The rule of law must operate within its proper constitutional limits; anything less erodes justice and public trust in our institutions. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: LADY rants on social media after a man she met online cancels their planned date after seeing her full-body PHOTO – “I prefer lean and petite ladies, you are thicker than I expected” (SCREENSHOTS)
description: Sunday, November 22, 2026 - A heartbroken lady has sparked debate on social media after exposing a man who cancelled their first date because he did not like her body size. The lady had met the man on Facebook Dating, and the two had agreed to meet for a face-to-face date at a restaurant. However, things took an unexpected turn after she sent him a full-length mirror selfie. Rather than complimenting her, the man questioned her body size, claiming she was much thicker than he had anticipated based on the pictures on her dating profile. "Actually hold on before you leave your house. Seeing a full-length photo like this, you are way thicker than I expected from the pictures on your dating profile," he texted her. The man went on to explain that he preferred lean and petite women, adding that they could reschedule their date in the future if she lost some weight. His remarks did not sit well with the lady, who questioned his audacity to expect her to lose weight for the privilege of going on a date with him. "The audacity to think I would ever lose weight just for the privilege of going on a first date with you is genuinely hilarious," she responded. The guy responded, "No need to get defensive. Plenty of men out there like thicker women. It is just not my personal preference.” She subsequently told him that she was comfortable in her body and asked him to delete her number, wishing him a good night dining alone. 💔 The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: “She is a bully and very arrogant”- Photographer DANITO KINYANJUI narrates his experience working with MARTHA KARUA during 2022 campaigns
description: Tuesday, November 24, 2026 - Photographer Danito Kinyanjui, who currently works at the Presidential Delivery Unit, has launched a scathing attack on People’s Liberation Party leader Martha Karua, accusing her of being arrogant and mistreating people who worked with her. In a lengthy Facebook post, Kinyanjui recalled his experience covering Karua’s campaigns across the Mt Kenya region during the 2022 General Election, claiming he witnessed behaviour that left him deeply disappointed. He said the State had paid him well to cover her campaigns but described her as one of the rudest people he had ever encountered, alleging that she mistreated both her staff and members of the public. Kinyanjui further claimed that Karua would sometimes bar political aspirants from addressing supporters at her rallies. He narrated an incident where Karua pulled him down from the top of her campaign vehicle as he attempted to capture a photograph of her rallying the crowd to raise their hands. However, he said his biggest disappointment came during the final days of the campaign at Nyambari in Kiambu County, where thousands of supporters had gathered to receive her entourage. According to Kinyanjui, upon arrival, Karua took the microphone and announced that nobody would be allowed to address the crowd because it was 20 minutes to 6pm and she had to catch a helicopter back to Nairobi. He claimed she then instructed her driver to head straight to where the helicopter was parked before flying back to Nairobi, leaving the waiting supporters without addressing them. Check out his post below. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: MOSIRIA pays surprise visit to MARTHA KARUA after Kirinyaga humiliation – See how the PLP leader warmly received him (PHOTOs)
description: Tuesday, November 24, 2026 – Former Nairobi County Chief Officer Geoffrey Mosiria paid a courtesy call to Martha Karua, the Party Leader of the People’s Liberation Party (PLP), at the party’s headquarters in Nairobi. Taking to social media, Mosiria shared photos of himself presenting a bouquet of flowers to the veteran politician, accompanied by a message detailing their meeting. “This morning, I paid a courtesy call to H.E. Martha Karua, Party Leader of the People’s Liberation Party (PLP), at the party headquarters in Nairobi. "We held fruitful discussions on national and county politics, particularly on how we can work together to transform Nairobi,” he wrote. Karua also took to X to acknowledge Mosiria’s visit, referring to him affectionately as her son. “With my son Hon Mosiria who paid me a courtesy call at Liberation House this morning. #TuunganeTujikomboe,” she posted. The meeting comes shortly after Karua appeared to dismiss Mosiria’s political ambitions during a rally in Kirinyaga County, where she told him that he had no votes in the region as he sought to drum up support for his 2027 Nairobi gubernatorial bid. Her remarks attracted criticism from a section of Kenyans, with some questioning why she had publicly embarrassed the former county official. However, Mosiria’s latest visit and Karua’s warm reference to him as her 'son' appear to have eased any perceived tension. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: SHAME! MP caught on CCTV stealing fellow MP’s phone in Parliament – Speaker WETANGULA calls him out (VIDEO)
description: Wednesday, November 25, 2026 - National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetangula has called out a Member of Parliament who was reportedly captured on CCTV stealing a phone belonging to a fellow MP inside Parliament. According to Wetangula, the incident happened during a commotion that erupted as MPs were debating in the House. The MP took advantage of the chaos to pocket his colleague’s phone, unaware that CCTV cameras installed inside Parliament were capturing his every move. When the footage was later taken to the Speaker’s office for review, the MP was reportedly summoned to explain himself. Despite the CCTV footage showing him taking the phone, the lawmaker denied stealing it. Wetangula, while addressing MPs, urged lawmakers to conduct themselves with dignity and respect, highlighting the incident as an example of unbecoming behaviour among elected leaders. Watch the video. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Milimani magistrate DIANA WIKUNZA’s estranged husband, EDWIN WAFULA, shares photos of the lavish houses he built for her, only for their marriage to crumble after cheating on him - “I was stupid”
description: Wednesday, November 25, 2026 - Kakamega-based lawyer Edwin Wafula, the estranged husband of Milimani Magistrate Diana Wikunza, has taken to social media to reflect on his failed marriage, sharing photos of lavish houses he claims he built for her during their relationship. In a lengthy post, Wafula lamented that men work hard to make money but end up investing heavily in building expensive homes for women instead of spending their fortunes enjoying life through holidays and travelling to exotic destinations. He cited destinations such as the Maldives, Seychelles, Mauritius, Costa Rica and Morocco, arguing that men should enjoy the fruits of their labour rather than spend their money trying to secure relationships through material possessions. Wafula claimed that he built the first house for Wikunza in Navakholo when she was a third-year law student at Moi University Law Annex. He further alleged that he later built her a second house within Kakamega town after she completed her studies at the Kenya School of Law while awaiting admission to the Roll of Advocates. The lawyer argued that building palatial homes and providing financial security cannot guarantee loyalty or save a troubled relationship. “We men can be stupid. We work hard to make money. Instead of enjoying the money by taking holidays in exotic places, we foolishly get busy pouring our hard-earned money into brick and mortar,” he wrote. He went on to advise men against trying to tame women through expensive gifts and property investments, insisting that they should prioritise enjoying their wealth. Check out his post. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

description: Wednesday, November 25, 2026 - A youthful preacher identified as Apostle Ushindi is trending after being captured on camera instructing his followers, the majority of them women, to beat up their enemies with sticks during a prayer session. The preacher had taken the congregants to a mountain for prayers, where they were seen wielding sticks and beating imaginary enemies as he led them through what appeared to be a dramatic spiritual session. “Piga adui yako,” the preacher is heard telling members of his congregation as they swing the sticks in the air, seemingly acting out the instruction to fight their perceived enemies. bizarre prayer session has sparked an online buzz, with many Kenyans questioning the preacher’s teachings and likening the church to a cult. Others have expressed concern over the kind of spiritual guidance being offered to unsuspecting followers, particularly women who appear to be deeply engrossed in the unusual ritual. Speaking during an interview with Citizen TV journalist Jeff Koinange, Gachagua revealed that his relationship with President William Ruto began deteriorating shortly after they assumed power in 2022. The Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader said the two frequently disagreed over how the government should be run, adding that he occasionally confronted Ruto over decisions he considered wrong. He further accused the President of repeatedly humiliating him, both publicly and during Cabinet meetings, deepening the divisions within the Kenya Kwanza administration. However, Gachagua's most shocking revelation was his claim that there were three attempts on his life, including an alleged poisoning attempt during an official visit to Kisumu. He claimed that an officer from the National Intelligence Service (NIS) brought him dinner at his hotel, but he did not eat the food after an Indian friend invited him for dinner. Gachagua alleged that he later discovered the food had been poisoned. “I would have died when I was Deputy President. “There were three attempts on my life. “An NIS officer attempted to poison me, but luckily, an Indian friend of mine had prepared dinner for me,” he said. description: Thursday, November 26, 2026 - A man who was caught stealing at a construction site was subjected to a humiliating punishment after being ordered to hold a banner publicly declaring himself a thief. In a video circulating on social media, the suspected thief is seen standing while holding a banner boldly written, “I am a big thief.” The site manager, armed with a loudspeaker, then proceeds to publicly announce that the man had been caught stealing at the construction site. “Huyu ndiye mwizi wetu wa leo,” the site manager is heard declaring over the loudspeaker. The man appears helpless as the site manager continues exposing him. Watch the video. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

Ebola cases cross 12,000 in DR Congo

KIGALI, Rwanda – The number of confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo has crossed 12,000 since the outbreak declaration in May, official data showed on Thursday as health authorities struggle to contain the largest outbreak in the country amid response disruptions due to insecurity.

The cumulative caseload has reached 12,021, including 5,904 related deaths, the Health Ministry's update showed.

Conflict and community resistance have been blamed for the more rapid spread of the virus from a single province in May to eight provinces now: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele, Tshopo, South-Ubangi and North Ubangi.

The World Health Organization (WHO) said early this week that heavy fighting in the vicinity of a hospital in Ituri province had disrupted the Ebola response, and its Ebola team was temporarily relocated from the Mongbwalu area until the situation calms.

In the viral clip, the lady gets emotional as the DJ plays the song and bursts into tears as a female friend tries to comfort her and offer. However, instead of holding back, the visibly emotional lady joins in singing the lyrics, seemingly pouring out her heart as the song takes her down memory lane. The touching yet amusing moment has since attracted widespread reactions, with social media users speculating that she could be nursing a broken heart. Some netizens had a field day cracking jokes at her expense, with several suggesting that whoever broke her heart must have put her through a difficult experience. Watch the video below. title: UNCLE FELO, the man arrested in Kangemi over claims that he took advantage of his neighbours daughter locked up at Industrial Area Prison - He insists he is innocent! Was it a set up?
description: Saturday, November 28, 2026 - Felix Anusu, popularly known as Uncle Felo, has been arraigned at Dagoretti Law Courts after being arrested in Kangemi over claims that he preyed on his neighbour’s daughter and did the unthinkable to her. Anusu was arrested on Wednesday by former Nairobi County official Geoffrey Mosiria following allegations that he had committed an offence against the little girl. He was presented before Dagoretti Law Courts on Friday and charged before being remanded at Industrial Area Prison as the court awaits a pre-bail probation report to guide further directions on his bail application. The matter is scheduled to come up again on December 2, 2026, at Dagoretti Law Courts. However, Anusu has denied the allegations, insisting that he is innocent and that the accusations against him are untrue. Speaking about his situation, he maintained that he was at work throughout Saturday and Sunday, working until late at night, and could not have committed the alleged offence. The embattled man is now seeking legal representation to respond to the allegations through the appropriate legal channels, as he maintains he has been wrongly accused. The court is expected to give further directions on his bail application after receiving the probation report. Watch the video of his arrest here: Link>> The Kenyan DAILY POST.
